(p-104) Sūrat al-An'ām

(Meccan, except for six or three verses, from His saying, "Say: Come, I will recite..." [6:151]. It has one hundred and sixty-five verses.)

﴿All praise belongs to Allah﴾. The praise, defined by the article of reality (al-ḥaqīqah), is first attached to the Essential Name (ism al-dhāt), on which all the attributes of perfection that it entails depend, and to which all the descriptions of majesty and beauty ultimately return. This is to signal that He, glorified and exalted is He, is the one deserving of it by His very essence, because the reality (of praise) requires that it be exclusively His, since all its individual instances are confined to Him by way of demonstration (al-ṭarīq al-burhānī).

Second, He is described by that which reveals some detail of its requirements, which are summarized in the category of general matters, of great effects and magnificent acts, in His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth﴾. This is to draw attention to His deserving it and to His being independent in it, by considering His magnificent acts and His vast blessings as well. The specification of their creation for mention is because they comprise the whole of the upper and lower effects and the general blessings, both manifest and hidden, the most excellent of which is the blessing of existence, which is sufficient to make the praise of Him, exalted is He, obligatory upon every existent. How much more so, then, for what branches from them of the various kinds of blessings, both personal and external, upon which the interests of the servants in this life and the Hereafter depend. That is: He brought them into being in the state they are in, of the most superior pattern and the most exquisite design, containing kinds of wonders and categories of marvels, such that minds and thoughts are bewildered by the wondrous lessons and effects, as an insight and a reminder for those who have vision. The plural "the heavens" (al-samāwāt) is used to show the multiplicity of their layers and the diversity of their effects and movements, and it is placed first for their nobility and the elevation of their place, and for their preceding the earth in existence, as it is.

﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾. This is coordinated with "﴿created﴾" and follows from it, because their making is preceded by the creation of their origin, and their place is included along with it in the sense of indicating the cause of praise. Just as the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, being a great effect and a magnificent blessing, necessitates that praise be exclusive to their Creator, exalted is He, so too the making of the darknesses and the light, being a weighty matter and a great blessing, necessitates that He alone be exclusively praised as their Maker.

Making (al-ja'l) is the bringing into being and origination, like creation (al-khalq), except that the latter is specific to creation in the existential sense (al-takwīnī), whereas making has in it the meaning of determining and arranging. This [making] is general in that it applies to this sense, as in the noble verse, and it also applies to the legislative sense (al-tashrī'ī), as in His saying: ﴿God did not appoint any bahīrah...﴾ [5:103], the verse.

In any case, it indicates that its object is connected with something else, either by being in it, or belonging to it, or proceeding from it, or the like, a connection that justifies a certain adverbial phrase (ẓarf) coming between the two, whether it is an incomplete (lagw) or a complete (mustaqarr) phrase. However, this is not in the sense of being the principal element of the sentence, but rather a qualifier within it, as in His glorified and exalted saying: ﴿And made between them a barrier﴾ [25:53], and His saying: ﴿And made in it firm mountains﴾ [41:10], and His saying: ﴿And appoint for us from Yourself a guardian...﴾ [4:75], the verse. (p-105)

For each of these adverbial phrases is either attached to the making itself, or to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial (ḥāl) of its object, which is placed before it because it is indefinite (nakirah). In either case, it is a qualifier in the sentence. Only when the context requires it to be the principal element does the making take two objects, the second of which is that element, as in His saying: ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾ [2:19].

Sometimes the matter becomes confused, and one supposes it to be the principal element, while in reality it is a qualifier in one of the two respects, as previously in His saying: ﴿Indeed I am making on the earth a successor﴾ [2:30], where it was said that the adverbial phrase is the second object of "jā'il." It was indicated there what sound taste dictates and what the eloquence of the noble composition requires: that it is attached to "jā'il," or to an omitted element occurring as a circumstantial of the object, and that the second object is "khalīfah" (successor), and the first is omitted, according to what was explained there in detail.

The plural "the darknesses" (al-ẓulumāt) is used to show the multiplicity of their causes and locations among people and their observation of them in detail. It is placed before "the light" because privation precedes possession (taqaddum al-i'dām 'alā al-malakāt), together with the observance of the fine correspondence between the two counterparts.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals [to Him]﴾ is coordinated with the preceding sentence, which states the causes that necessitate His exclusive right to praise, which in turn requires that worship be confined to Him, as has been verified in the commentary on the noble Fātiḥah. It is brought to deny what the disbelievers hold and to regard as remote their opposition to its meaning and their audacity in what the evidence of reason declares false. The meaning is: He is exclusively deserving of praise and worship by virtue of His essence and by virtue of the great attributes specific to Him that He has detailed, which necessitate confining praise and worship to Him. Yet these disbelievers do not act in accordance with this and ascribe equals to Him, glorified is He; that is, they make others equal to Him in worship, which is the ultimate goal of gratitude, whose head is praise, although everything other than Him is created by Him and possesses none of the bases of praise.

The word "thumma" (then/yet) is for expressing the remoteness of associating partners after the clarity of the aforementioned cosmic signs that refute it, not after its explanation by the revealed verses. The relative pronoun is an expression for the group of disbelievers, functioning as their name, without making their disbelief in what must be believed, wholly or partly, a designation of the subject, since that would undermine the remoteness of what is attributed to them of associating partners.

The preposition "bi" is connected to "ya'dilūn" (ascribe equals), and placing "the Lord" in the position of His pronoun is for added reproach and condemnation. The fronting [of the preposition] is for greater emphasis and haste in establishing the pivot of denial and remoteness, and for preserving the rhyme (fawāṣil). The object is omitted for its being evident, or to direct the denial at the act itself by treating it as intransitive, signalling that this is the pivot of the remoteness and the reprehensibility, not the particularity of the object. This is what is fitting for the eloquence of the revelation and worthy of the grandeur of its magnificent status.

As for making "bi" a complement of "kafarū" with "ya'dilūn" meaning "to deviate," so that the meaning is: God is worthy of praise for what He created as a blessing for the servants, then those who disbelieve in Him deviate, thereby denying His blessing, this is refuted by the fact that their disbelief in Him, exalted is He, especially with regard to His lordship over them, is more heinous and a greater crime than their deviation from praising Him, glorified and exalted is He, since it occurs together with their neglect of it as well. Thus making the lesser of the two evils the principal element of the sentence, with the intended benefit, and relegating the greater of them to the status of a qualifier that is presupposed, is something unknown in sound speech, let alone in the revealed composition.

It has also been said that it is coordinated with "﴿created the heavens﴾", and the meaning is: He, exalted is He, created what He created, of which none other than Him is capable, and then they ascribe to Him, glorified is He, what has no power over anything of it. But this is not on the understanding that it is an independent relative clause, such that it would be as if one said: "All praise belongs to God, whom they equated with others," but rather that it falls under the relative clause, so that the whole is one relative clause, as if it were said: "All praise belongs to God, from whom came those great blessings, and then from the disbelievers came disbelief."

You know well that what is included in the relative clause, which indicates the requirements of His praise, glorified and exalted is He, must have some role in that indication, even if partial. There is no doubt that their disbelief is far removed from this, and the claim that it has a role in it, on the grounds that it indicates perfect generosity, as if it were said: "All praise belongs to God, who bestowed such great blessings upon one who does not praise Him," is an forced interpretation that the composition does not support, and an inversion that the context rejects. How could it be otherwise, when the thrust of the noble composition, as the following verses reveal, is the censure and rebuke of the disbelievers, by showing the extent of their wrongdoing together with the utmost of His goodness toward them, not by showing the utmost of His goodness toward them together with the extent of their wrongdoing against His right, as the aforementioned claim requires.

Thus it becomes clear that there is no way to make the coordinated element one of the complements of the principal element, since the rule for a relative clause is that it should not be intended for its own benefit; so what then of what is among its complements? You know that the coordinated element is what the speech is directed toward. So reflect, and be upon the manifest truth.

He is the One who created you from clay. This is a resumptive sentence, brought in to demonstrate the falsity of their denial of the Resurrection, even though they witness what necessitates belief in it. It follows the demonstration of the falsity of their associating others with Him, Exalted is He, even though they observe what necessitates His unity. The specific mention of their creation, from among the rest of the proofs for the validity of the Resurrection, is because the creation of the heavens and the earth, which is mentioned, is among the clearest and most evident of them, as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?﴾. This is because the point of dispute is their resurrection, so the indication of the beginning of their creation for that is more evident, and they know more about their own affairs, and turning a blind eye to the luminous proof is more shameful.

The shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical address from third person to second) is for added censure and rebuke. That is: He began your creation from it (clay), for it is the first material of everything, because it is the origin of Adam, who is the father of mankind. This creation is attributed to the addressees and not to Adam, peace be upon him, although he is the one actually created from it, such that it would be said: "He is the One who created your father..." etc. This is sufficient because they already know of his creation, peace be upon him, from it, in making belief in the Resurrection obligatory and nullifying doubt. This clarifies the method of analogy (qiyas), and for the sake of thoroughly removing confusion and ambiguity, along with what this contains of establishing the truth, and drawing attention to a hidden wisdom: that every individual of mankind has a share in his creation, peace be upon him, from it, since his wondrous nature was not confined to himself, but was a model containing within it the nature of all the individuals of the species, in a general (ijmali) enfolding that necessarily entails the operation of its effects on all of them. Thus his creation, peace be upon him, from clay was the creation of every one of his descendants from it. And since his creation was upon this pattern that extends to all the individuals of his offspring, it is more fitting than that this should be confined to himself, as is the understood meaning from attributing the aforementioned creation to him, and more indicative of the greatness of the power of the All-Creating, the All-Knowing, and the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom.

The beginning of the state of the addressees is more fitting to be a standard for its end, so He did what He did. How excellent is the wisdom of the revelation! Upon this secret depends His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you...﴾ etc., and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I had created you before, when you were nothing﴾, as will come.

It is said: the meaning is: He created your father from it, with an omitted modifier (elision of the mudaf). It is also said: the meaning of their creation from it is: their creation from the sperm drop resulting from foods formed from the earth. In any case, there is in it, from the clarity of the indication of His complete power over the Resurrection, what is not hidden, for whoever is able to bring back to life what never smelled the scent of life at all, is more able to bring back to life what has been accompanied by life for a period.

﴿Then He decreed a term﴾; that is, He wrote the death of each one of you.

﴿A term﴾ specific to him; that is, a specific limit of time in which he will certainly perish upon its arrival. The word "then" (thumma) is to indicate the disparity between their creation and the determination of their terms, according to what the profound wisdoms require.

﴿And a named term﴾; that is, a specific limit for your resurrection all together. It is an inchoative (mubtada') because it is specified by the attribute, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And a believing slave is better﴾, and because it occurs in the position of detail, as in the saying of one who said:

When she weeps behind her, she turns toward him with one half, and the other half with us is not turned.

Its being indefinite is to magnify its status and emphasize its matter. For this reason the predicate, which is ﴿with Him﴾, was given precedence, although the common and widespread usage is to delay it, as in your saying: "I have a true word," and "I have a precious book." It is as if it was said: And what named term is established, specified in His knowledge, which does not change, and no one knows the time of its arrival, neither in general nor in detail? As for the term of death, it is known in general and approximately, based on the manifestation of its signs, or on what is customary in human lifespans. Its being called a term is only in consideration of it being the endpoint of the duration of their stay in the graves, not in consideration of it being the beginning of the duration of the Resurrection. Just as the basis for naming in the first term is that it is the last period of life, not that it is the first period of death, because the term in language is an expression for the last part of a duration, not its first part.

It is said: the first term is what lies between creation and death, and the second is what lies between death and resurrection, from the barzakh. For the term, just as it is applied to the last part of a duration, is also applied to all of it. This is most agreeable with what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Allah, Exalted is He, decreed for each person two terms: a term from his birth to his death, and a term from his death to his being raised. If he is righteous, pious, and maintains ties of kinship, something is added to him from the term of resurrection to the term of life. If he is wicked and severs ties, something is reduced from the term of life and added to the term of resurrection. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no one is granted a long life, nor is anything reduced from his life, except that it is in a Book﴾. So the meaning of the term not changing then is: the non-change of its end.

The first is the more well-known and more suitable to magnify the second term, which is contingent upon its being specific to His knowledge, and more fitting to its being emphasized, which is based on its being accompanied by the great calamity. For the fact that part of it is known to creation, and that it passes without any of the calamities occurring in it, as the reading of the second meaning necessarily implies, definitely undermines that emphasis. The meaning of the increase and decrease of the term in what is narrated is: the postponement and advancement of the first term.

﴿Then you doubt﴾: this is an expression of astonishment and denunciation of their doubting the Resurrection, after witnessing the dazzling proofs indicating it that have been mentioned; that is, you doubt its occurrence and its realization in itself, even though you witness within yourselves evidence that completely cuts off the root of doubt. For whoever is able to bestow life and what branches from it of knowledge, power, and the other human perfections upon a material that is not prepared for any of them at all, is clearly more capable of bestowing them upon a material that has been prepared for them and has been accompanied by them for a period.

From here it becomes clear that what has been said, that the first term is sleep and the second is death, or that the first is the term of those who have passed away and the second is the term of those who remain, or that the first is the amount of what has passed of each person's life and the second is the amount of what remains of it, has no basis whatsoever. This is because, as you have seen, the context of the noble composition is to express astonishment at their doubt about the Resurrection, whose time is expressed by the named term. So if it is meant by one of the three matters mentioned, then about what would they be in doubt?

Describing them with doubt, which is uncertainty, and directing the astonishment at it, even though they are firmly certain of the negation of the Resurrection, persistent in denying it, as their saying indicates: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ and its counterparts, is to indicate that their firm certainty mentioned is at the furthest degree of astonishment and denunciation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is Allah﴾ is a nominal clause (jumlah ismiyyah) consisting of a subject (mubtada', "the subject") and predicate (khabar, "the predicate"). It is conjoined (ma'tufah) to what precedes it, and it is brought to explain that the rulings of His divinity (ilahiyyah) extend to all created beings, and that His knowledge encompasses the details of the states of the servants and their deeds that lead to recompense. This follows the indication, within the explanation of how they were created and how their terms were determined, to the realization of the Return (ma'ad).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in the heavens and in the earth﴾ is related (muta'alliq) to the descriptive meaning (al-ma'na al-wasfi) that the majestic name (al-ism al-jalil) indicates. This is either in consideration of the root of its derivation and its being a proper name (alam) for the One worshipped in truth, as if it were said: "He is the One worshipped in them both." Or it is in consideration of its being a name that has become famous for what the Essence is famous for of the attributes of perfection, so that there is taken into account with it what the situation requires of absolute ownership (al-malikiyyah al-kulliyyah) and perfect disposal (al-tasarruf al-kamil), in accordance with what the will requires, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdoms. Thus the adverbial phrase is attached to it from that aspect, and it becomes as if it were said: "He is the Owner, or the Disposer, the Manager, in both of them," as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He is the One who is in the heaven a god, and in the earth a god﴾.

What is meant by the two considerations mentioned is not that the majestic name is to be taken in its linguistic meaning, or in the meaning of "owner," or "disposer," or the like. Rather, it is merely the noting of one of the meanings mentioned within it, just as there is noted with the name "lion" (asad) in the saying of the poet: "A lion against me..." etc., the attribute of boldness for which its referent is famous, so that it takes the place of "bold against me."

By this it becomes clear that what has been said concerning the depiction and interpretation, namely: He is the One known by that in the heavens and in the earth; or He is the One known and famous for the attributes of perfection; or He is the One known for divinity in both of them; or the like, is far from verification. For what is taken into account with the name is the very attribute for which it has become famous, since it is that which the situation requires, as has been explained just above, owing to its being famous for it. Do you not see that the word "against me" in the example mentioned cannot be attached to the name's fame for boldness, with certainty?

It has been said: it is related to what the exclusive construction (al-tarkib al-hasri) conveys of oneness and singularity, as if it were said: "He is the One uniquely (mutawahhid) in divinity in both of them."

It has been said: it is related to what is established for all of them concerning the application of this name to Him exclusively, as if it were said: "He is the One who is called Allah in both of them, none shares with Him in this name," in the manner preceding of taking into account the meaning of oneness, or of stating it within the implication of the speech by way of consequence (istitba'), not by taking the majestic name to mean "the one uniquely divine," nor by positing an implied saying.

It has been permitted that the adverbial phrase be a second predicate (khabar thani), on the basis that His, glorified be He, being in both of them is an expression of His, exalted be He, being extremely knowledgeable of what is in them. This is based on treating His sanctified knowledge, which is free from the acquisition of images and forms, because it is presential (huduri), as the station of His being in them, and depicting it through that by way of figurative representation (tamthil), founded on likening the state of His knowledge of what is in them to the state of His being in them.

For when a knower is in a place, he knows it and what is in it in such a way that nothing of it is hidden from him. Accordingly, His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿He knows your secret and your open﴾ means: what you conceal and what you disclose of sayings, and what you hide and what you make public, whatever it is of sayings and deeds, as an explanation and confirmation of its content, and a realization of the meaning intended by it. The restriction of His, mighty and majestic, knowledge to what is mentioned, specifically, despite its inclusion of all that is in them, is in accordance with what the preceding clause conveys, since the noble composition leads to the explanation of the state of those addressed.

The same holds on the second aspect: for taking the majestic name in consideration of absolute ownership and perfect disposal running in the mentioned pattern necessarily entails taking into account His all-encompassing knowledge, so this is undoubtedly an explanation and confirmation of it.

As for the remaining three aspects, there is no way for it to be an explanation. But this is not because of what has been said, that the equality of secret and open in His knowledge does not indicate what is considered in them of worship and being specific to this name, since perhaps one who lacks perfect knowledge may be worshipped and singled out with it. That is certainly false, for what is meant by what was mentioned is worship in truth and specificity to the majestic name.

There is no doubt that these two are things not conceivable in one who lacks perfect knowledge, self-evidently. Rather, it is because the knowledge mentioned is not taken into account in the meaning of any of the worship in truth and the specificity to the name, so that this would be an explanation of it. And by this it becomes clear that it is not an explanation on the third aspect either, since the singleness in divinity does not have perfect knowledge taken into account in its concept, for this to be an explanation of it. Rather, it is taken into account in what the singular one applies to, and that is not sufficient for the explanatory relation (al-bayaniyyah).

It has been said: it is a predicate after a predicate, according to those who permit the second predicate to be a clause, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿then behold, it was a serpent running﴾.

It has been said: it is the predicate, and the majestic name is a substitute (badal) for "He," and the preceding adverbial phrase is attached to it. For this, it suffices that the object of knowledge is in both of them, as in your saying: "I shot the game in the sacred precinct (haram)" when it is inside and you are outside it.

Perhaps the placing of their secret and their open in both of them is for broadening the circle, and depicting that nothing of them escapes His knowledge in whatever place they may be, not because they may also be in the heavens. And generalizing the address to the people of the heavens is an unlikely far-fetched interpretation, which is not hidden.

﴿and He knows what you earn﴾; that is: what you do to bring benefit or to avert harm, of the deeds earned by the hearts or by the limbs, secretly or openly. Specifying them by mention, despite their inclusion in what preceded on the second interpretation of secret and open, is to show complete concern for them, because they are what recompense is connected to, and this is the reason for the repetition of "He knows."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 4:

﴿And there does not come to them any sign from the signs of their Lord﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaP'naf), coming to explain their disbelief in the signs of Allah and their complete turning away from them, after the first verse had explained their association of partners with Allah, Glorified is He, and their turning away from some of the signs of Tawhid (divine oneness), and the second verse had explained their doubt concerning the Resurrection and their turning away from some of its signs.

The shift in address (al-iltifat) serves to indicate that the mention of their ugly deeds has required that address be turned away from them altogether (yudrab 'anhum al-khitab safhan), and that their crimes be enumerated to others as a censure of them and a condemnation of their state. Here "ma" is a negation particle, and the present-tense form is either to narrate a past state or to indicate continuity in renewal (al-istimrar al-tajaddudi).

The first "min" is extra (mazidah) for comprehensiveness (li'l-istighraq), and the second is partitive (tab'idiyyah), forming together with its genitive complement a qualifier of "ayah." The attribution of the signs to the name of the Lord, attached to the pronoun "hum," serves to magnify their status, which entails the magnification of the enormity of what they dared to do against them. What is meant by them is either the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanziliyyah), so that their "coming" means their descending, and the meaning is: no sign of the Qur'anic signs descends to them, of which those signs are part, speaking of what has been detailed of the wondrous workmanship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, announcing the operation of the rulings of His divinity, Exalted, over all created beings, and the encompassing of His knowledge over all the conditions of creation and their deeds, which necessitate turning toward them and believing in them.

﴿except that they were turning away from it﴾; that is, in the manner of denial and mockery, as you will see explained. As for the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), which include the miracles and other wonders of created things, their "coming" means their appearing to them, and the meaning is: no sign appears to them from the created signs, of which is what has been mentioned of the sublime matters of His, Exalted, which bear witness to His oneness, except that they were turning away from them, abandoning the correct reflection upon them that leads to belief in their Creator.

The choice of this wording over saying "illa a'radu 'anha" (except that they turned away from it), as occurs similarly in His, Exalted, saying: ﴿And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, "This is continuous magic"﴾, is to indicate the continuity of their turning away in accordance with the continuity of the coming of the signs.

"'an" is connected to "mu'ridin" (turning away), and it was placed before it for the sake of the rhyme (li-murá'at al-fawasil). The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the object of "ta'ti" or from its subject, being specific by description, because it includes a pronoun referring to each of them. In either case, there is clear indication of the completeness of their haste to turn away and their carrying it out at the very moment of the coming.

Like the word "lamma" (when/since) reveals in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So they have denied the truth when it came to them﴾. The truth here is an expression for the Qur'an, from which they turned away, when they turned away from each and every one of its verses. He expressed it this way to show the complete ugliness of what they did, for denying the truth is something that cannot be conceived of as proceeding from anyone (p-110).

The fa' (so/then) indicates that what follows it is arranged upon what precedes it, but not on the basis that the latter is something different from the former in reality and occurs after it or is caused by it. Rather, the first is in reality the very same as the second, and the ordering is only according to a conceptual difference. The fa' may also serve to establish this meaning, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So they have come with injustice and falsehood﴾ after His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved said, "This is not but a fabrication he has invented, and other people have helped him with it."﴾ For what they came with, i.e., what they did of injustice and falsehood, is the very same as their stated speech, but since it differs from it in concept and is more heinous in state, it is arranged upon it with the fa' as the arrangement of what necessarily follows upon what necessitates it, to magnify its matter. Likewise, the concept of denying the truth, since it is more heinous than the concept of the aforementioned turning away, is presented in the manner of a clearly invalid necessary consequence, and so it is arranged upon it with the fa' to make manifest the extreme of its invalidity. Then this is qualified by its being without reflection, to emphasize its heinousness and to pave the way for explaining that what they denied is of great consequence, having sublime outcomes that will certainly become apparent to them. The meaning is: when they turned away from those verses at the time of their coming, they denied what cannot be denied at all, without reflecting on its state and outcome, and without taking note of the evidences within it that necessitate its verification, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, they denied what they did not encompass in knowledge, and its interpretation has not yet come to them﴾.

As His statement indicates, exalted is He: ﴿Soon there will come to them the news of what they used to mock﴾. Here "mā" is an expression for the aforementioned truth, expressed thus to magnify its matter by its vagueness, and to give the reason for the ruling by what is within the relative clause. Its "news" is an expression for the immediate punishments that are coming upon them, which the verses of threat have declared.

The word "news" implies the utmost greatness, since nabaʾ (news) is not applied except to a report of great weight. Interpreting it as the delayed punishments, or as the rise of Islam and the exaltation of its word, is contradicted by the verses that follow.

"Sawfa" (soon/surely) serves to affirm and establish the content of the sentence; i.e., it will certainly come to them, even if the realization of the news of the thing they denied before, without reflecting on its outcomes, is delayed. It was said "yastahziʾūn" (they mock) to indicate that their denial was accompanied by mockery, as has been pointed out. This is on the reading that by "the verses" is meant the Qur'anic verse, which is the more apparent.

As for if by them is meant the cosmic signs, then the fa' enters upon the cause of the answer of an elided conditional clause, and the turning away is in its literal sense, as if it were said: if they are turning away from those signs, then do not be surprised, for they have done what is greater than that, of turning away, in that they have denied the truth which is the greatest of the signs. There is no room to take the signs in this sense as all of them at all. As for what has been said, that the meaning is: since they were turning away from all the signs, they denied the Qur'an, this is something the revelation ought to be exalted above such things.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 6:

﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to specify what is meant by the "news" (anba') whose warning was previously given, and to establish its occurrence by way of citing evidence. The hamza is an interrogative of rebuke (inkar) used to affirm the seeing (ru'yah). It is a seeing of recognition (irfaniyyah, i.e., the verb means "to know/recognize"), which requires a single object. The word ﴿kam﴾ ("how many"), whether interrogative or declarative, suspends the verb from acting on it (mu'allaqah 'an al-'amal), and indicates multiplicity (li-al-taktir). Together with what follows it in its scope, it serves as the object of the verb. It is in the accusative governed by ﴿ahlaknا﴾ ("We destroyed") as its object, on the understanding that it refers to persons. The phrase ﴿min qarn﴾ ("from a generation") is a specifier (mumayyiz) for it, on the understanding that qarn refers to the people of an age (asr) among the ages. They were so called because of their being joined together (iqtiran) for a span (burhah) of time, as in the statement of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them," and so on.

It has been said: qarn refers to a period of time, and the noun it modifies is elided, i.e., "from the people of a generation." As for its being in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (masdariyyah) or of time (zarfiyyah), on the understanding that it refers to the verbal noun or to time, this is an evident forced interpretation (ta'assuf).

The first ﴿min﴾ is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah), connected with ﴿ahlaknا﴾. That is: Did they not come to know, through observing the remains and hearing reports, how many nations We destroyed before the people of Makkah; that is, before their creation, or before their time, with the noun elided and the noun of the genitive put in its place, such as 'Ad, Thamud, and their like.

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿We established them on the earth﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining the manner of the destruction and detailing its beginnings, based on a question arising from the opening of the speech, as if it were said: How was that? So it was said: "Their establishment..." etc.

It has been said: it is an attribute (sifah) of qarn, because an indefinite noun requires a specifier, and when what is suitable as a specifier follows it, its being an attribute is determined.

You know that its magnifying tanwin (tanwin al-tafkhim) makes this unnecessary, to the requirement of an attribute. Moreover, that would require that its content and the content of the four clauses conjoined to it be a settled matter not intended by the structure of the discourse, leading to discord in the noble composition. How could it not be so, since the meaning then would be: Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them, described as such and such, and by Our destruction of them for their sins, and that it is evident corruption? Establishing something in the earth means making it settled therein; and since it entails making the earth its place of settlement, usage has come with both. Sometimes it is said "He established him in the earth" (makkanahu fi al-ard), as in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿We had established them in that wherein We have not established you﴾; and sometimes "He established for him in the earth" (makkana lahu fi al-ard), as in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, until each of them was treated as the other.

From it is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿what We have not established for you﴾, after His statement: "﴿We established them in the earth﴾," as if it were said in the first: "We established for them," or in the second: "what We have not established you." The word ﴿ma﴾ is an indefinite noun described by the negative clause following it, and its returning pronoun is elided; its place is accusative as a verbal noun; that is, "We established them an establishment which We have not established for you."

The shift to address (iltifat) is for the sake of addressing them with the weakness of their condition, as additional clarification of the state of both groups, and to remove confusion from the outset regarding the referents of the two pronouns.

﴿And We sent the sky﴾; that is, the rain, or the clouds, or the canopy, since it is the origin of rain.

﴿upon them﴾ is connected with ﴿We sent﴾.

﴿in abundance﴾; that is, in torrents, a circumstantial state (hal) of "the sky."

﴿And We made the rivers﴾; that is, We made them, so the statement of the Exalted: ﴿flowing beneath them﴾ is a second object of "We made," or We brought them into being, in which case it is a circumstantial state of its object. ﴿Beneath them﴾ is connected with ﴿flowing﴾. In it there is an indication that they are subjected to serve them and continue flowing in the stated manner, which is not present in saying "And We caused the rivers to flow beneath them."

The purpose of enumerating those great blessings poured upon them after mentioning their establishment is not to show the greatness of their offense in denying them and their deserving of the greatest punishments for that. Rather, it shows their possession of all the means of attaining their aims, and the foundations of security and salvation from hardships and perils, and that these did not avail them anything. The meaning is: We gave them of physical stature and breadth, of extended lifespans, of abundance of wealth, and of reliance upon worldly means in acquiring benefits and warding off harms, what We did not give the people of Makkah; yet they did what they did.

﴿So We destroyed them for their sins﴾; that is, We destroyed every generation of those generations because of the sins specific to them. Thus those numbers and means did not avail them, and so there will befall these people the like of what befell them of punishment. This, as you see, is the final point by which citation and admonition are made.

As for the statement of the Glorified: ﴿And We brought into being after them﴾; that is, We created after the destruction of every generation.

﴿other generations﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "those who perished." It is for showing the perfection of His power and the breadth of His dominion, and that what has been mentioned of the destruction of many nations has not diminished His kingdom in anything; rather, whenever He destroyed a nation, He brought another in its place.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 7:

﴿And if We had sent down to you﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumla musta'nafa), brought in by way of a shift of address (talwin al-khitab), to show the severity of their obstinacy (shikima) in stubborn denial, and the false assertions that branch out from it, following the statement of their turning away from the signs of God Most High and their denial of the truth, and their deserving, by that, the descent of punishment. The attribution of the sending down here to him, peace be upon him, together with the attribution of the coming of signs and the arrival of the truth in what preceded concerning them, serves to indicate that they were disparaging his prophethood (nubuwwa) implicitly, within their explicit disparagement of what was sent down to him.

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, and Nawfal ibn Khuwaylid, when they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not believe you until you bring us a book from God, and with it four angels testifying that it is from God Most High and that you are His messenger."

﴿a book﴾ (kitaban): if it is taken as a noun like "imam," then His saying, ﴿on parchment﴾ (fi qirtas), is connected to an omitted word that falls as a qualifier of it; that is, a book existing in a sheet. If it is taken as a verbal noun in the sense of "the written," then it is connected to itself.

﴿and they touched it﴾ (falamasuhu); that is, the book. It was said: the parchment.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿with their hands﴾ (bi-aydihim), despite it being evident that touching is customarily not done except with the hands, is for the sake of added specificity and to repel the possibility of the figurative usage found in His saying, ﴿and we touched the heaven﴾ (wa-anna lamasna al-sama'); that is, we searched (tafahhasna). That is: they touched it with their hands after they had seen it with their eyes, such that no doubt about its matter remained for them, and they were unable to make the excuse of having their eyes blinded (taskir al-absar).

﴿those who disbelieved would have said﴾ (laqala alladhina kafaru); that is, they would have said. The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to specify their being characterized by the disbelief contained in the relative clause, which is not hidden; its placement is also fitting in terms of its linguistic meaning (mafhumuhu al-lughawi) as well.

﴿this is not﴾ (in hadha); that is, "this is nothing but," pointing, with this, to that book.

﴿except clear magic﴾ (illa sihrun mubin); that is, its being magic is clear, out of wilful obstinacy and opposition to the truth after its manifestation, as is the habit of the defeated and the rejected, and the custom of the stubborn and the contentious.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 8:

﴿And they say: Why has an angel not been sent down to him?﴾ This begins their explicit denunciation of his prophethood, peace be upon him, after their denunciation of it had been hinted at implicitly. It has also been said that it is coordinated with the answer of "law" (lau), but this is not the case, because that outrageous statement is not something that could be expected from them under the supposition of sending down the mentioned Book. Rather, it is among their manifest falsehoods and fabricated superstitions, with which they make excuses whenever their stratagems run out and their pretexts fail them. That is: why has an angel not been sent down to him, peace be upon him, such that we see him and he speaks to us that he is a prophet? This is as reported from them through al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and its parallel is their saying: ﴿Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾

Since the basis of this suggestion rests on two things, the sending down of the angel as he is, and his being made a warner along with him, peace be upon him, the answer to it is that this is something that scarcely falls within existence at all, because it comprises two mutually incompatible matters that cannot coexist in existence: the sending down of an angel in his own form necessarily entails the absence of his being made a warner, and his being made a warner necessarily requires that he not be sent down in his own form.

The first was alluded to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would certainly have been decided﴾; that is, had We sent down an angel in his own form, as they proposed, while the reality is that, because of the terror of the sight, human powers cannot endure beholding him. Do you not see that the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, used to see the angels and converse with them in human forms, like the guests of Abraham and Lot, and the litigants of David, upon them be peace, and others? And since their condition was thus, though they were supported by holy powers, what then do you think of those others among the common people? Had they seen him thus, the matter of their destruction would have been decided entirely, and his being made a warner would have been impossible. And this, besides being contrary to what they desire, necessarily entails emptying the world of that upon which the order of this world and the Hereafter revolves, namely the sending of messengers and the establishing of laws.

And He, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾, and in it, as you see, is an announcement that in that suggestion they were like one who seeks his own death with his own hoof, and that not granting their request was for the sake of sparing them.

The verb in the first part of the answer is in the active voice with the subject being the "we" of majesty, although in the question it was in the passive voice, in order to magnify the matter and instill awe. The second is in the passive voice, to follow the customary manner of majesty.

The word "then" (thumma) in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they would not be respited﴾; that is, they would not be granted a respite after its descent even for the blink of an eye, let alone be warned by it, which is the purpose of warning. This is to draw attention to the difference between the decision of the matter and the absence of respite, for the suddenness of punishment is greater than the punishment itself and more grievous.

It has also been said regarding the cause of their destruction that if they witnessed the angel descended upon the Messenger of God ﷺ in his form, and that is a sign than which nothing is clearer, and then they did not believe, there would have been no alternative to their destruction.

It has also been said that if they saw him, the faculty of choice, which is the foundation of obligation, would cease, and so their destruction would become obligatory.

And for the second [meaning], by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾. [This is] on the basis that the first pronoun refers to the warner (nadhir), which is understood from the context of the speech with the help of the situation (maqam). The reason the angel mentioned before it was not made the referent, by reversing the order of the two objects so that one would say, "Had We made him a warner, We would have made him a man," while the intended meaning is still understood, is to establish that the criterion for presenting the first act of making (ja'l) in the form of a supposition and hypothesis (fard wa-taqdir) is [the following]:

The basis for the implication of the second [clause] by the first is only the angelhood of the warner, not the warner-hood of the angel. This is because the verb "ja'l" (to make) by its nature requires that its first object be a subject (mubtada') and its second a predicate (khabar), since it carries the meaning of "taṣyīr" (to render/make into), transferred from "ṣāra" (to become) when it enters upon a subject and predicate.

There is no doubt that the locus of the benefit and the basis of the necessary connection between the two parts of the conditional sentence is the predicate of the antecedent, not its subject. Since the conditional here is counterfactual (imtina'iyya), it is intended to show the negation of the first making, because it entails the impossible consequence, which is the second making. Therefore the basis of the implication must necessarily be made the second object in the first [clause]. For this reason its counterpart was made likewise in the second making, to make clear the complete incompatibility between them, which necessitates the negation of the consequent.

The second pronoun refers to the angel, not to what the first refers to. The meaning is: "Had We made the warner they proposed an angel, We would have represented that angel as a man," because of what has passed concerning the inability of individuals to witness the angel in his true form. The preference of "rajulan" (a man) over "basharan" (a human) indicates that the making is by way of representation (tamthil), not by way of changing the reality, and it specifies the means by which the representation occurs.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We would have confused them﴾ is a conjunction upon the answer of "law" (lau), built upon the first answer. It was also read with the elision of the answer's lam, being sufficient with what is in the conjoined [clause]. One says: "labastu al-amra 'ala al-qawm, albisuhu" (I confused the matter for the people, I confuse it), when I make it resemble something else and make it difficult, and its original meaning is covering with a garment. It was also read with both verbs doubled (tashdid) for emphasis; that is: "We would have mixed up for them, by His representing him, a man."

﴿what they confuse﴾ upon themselves at that time, by saying to him: "You are only a human, and you are not an angel." And if his angelhood were established by the inimitable, explicit Qur'an, or by other miracles that do not compel assent, they would have denied him just as they denied the Prophet, peace be upon him. And if He had shown them his original form, the first matter would have followed.

The expression of His exalted representation of him as a man by "confusion" (labs) is either because it is in the form of confusion, or because it is the cause of their confusion, or because it occurs in his company by way of mushakala (a rhetorical device of association in which one term is used for another because of its proximity). In it is an emphasis on the impossibility of making the warner an angel, as if it were said: "Had We done it, We would have done what is not fitting to Our dignity, namely confusing the matter for them."

It has also been permitted that the meaning be: "And We would have confused for them at that time like what they now confuse upon themselves in their disbelief in the manifest signs of God."

Abu al-Su'ud, *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*, on Surah 6, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾. This is a consolation to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he suffers from his people. The opening of the sentence with the oath particle (*lam al-qasam*, the "lam of oath") and the emphatic particle (*harf al-tahqiq*, the particle of affirmation) shows clear emphasis. The tanwin on "messengers" (*rusul*) is for magnification and multiplication. The "min" (﴿from﴾) is ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin) and is connected to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "messengers". The meaning is: "By God, indeed messengers of great importance and great number were mocked, who existed from a time before your time." This is an ellipsis of the modified noun (*hadhf al-mudaf*), with the modifier placed in its position.

﴿So there encompassed﴾ it after it, i.e., it surrounded, or descended, or befell, or something similar. Its meaning revolves around comprehensiveness and inevitability, and it is hardly used except for evil. *Al-hayq* is what encompasses a person of the harm of his own action.

God's statement ﴿those who mocked them﴾, i.e., those who mocked those messengers, peace be upon them, is connected to "encompassed".

Placing it before its agent, which is God's statement ﴿what they used to mock﴾, is for haste in declaring that evil overtook them. The word "what" (*ma*) may be a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) conveying terror: "So there encompassed them that at which they used to mock, since they were destroyed on account of it." Or it may be a verbal-source particle (*masdariyyah*): "So there descended upon them the consequence of their mockery." Placing the prepositional phrase before the verb is for the sake of the rhyme endings (*ri'ayat al-fawasil*).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 11:

﴿Say: Travel through the earth⁠﴾ after the explanation of what the earlier nations did and what was done to them, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was addressed with warning his people and reminding them of their dreadful circumstances, as a caution to them regarding what they were upon, and as a completion of consolation, by what it contains of the subtle assurance that there will befall them the like of what befell their predecessors. This indeed was fulfilled on the Day of Badr in a most remarkable fulfilment. That is: travel through the earth to learn the conditions of those peoples.

﴿Then look⁠﴾; that is: reflect.

﴿how was the end of those who denied⁠﴾. The word "then" (thumma) is either because looking at the traces of the perished cannot be accomplished except after the completion of the journey to their places, or to show the difference between the two in degrees of obligation, and this is the more apparent. For the obligation of travelling is only because it is a means to looking, as the conjunction with "fa" (then) in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, "fa-unzuru" (so look) ... the verse, makes clear.

As for the view that the first command is a permission to travel for trade and the like, and the second an obligation to look at their traces, and that "thumma" serves to distance what lies between the obligatory and the permissible, this does not suit the context.

The word "kayfa" (how) is an interrogative that suspends the verb of looking, and the clause occupies a place in the accusative by the removal of the preposition; that is: reflect upon how they were destroyed by a punishment of annihilation. The word "al-'aqibah" (the end) is a verbal noun like "al-'afiyah" and its like, and it is the final outcome of a matter and its result. Placing "those who denied" in the position of "those who mocked" is to establish that the basis on which what befell them came about is denial, so that the listeners may be restrained from it and not from mockery alone, while denial remains as it is, on the assumption that it is the basis of that.

[Say] to them, by way of compulsion and rebuke (*ilja'*, *tabkit*): ﴿To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ That is, among the rational beings and others: to whom belong all existing things, in creation, ownership and disposal?

His saying, ﴿Say: "To God."﴾ is a confirmation of them and an alert that He is the one specified for the answer by agreement, such that it is not possible for anyone to answer with other than Him. This is as His saying expresses: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "God."﴾

His saying, ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾ is an independent sentence, included under the command, stating that His vast mercy encompasses all creation, in the same way as His dominion and power encompass everything. It is brought to explain that He, exalted is He, is kind to His servants: He does not hasten punishment against them, and He accepts repentance and turning back from them.

And what has been mentioned before and what follows of the rulings of wrath is not among the requirements of His own essence, exalted is He, but comes from the side of the creatures. How could it not be so, when it is from His mercy that He created them upon the sound *fitrah* (primordial nature), guided them to knowing Him and believing in His oneness by setting up the signs within themselves and in the horizons, sending the messengers, and sending down the books filled with the call to what brings about His good pleasure and the warning against what brings about His anger? Yet they changed God's *fitrah*, turned away entirely from the signs, denied the books, and mocked the messengers. ﴿God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Were it not for the comprehensiveness of His mercy, He would have dealt with these people too in the way of those who went before. The meaning of "He has prescribed mercy for Himself" is that He, exalted is He, decreed it and made it obligatory by way of grace and kindness upon His holy essence itself, directly, without any intermediary at all.

It has been said: [it is] what is narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When God, exalted is He, finished creating, He wrote in a book which is with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath."

And from him, in another narration, that he (ﷺ) said: "When God, exalted is He, finished creating, He wrote a book which is with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath."

And from 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Ka'b: "What is the first thing God, exalted is He, began of His creation?" Ka'b said: "God wrote a book, not with a pen or ink, but with the writing of chrysolite, pearl and ruby: Indeed I am God, there is no god but I; My mercy precedes My wrath."

The meaning of the precedence and overcoming of mercy is that it is earlier in its relation to the creatures and more widespread in reaching them, while it is also among the requirements of the essence that bestows good. In the expression of the essence by "self" there is evidence against those who claim that the word "self" (*nafs*) is not applied to God, exalted is He, even if the essence is meant by it, except by *mushakalah* (correspondence of wording), since the correspondence is absent here in both its kinds.

His saying, ﴿He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and the sentence is a resumption brought to threaten them for their associating (others with God) and their neglect of reflection. That is: "By God, He will surely gather you in the graves, raised up, or assembled, until the Day of Resurrection, and then He will recompense you for your polytheism and all your other sins, even if He grants you respite by the requirement of His mercy and does not hasten the worldly punishment upon you." It has been said: "ilā" here means "li" (for), that is: "He will surely gather you for the Day of Resurrection," like His saying: ﴿Indeed you will gather the people for a day about which there is no doubt.﴾ It has been said: it means "fī" (in), that is: "He will surely gather you on the Day of Resurrection."

﴿There is no doubt about it﴾: that is, about the day, or about the gathering.

His saying, ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾: that is, by wasting their capital, which is the original *fitrah*, the sound intellect, and the near readiness that comes from witnessing the Messenger (ﷺ), hearing the revelation, and other traces of mercy. [The phrase is] in the accusative position, or the nominative position, as a censure; that is: "I mean: those who... etc."

Or "they" (*hum*) is a subject, and the predicate is His saying, ﴿so they do not believe﴾, with the "fa" (so) because the subject includes the meaning of a condition, and to indicate that their not believing is due to their loss. For the nullification of the intellect by following the senses and imagination, immersion in imitation, and neglect of reflection led them to persist in disbelief and to refrain from belief. The sentence is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) brought from His side, exalted is He, to them, to condemn what is not included under the command

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 13:**

﴿And His﴾; that is, to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, exclusively.

﴿whatever dwells in the night and the day.﴾ The two periods (al-malawan, lit. "the two smooth ones," i.e. night and day) are treated as if they were a place, so the attribution of temporal things to them is expressed by "dwelling" in them, and the verb is construed with the particle "fi" (in), as in His Exalted saying: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾. Alternatively, "sukun" (dwelling/rest) is the opposite of "harakah" (movement), and the intended meaning is: whatever rests in them or moves, so one of the two opposites is mentioned and the other is omitted.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾, the one who exceeds in hearing everything that is heard.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾, the one who exceeds in knowing everything that is known, so that nothing whatsoever of sayings and deeds is hidden from Him.

**Ask them (﴿قُلْ﴾)**, after having rebuked them with what preceded in the address.

﴿Shall I take as a protector (walī) other than Allah?﴾ That is, as an object of worship (ma'būd), either independently or as a partner. The interrogative hamzah (hamzat al-istifhām, the question particle) was placed on the first object (the maf'ūl awwal) and not on the verb, to indicate that what is being denied is taking someone other than Allah as a protector, not taking a protector in general. This is like His saying ﴿Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?﴾ and His saying ﴿Do you then order me to worship other than Allah...?﴾ and so on.

﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, their originator (mubdi'uhumā). It is in the genitive as an epithet (ṣifah) of the Divine Name (al-jalālah), emphasizing the denial, because it carries the sense of the past tense. For this reason it is also recited as (faṭara). The separation between them by the sentence does no harm, because the sentence is not foreign (ajnabiyyah), since it governs the operator of the qualified noun (ʿāmil fī ʿāmil al-mawṣūf). Or it is an apposition (badal), since separating a substitute from what it substitutes is easier, because the apposition is intended as a repetition of the governing element (taknīr al-ʿāmil).

It is also recited in the nominative and accusative as a laudatory epithet (ʿalā al-madḥ). Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I did not know the meaning of al-Fāṭir until two Bedouins disputed with me over a well, and one of them said: 'I originated (fṭartuhā) it'; that is, I began it."

﴿And He feeds and is not fed﴾, that is, He provides sustenance to creation and is not provided for. The mention of food specifically is due to the intense need for it, or because it is the greatest part of the provision that reaches the one who is provided for. The position of the sentence is accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), since its content establishes the necessity of taking Him, glory be to Him and exalted, as a protector.

It is also recited (﴿وَلا يَطْعَمُ﴾) with a fatḥah on the yā' (yaṭʿamu), and with the reverse of the first reading as well, on the basis that the pronoun refers to other than Allah. The meaning would be: "Shall I associate (partners) with one who is the originator of the heavens and the earth? Something that has fallen below the rank of animal life?" And it is read with the two verbs in the active voice, with the second meaning "seeks food" (yastaṭʿimu), or with the meaning that He sometimes feeds and sometimes does not feed, like His saying ﴿He withholds and expands﴾.

**Say (﴿قُلْ﴾)**, after the clarification that taking anyone other than Him as a protector is something which the immediate reasoning of minds judges to be null.

﴿Indeed, I have been commanded﴾ from His presence, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿To be the first to submit﴾, with my face turned to Allah, sincere to Him. This is because the Prophet is the leader of his community in Islam, like His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to this, and I am the first of the Muslims﴾, and His saying ﴿Glory be to You; I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers﴾.

﴿And never be﴾; that is: and it was said to me: "And never be."

﴿among the polytheists﴾; that is, in any matter of the affairs of religion. Its meaning is: I have been commanded to submit to Islam and forbidden from associating partners with Allah. It has been permitted to make this (negative prohibition) coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the command.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 15:

﴿Say: Indeed I fear, if I disobey my Lord,﴾; that is: by opposing His command and His prohibition, whatever disobedience it may be. Thus what has been mentioned enters into it as a primary inclusion, and in it is a clarification of the complete avoidance by him (ﷺ) of sins in every respect.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾; that is: the punishment of the Day of Resurrection. It is the object of "fear" (khāfa), and the conditional clause is interposed between the two, while the response (jawab) is omitted, the preceding context indicating it. In it is a severing of their vain hopes, and an allusion that they are sinners deserving of the great punishment. (p-117)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 16:

﴿Whoever is turned away from it﴾ is in the passive form (al-bina' li-l-maf'ul); that is, the punishment. It has also been read in the active form (al-bina' li-l-fa'il), with the pronoun referring to Allah, glorified is He, and it has been read with the explicit noun (bi-l-idhhar), with the object omitted.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on that day﴾ relates to the turning away; that is, on that great day. It has also been permitted that it be the object (al-maf'ul) when read in the active form, by omitting the genitive-noun (al-mudaf) so that the sense is: a punishment on that day.

﴿then He has shown him mercy﴾; that is, He has saved him and bestowed favour upon him. It was also said: then He has caused him to enter Paradise, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed succeeded﴾. The clause is a resumptive (mustanafah) clause, emphasising the terror of the punishment. The pronoun in ʿanhu and rahimahu refers to man (man), and it is an expression for one other than the disobedient.

﴿That﴾ is a reference to the turning away or to the mercy, since it is interpreted as an (an) clause with the verb, and what it contains of the meaning of distance, to signal the loftiness of its rank and the remoteness of its place in virtue. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the manifest triumph﴾; that is, its being manifestly a success, which is attaining the desired goal. The definite article (al-alif wa-l-lam) is for restricting it to that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 17:

﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾; i.e., with an affliction, such as sickness, poverty, and the like.

﴿then there is none who can remove it﴾; i.e., there is none able to remove it from you, ﴿except Him﴾ alone.

﴿And if He touches you with good﴾ such as health, blessing, and the like.

﴿then He is over all things competent.﴾ And among the totality of all things is this: He is able over it, so He holds it fast for you and preserves it for you, and no one is able to repel it or to lift it. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So there is no repeller of His bounty﴾. And taking it to be an emphasis of the two responses is refuted by the fa' (the particle "then", fa').

Reminder: It is related "from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: A mule was presented as a gift to the Prophet (ﷺ), which Kisra had sent him. He rode it with a rope of hair, then had me ride behind him, then he traveled with me a mile. Then he turned to me and said: 'O boy!' I said: 'At your service, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Guard Allah and He will guard you; guard Allah and you will find Him before you. Get to know Allah in ease and He will know you in hardship. When you ask, ask Allah; and when you seek help, seek help from Allah. The pen has already dried over what is to be. If all creation were to strive to benefit you with something Allah has not decreed for you, they would not be able to do it; and if they strove to harm you with something Allah has not written against you, they would not be able to do it. If you are able to act with patience together with certainty, then do so; and if you are not able, then be patient, for in patience over what you dislike there is much good. Know that victory comes with patience, that relief comes with distress, and that with hardship comes ease.'"

And He is the Subduer over His servants, above them. (This is a depiction of His dominance and His exaltedness through overpowering and capability.)

And He is the All-Wise in everything He does and in what He commands.

The All-Aware of the conditions of His servants and the hidden matters of their affairs. The lam in the three places is for restriction (al-qasr).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 19:

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ (p-118) It is related that the Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, we asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that you have no mention or description among them. So show us who will testify for you that you are the Messenger of Allah." Then this was revealed.

Ayyu (أيّ) is the subject (mubtada'), akbaru (أكبر) is its predicate (khabar), and shahadatan (شهادة) is in the accusative as a specifier (tamyiz).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Allah"﴾ is a command to him (ﷺ) to give the answer himself. This is either to announce that the answer is determined and that they are unable to answer with anything other than it, or because they might stammer over it, not out of hesitation about whether it is greater than everything, but about whether it is a witness in this matter.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Witness﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada'), meaning: He is a witness.

﴿between me and you﴾. It is also permissible that "Allah is a witness between me and you" is the answer; for since He is the witness between him and them, the greatest thing in testimony is a witness for him (ﷺ). The repetition of "between" (bayn) is to establish the correspondence.

﴿And it has been revealed to me﴾; that is, from Him, exalted is He.

﴿this Qur'an﴾, which testifies to the truth of my message.

﴿so that I may warn you thereby﴾ with what it contains of threat. The restriction to mentioning warning is because the address is with the disbelievers.

﴿and whoever it reaches﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun of those addressed; that is: so that I may warn you thereby, O people of Makkah, and all others it reaches of the black and the red, or of the two species (jinn and humankind), or: so that I may warn you thereby, those present and whoever will exist until the Day of Resurrection. This is evidence that the rulings of the Qur'an encompass those present on the day of its revelation and whoever will exist afterward until the Day of Resurrection, except that this is by way of implication (ibarah) for all according to the Hanabilah, and by consensus according to us, regarding those not present and those not obligated on that day, as has passed at the beginning of Surah an-Nisa'.

﴿Do you indeed testify that there are other gods with Allah?﴾ This is a confirmation to them, together with denial and disapproval.

﴿Say: "I do not testify"﴾ to that; and even if you testify to it, it is pure falsehood.

﴿Say﴾ is a repetition of the command for emphasis.

﴿Indeed He is only one God﴾; that is: rather, I testify only that He, exalted is He, there is no god but Him.

﴿And indeed I am free from what you associate﴾ with Allah, of idols, or of your associating.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 20:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ is an answer to what preceded from their saying: "We have asked about you the Jews and the Christians." It has been delayed from specifying the witness, in haste to bind them to an answer regarding their arbitrariness in saying: "Show us someone who testifies for you?" ... etc.

The intended meaning of the relative pronoun is the Jews and the Christians, and by "the Book" is meant the category that includes the Torah and the Gospel.

Their designation by the title "the giving of the Book" serves to indicate the basis of what is attributed to them by the words of the Exalted: ﴿they recognize him﴾; that is, they recognize the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through the two Books by his description and his attributes mentioned in them.

﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾ by their features, to the extent that they have no doubt in that at all. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to 'Abd Allah ibn Salam: "Allah the Exalted revealed this verse to His Prophet. How is this recognition?" He said: "O 'Umar, I recognized him among you when I saw him just as I recognize my son, and indeed I am more certain of Muhammad than I am of my son, because I do not know what women have done, and I testify that he is the truth from Allah the Exalted."

﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ from among the People of the Two Books and the polytheists, in that they wasted the fitrah of Allah upon which He created people, and turned away entirely from the clear proofs that necessitate faith.

﴿So they do not believe﴾ because their hearts have been sealed. The position of the relative pronoun is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is the clause introduced by the particle "fa" (so), due to the resemblance of the relative pronoun to the conditional.

It has been said: it is accusative, as the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, "they are those who have lost..." etc. It has also been said: it is in apposition as an attribute of the first relative pronoun. It has also been said: it is accusative by way of censure. According to the last opinions, the saying of the Exalted "so they do not believe" is a conjunction upon the clause "Those to whom We gave the Book" ... etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 21:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ By their describing the Prophet (ﷺ), who is promised in the two Scriptures, with attributes other than his (ﷺ) true attributes, which is a fabrication against Allah, Glorified is He; and by their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and their saying: "These are our intercessors with Allah," and the like. This is a denial and a declaring far-fetched, that anyone should be more unjust than those who did that, or equal to them in injustice. Although the structure of the expression does not explicitly address the denial of equality, its negation is witnessed by common usage and consistent practice: when it is said, "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "There is no one more virtuous than so-and-so," what is definitively meant is that he is more generous than every generous person and more virtuous than every virtuous person. Do you not see the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Without doubt, they are in the Hereafter the greatest losers﴾ after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah...﴾ and so on.

The reason for this is that a comparative relation between two things is generally conceived only in terms of differing degrees, especially in the domain of competition by excess, in increase and decrease. So when neither of them is greater, a deficiency necessarily arises.

﴿Or denies His signs﴾, such as when they denied the Qur'an, of which is the verse that states they recognize him (ﷺ) as they recognize their own sons, and denied the miracles, calling them sorcery; and they distorted the Torah and altered its descriptions of him (ﷺ). Indeed, that is a denial of the signs of Allah, Exalted is He.

The word "or" (أو) serves to indicate that each of fabricating and denying, on its own, reaches the extreme of excess in injustice. How much more so when they have combined both, affirming what Allah has negated and negating what He has affirmed. ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they deluded?﴾

﴿Indeed, He﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n), and the reason for placing it in this position is the claim that its fame makes mention of it unnecessary. The benefit of beginning the sentence with it is to indicate the grandeur of its content, together with the increased fixing of it in the mind. For the pronoun, at first, conveys only an undefined matter of importance, so the mind remains awaiting what follows, and so when it arrives it becomes firmly settled with especially great firmness. It is as if it were said: "The momentous matter is this."

﴿The wrongdoers will not prosper﴾; that is, they will not be saved from what is disliked, nor will they attain what is sought. If this is the condition of wrongdoers, then what do you think of one who is at the furthest extreme of injustice?

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 22:**

﴿And the Day We gather them all﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarfiyyah*), governed by a deleted verb placed later in the sentence. It has been omitted to indicate that the expression is too narrow to explain and clarify it, and as a hint that the listeners cannot bear to hear it, because of the extreme horror of the catastrophe and the complete calamity that will befall them. It is as if it had been said: "And the Day We gather them all."

﴿Then We will say﴾ to them what We will say. There will be such states and terrors that the range of speech cannot encompass them. The verb is taken in the past form to indicate certainty, and for the good placement of the conjunction in the Almighty's words: ﴿Then it will not be [that their trial was] ...﴾ etc., coordinated with it.

It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a direct object (*maf'ūliyyah*) governed by a verb placed earlier. That is: "And mention to them, for the sake of warning and admonition, the Day We gather them ..." etc. It has also been said: "and so that they may be wary of," or "so that they may beware of, the Day We gather them ..." etc.

The pronoun (in *naḥshuruhum*) refers to all of them, and *jamī'an* ("all") is a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of it. It has been read as *yaḥshuruhum jamī'an thumma yaqūlu* with the *yā'* (third person) in both places.

﴿To those who associated partners﴾; that is, We will say to them specifically, for rebuke and reproach before the heads of the witnesses.
