﴿Where are your partners﴾; that is, your gods whom you made partners with God, exalted is He. Their attribution to them (as "your partners") is because their partnership is nothing but their naming and their false fabrication.

As His Almighty's words indicate: ﴿Those whom you used to claim﴾; that is, you used to claim them to be partners. So both objects are omitted together. This question, which indicates the absence of the partners despite the general gathering that includes them, is based on the Almighty's words: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, their spouses, and what they used to worship﴾ ﴿besides God﴾. Other texts besides this occur only after what took place between them and the partners of disavowal from both sides, and the severing of the ties and connections between them, as His Almighty's words narrate: ﴿And We will separate them ...﴾ etc., and similar noble verses. This is either by their not actually being present at that time, through their being removed from that station, or by treating (p-120) their non-presence under the title of partnership and intercession as equivalent to their non-presence in reality. For the question is not about them in terms of their essences, but in terms of their being partners, as the description by the relative clause expresses. There is no doubt that the absence of the attribute necessitates the absence of the thing described insofar as it is described. Thus they, insofar as they are partners, are necessarily absent, even though they may be present insofar as their essences are concerned, whether they were idols or otherwise.

As for what is said, that they will be kept away from them at the time of rebuke, so that they will lose them at the very hour in which they had placed their hope, and thus see the place of their disgrace and regret, this perhaps implies that they do not perceive the true state of affairs, and that the ropes of their hope in them have not yet been cut. Yet you know that they witnessed them before that, and that the handhold of their desires in them had been completely severed, since it is known to them from the moment of death and the affliction of punishment in the barzakh. What occurs on the Day of Gathering is only the clear unveiling and the strong certainty that results from direct presence and dialogue.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 23:

﴿Then their fitnah (trial, test; here, their response) will not be but that they say﴾ With the verb read in the feminine form and with "fitnatuhum" in the nominative, taking it as the subject (ism) of the verb, and the predicate (khabar) being ﴿but that they say﴾. It is also read with "fitnatahum" in the accusative, taking it as the predicate, while the subject is ﴿but that they say﴾. The feminine form of the verb is for the predicate, as in the expression "man kānat ummuka?" (who was your mother?). It is also read in the masculine form with "al-fitnah" in either the nominative or the accusative. The nominative is more fitting according to the meaning. The clause is coordinated with what was assumed to govern "the day We gather them" (yawma nahshuruhum), as indicated earlier. The exception (istithna') is an incomplete exception (mufrigh) from the most general of things.

As for "fitnatuhum": it is either their disbelief (kufrahum), meant in the sense of its consequence (aqibah), i.e., the consequence of their disbelief, to which they clung throughout their lives and on which they prided themselves, will be nothing except denial of it and disavowal of it, by saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. As for their answer, it is expressed as a "fitnah" because it is a lie, and describing Him, exalted is He, with His lordship over them is for emphasis in disavowing polytheism.

It is also read as an address (nida'), in which case it is to display humility and supplication in seeking the acceptance of the excuse. They say this while knowing that it is entirely useless, out of extreme bewilderment and astonishment. Interpreting it as meaning: "We were not polytheists in our own estimation, and in the world we did not know that we were in error regarding our belief," is something that should not be supposed at all, for it would imply that they have an excuse.

Oh, and as for their being able to offer some excuse in general: that certainly detracts from the full awfulness of that Day, and it is definitively refuted by His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾. For this is an expression of wonder at their blatant lie in denying that they had ever associated partners (with God) in the world. That is: look how they lied against themselves in their saying that, for this is an extremely astonishing matter. As for interpreting it as referring to their lying in the world, that is a far-fetched strained reading, from which the sanctity of the revelation must be kept clear.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾ is coordinated with "﴿they lied﴾" and falls under the same rule of expressing wonder. The "﴿what﴾" is either a verbal noun (masdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (mawsulah), whose returning pronoun has been omitted. The meaning is: look how they lied, by the wicked and emphatic oath, against themselves by denying that what had proceeded from them had proceeded from them, and how their fabrication went astray from them; that is, it vanished and disappeared, or (it means) what they used to fabricate of associating partners, so that they denied its having proceeded from them altogether and disowned it entirely.

It has been said: "﴿what﴾" refers to the partners, and attributing the fabrication to them, although in reality it falls upon their states of divinity, partnership, intercession and the like, is for the sake of emphasis regarding their matter, as if they themselves were the thing fabricated. And it has been said: the sentence is an independent statement, not falling within the scope of the expression of wonder.(p-121)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 25:

﴿And among them are those who listen to you.﴾ This is a fresh sentence (kalam mubtada') brought in to narrate what some of the polytheists did in this world of the rulings of disbelief, and then to state what will proceed from them on the Day of Gathering, as a confirmation of what came before and a verification of its content. The pronoun refers to those who associated partners (with God). The place of the adverbial phrase (zarf) is nominative, on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada') in terms of its content, or by way of an implied described noun, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among us are some who are otherwise than that﴾; that is: "and a group among us..." etc.

"Man" (من) is either a relative pronoun (mawsula) or a descriptive (mawsufa), its position being nominative as a predicate (khabar). The meaning is: "And some of them, or some of them, are those who listen to you," or "a group who listen to you," on the basis that the point of the statement is their being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause or the descriptive, not that they are the very persons so named. This has been discussed in the explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among people is one who says...﴾ etc.

It is narrated that Abu Sufyan, al-Walid, al-Nadr, 'Utba, Shayba, Abu Jahl and their likes gathered, listening to the recitation of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said to al-Nadr, who was a man of tales: "O Abu Qutayla, what does Muhammad say?" He said: "By Him who made it His house, I do not know what he says, except that he moves his tongue and says the fables of the ancients, like what I have told you of the past generations." Abu Sufyan said: "Indeed I see that it is true." Abu Jahl said: "No!" Then it was revealed.

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾: "placing" (ja'l) here carries the sense of creating (al-in'sha'), and "over" (ʿala) is attached to it. The pronoun in "their hearts" refers to "man," and its plural form is in view of its meaning, just as the singular pronoun in "listens" is in view of its wording. The consideration of meaning has been observed in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾... the verse.

"Akinna" is the plural of "kinan," which is that by which a thing is covered. Its tanwin is for magnification. The clause is either a new independent sentence informing of the sealing it contains, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "listens," with "qad" implied according to those who regard it as preceding the past tense that serves as a circumstantial clause; that is: they listen to you while We have placed over their hearts coverings in great number, whose extent cannot be measured, beyond what people are accustomed to.

﴿Lest they understand it﴾; that is: out of aversion to their understanding what they hear of the Qur'an, indicated by the mention of listening. It may also be that it is an object (maf'ul) of what the statement points to; that is: We have prevented them from understanding it.

﴿And in their ears is a heaviness﴾: deafness and a weight that prevents hearing it. The discussion of it is as in His words: ﴿over their hearts coverings﴾.

This is an image that indicates the extent of their ignorance of the affairs of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the excessive distance of their hearts from understanding the noble Qur'an and their rejection of hearing it. Its verification has been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara.

It has been said: it is a report of what they said: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is a heaviness...﴾ the verse.

You know well that their intention in this was to report what they believed about the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ), out of ignorance and disbelief, of attributes of them both that prevent acceptance and faith, such as the Qur'an being magic, poetry, and fables of the ancients; and measure what they imagined concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) by this. It is not a report that there was some matter beyond that which a barrier from their side had come between them and perceiving, such that the noble text could be taken to mean that.

﴿And if they see every sign﴾ of the Qur'anic signs; that is: they witness them by hearing them.

﴿they will not believe in it﴾: this is a general negation, not a negation of generality; that is: they disbelieve in each one of them, because they do not perceive them as they truly are, given their state as already described.

﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you﴾: this is the "until" that is followed by clauses, and the clause is ﴿when they come to you﴾.

﴿those who disbelieve say﴾, and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "came." The relative pronoun was placed in the position of the pronoun to censure them through what is within the scope of the relative clause, and to indicate the cause of the ruling; that is: they reached such a degree of denial and obstinacy that when they come to you disputing with you, they are not content merely with not believing what they heard of the noble verses, but say: ﴿This is not﴾; that is: this is nothing.

﴿except the fables of the ancients﴾. For counting the best and truest of speech, which falsehood cannot approach from before it or from behind it, among the falsehoods and fables, is a degree of disbelief beyond which there is no further degree. "Until" may be a preposition (jarra), and "idhā" may be temporal, meaning "at the time of their coming," with "disputing with you" as a circumstantial clause as already mentioned.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿those who disbelieve say﴾... etc., are an explanation of the disputing. "Asatir" is the plural of "ustura" or "usṭara," or the plural of "siṭar," which is the plural of "saṭar" with vowelling, and the root of all of these is "saṭr," meaning a line.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 26:

﴿And they forbid others from it﴾. The pronoun of subject refers to those previously mentioned, and the pronoun of object refers to the Qur'an. That is, they are not content merely with denying it and dismissing it as fables of the ancients; rather, they forbid people from listening to it, lest they come to recognize its truth and believe in it.

﴿And they keep away from it﴾: that is, they distance themselves from it personally, to show the utmost extent of their aversion to it and to reinforce their prohibition of it. For abstaining from what one forbids others from is among the completions of the prohibition itself. Perhaps this is the secret behind placing the "keeping away" after the "forbidding."

It is said: the pronoun of object refers to the Prophet ﷺ. It is also said: the pronoun of subject refers to Abu Talib. Perhaps its being in the plural is by way of considering that he was followed by those who followed him, for he used to forbid the Quraysh from confronting the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he kept away from him and did not believe in him.

It is narrated that they gathered around him and intended harm to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said:

By Allah, they will not reach you with their gathering
Until I am laid in the dust, buried.

So proclaim your matter; there is no shame upon you in it,
And rejoice in that, and let your eyes be refreshed by it.

You called me, and you claimed that you were my sincere advisor,
And indeed you spoke truly, and you were trustworthy there as a faithful one.

And you presented a religion which is undoubtedly
Among the best religions of mankind in religion.

Were it not for the reproach, or my fear of a disgrace,
You would have found me generous in that, clearly declaring it.

Then it was revealed.

﴿And they destroy none but themselves﴾: that is, they do not destroy by what they did of forbidding and keeping away.

﴿but themselves﴾, by exposing themselves to the most severe and dreadful punishment, both in this world and the next, which is the punishment of misguidance and misleading others.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they are not aware﴾, it is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "they destroy"; that is, they restrict the destruction to themselves, while in fact they are not aware, neither of their destroying themselves, nor of the restriction of that to themselves, without it harming anything of the Qur'an, the Messenger ﷺ, or the believers. The destruction was expressed thus, although what is negated of others is absolute harm, because the ultimate result of what they did, of disparaging the noble Qur'an and obstructing the implementation of its rulings and the manifestation of the matter of the religion, is destruction; this indicates that what befalls them is perdition, not mere harm. Moreover, their aim was not absolute obstruction in the matters mentioned, but rather they were seeking evils against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers.

It is also permissible that the destruction be considered in relation to those whom they misguide by forbidding, so restricting it to themselves then, together with its inclusion of both groups, is based on regarding the punishment of misguidance as equivalent to non-existence in comparison with the punishment of misleading others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 27:

﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾. This begins the narration of what they will say on the Day of Resurrection, a self-contradictory speech, in contrast to the ugly deeds they committed in the world that were related earlier, while the speech itself is a lie in its own right.

The address is either to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone (p-123) among those who are witnesses and observers, with the aim of showing the completeness of their wretched state and the extent of its horror and dreadfulness, to the point that its wonder is not confined to one who sees and not to another who sees among those accustomed to witnessing marvelous things; rather, everyone to whom sight is possible is amazed at its terror and dreadfulness.

The answer to "law" (lau, "if") is omitted, relying on its being evident, and to signal that expression falls short of detailing it. Likewise the object of "tara" (you see) is omitted, because what is in the adverbial phrase indicates it. The meaning: If you could see them when they are made to stand over the Fire, until they witness it directly, you would see what speech cannot encompass.

The past form of the verb (waqafu) indicates certainty, or [it means] "when they become aware of it, looking down upon it while it is beneath them," or "when they enter it and come to know the measure of its punishment," from the expression "waqaftuhu 'ala kadhā" meaning "when you have understood it and known it." It is also read "wuqifu" with the active form, from "waqafa 'alayhi wuqufan" (he stood over it / became aware of it).

﴿So they will say: "Oh, would that we were returned!"﴾; that is, to the world, wishing for a return and deliverance. "Hayhāt" (far-fetched, too late) and "wa-lā tanāṣ" (no escape) [come in as the response].

﴿And that we would not deny the signs of our Lord﴾; that is, the signs of His which speak of the states of the Fire and its terrors, commanding that one guard against it, since these are what come to mind at that time, and they lament over what they neglected regarding its right; or [it means] all His signs, which encompass those signs in a primary sense.

﴿And that we would be among the believers﴾ in them, acting in accordance with their requirements, so that we would not see this terrifying position; or that we would be among the group of believers who are saved from punishment and who attain a good return.

The two verbs are in the subjunctive as an answer to the wish, with "an" (that) implied after the "wa" (and), treating it as the "fa" (then) would be; this is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Ishaq: "fa-lā nukadhdhiba" (so we would not deny). The meaning: If we are returned, we will not deny and we will be among the believers.

It is said: from "an" (the verbal particle) and the verb after it a verbal noun is formed, and before it an implied verbal noun is assumed, so this is coordinated with it, as if it were said: "Would that we had a return, and no denial, and being among the believers."

It is also read with both verbs in the nominative, on the basis that it is a resumed statement, like the saying: "Leave me, and I will not return"; that is, "and I do not return, whether you leave me or do not leave me." Or it is coordinated with "nuradd" (we are returned), or is a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, so it falls within the ruling of the wish, like the last aspect of the subjunctive. The later statement of denial is connected to it because of what it implies of a promise of belief and non-denial, like one who says: "Would that I were given wealth so I could reward you for your kindness," for he is wishing in the sense of one making a promise; so if he were given wealth and did not reward his companion, he would certainly be a liar. It is also read with the first in the nominative and the second in the subjunctive, and the reasoning for both has already been mentioned.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 28:

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before.﴾ This is a turning away (idrab) from what the wish (tamanni) for the promise of affirming the signs and believing in them indicates. That is: it is not from a true resolve, arising from a desire for faith and a longing to attain it and to be characterized by it. Rather, it is because there became apparent to them, in that station of theirs, what they used to conceal in the world of the great calamity (al-da'hiya al-dahya'), and they thought that they were about to fall into it. So, from fear of it and the terror of its onset, they said what they said. What is meant by it is the Fire upon which they were made to stand, since it is the one about which the speech was brought to magnify its matter and to marvel at the horror of the state of those made to stand over it. And by concealing it, their denial of it is (established), for denying a thing is necessarily disbelief in it and concealment of it.

Its preference over the explicit denial found in His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny﴾, and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny﴾, although it is more suitable to what precedes it, namely their saying: ﴿and that we would not deny the signs of our Lord﴾, is for the sake of observing what corresponds to it in "appearance" (al-bud). This is what the eloquence of the noble arrangement (al-nazm al-karim) requires.

As for what has been said, that what is meant by "what they used to conceal" is their disbelief and their acts of disobedience, or their ugly deeds and disgraceful acts which they used to hide from people, so that they appear in their records and through the testimony of their limbs against them; or their polytheism, which they deny at some stations of the Resurrection by saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾, and then it becomes apparent through the testimony of the limbs against them as mentioned; or what the leaders of the disbelievers concealed from their followers regarding the matter of resurrection and rising again; or what the scholars of the People of the Two Books concealed from their common folk regarding the authenticity of the Prophet's prophethood (ﷺ) and his noble attributes, with the pronoun in the genitive referring to the common folk and the pronoun in the nominative referring to the elite; or their disbelief which they concealed from the believers, with the genitive pronoun referring to the believers and the nominative pronoun referring to the hypocrites. After overlooking in each of these the forced construction and the disorder, there is no path to any of that at all, because of what you have understood: that the course of the noble arrangement is for magnifying the matter of the Fire and depicting the condition of its people as dreadful, and their standing over it has been mentioned, and it has been indicated that there befell them at that time fear, dread, bewilderment and astonishment which description cannot encompass. And their aforementioned wish has been ordered upon it by the fa' which signifies that what precedes it is the cause of what follows. So the dropping of the Fire after that from that causal relation, while it is in itself the most calamitous of calamities and the most restraining of restraints, and attributing it to some of the aforementioned matters which are lesser in terror and restraint, while its mention does not run there, is a matter from which the sanctuary of the Revelation must be held free.

As for what has been said, that what is meant is the requital for what they used to conceal, it is of the kind of entering houses from their backs while their doors are open; so reflect.

﴿And if they were returned﴾; that is: from that station of theirs to the world, as they wished, and what they had witnessed of the terrors had been forgotten by them.

﴿they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ of the various kinds of ugly deeds, of which the aforementioned denial is part, and they would entirely forget what they had witnessed, because their gaze is confined to the visible and not the unseen.

﴿And indeed they are liars﴾; that is: they are a people whose habit is lying in everything they do and everything they leave undone.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 29:

﴿And they said﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to "they would return" (ʿādū), and falls within the scope of the answer (jawāb). The placing of the saying of Allah, exalted is He, "and indeed they are liars" (wa-innahum la-kādhibūn) between the two is because it is an interjection (iʿtirāḍ) brought to confirm what the conditional sentence (sharṭiyyah) conveys concerning their particular lying. Had it been delayed, it would have given the impression that the intended meaning was their being called liars for their denial of resurrection. The meaning is: if they were returned to the world, they would return to what they had been forbidden, and they would say: ﴿It is not﴾; that is, what is (mā) ...

﴿Only our life of this world, and we shall not be resurrected﴾ after we have departed this life, as if they had not seen what they had seen of the states whose first is resurrection and rising up.

﴿وَلَوْ تَرى إذْ وُقِفُوا عَلى رَبِّهِمْ﴾ The discussion of this is like what has passed regarding its counterpart, except that the standing (*wuqūf*) here is a metaphor (*majāz*) for being held back for reproach and questioning, as a guilty slave is made to stand before his master for punishment. It has also been said: they came to know their Lord with true knowledge. And it has been said: they were made to stand over the recompense of their Lord.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) built upon a question arising from the preceding discourse, as if it were said: "What did their Lord say to them at that time?" So it was answered: "He said," ﴿أَلَيْسَ هَذَا﴾ pointing to what they witnessed of the Resurrection and what follows it of great matters.

﴿بِالحَقِّ﴾ is a rebuke to them for their denial of it, and for their saying, when they heard what relates to it: "This is not true; it is nothing but falsehood."

﴿قالُوا﴾ is a resumptive clause, as before.

﴿بَلى ورَبِّنا﴾ They confirmed their acknowledgment with an oath, to show the completeness of their certainty of its truth, and to indicate that this acknowledgment came from them with eagerness and alacrity, hoping it would benefit them.

﴿قالَ﴾ is a resumptive clause, as has passed.

﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ﴾ which you have seen with your own eyes. The *fa'* (*fa'*) here indicates the sequence of the punishment upon their acknowledgment of the truth of what they disbelieved in during the world. However, the punishment does not revolve around their acknowledgment of it; rather, it is their earlier disbelief in what they now acknowledge as true.

As His words, mighty and majestic, express: ﴿بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾; that is: because of your disbelief in the world in that, or (p-125) in everything that it is obligatory to believe in, so their disbelief in it enters in the primary sense. Perhaps this rebuke and reproach occur only after they have been made to stand before the Fire, and then they said what they said, since it is apparent that after this matter nothing remains but the punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 31:

﴿Indeed, those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah﴾. They are the ones whose circumstances were related earlier, but the relative pronoun (al-ladhina, "those who") has been placed in the position of the pronoun, to give notice (li-l-idhan) that their loss is caused by what is contained in the relative clause (al-silah), namely their denial of the meeting with Him, the Exalted, by the establishment of the Hour (al-sa'ah), and what follows from it of resurrection (al-ba'th) and its consequent rulings, and their persistence in that. For the word "until" (hatta) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until, when the Hour comes upon them﴾, is a limit (ghayah) to their denial, not to their loss, since that loss is everlasting and has no limit.

﴿Suddenly﴾ (baghtatan). Al-bagt and al-baghtah: the surprising of a thing swiftly without awareness of it. It is said: "he surprised him (baghatahu) with bagt and baghtah", i.e., suddenly. Its being in the accusative may be either as a verbal noun (masdar) standing in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "came upon them", i.e., "surprising" (mubaghatatan), or from its object, i.e., "taken by surprise" (mabghutin). Or it may be a verbal noun emphasising a non-root meaning, since "came upon them" means "surprised them", like their saying: "I came to him running" (ataytuhu rakdan). Or it may be a verbal noun emphasising an omitted verb that stands as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "came upon them", i.e., "the Hour came upon them, surprising them with surprise."

﴿They say﴾ (qalu) is the answer (jawab) of "when" (idha).

﴿Alas for us!﴾ (ya hasratana). "Come, O regret, for this is your time!" Al-hasrah: intense remorse. Although this anguish overtakes them at death, since that is among the beginnings of the Hour it is named by its name. For this reason the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "Whoever dies, his resurrection has come" (man mata faqad qamat qiyamatuhu). Or the coming of the Hour after death is treated as though it happens without interval, because of its swiftness.

﴿For what we neglected concerning it﴾; i.e., for our neglect regarding the matter of the Hour, our shortcoming in observing its right and preparing for it by faith in it and by acquiring righteous deeds, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for what I neglected in regard to Allah's side﴾.

It is said: the pronoun refers to the worldly life (al-hayah al-dunya), though no mention of it has preceded, because it is known. Al-tafrit: falling short in a thing while having the ability to do it. It is said: it is wasting (al-tadyi'). It is said: al-farat is precedence, whence al-farit, i.e., the one who goes ahead; and the meaning of farrata is "he left the precedence to another"; so the doubling in it indicates removal (li-l-salb), as in "I stripped the camel" (jallattu al-ba'ir).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "they say". Its benefit is to give notice that their punishment is not confined to the anguish mentioned over what has passed and gone, but that they also suffer the bearing of heavy burdens; and it signals that this anguish is of such intensity that it does not cease nor is forgotten, because of the varieties of punishment they endure. The secret in this is that spiritual punishment is more severe than bodily punishment; we seek refuge in the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from both.

Al-wizr in origin is a heavy load; it is applied to sin and wrongdoing because of its extreme weight upon its bearer. Mention of the backs is like the mention of hands in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾; for the customary thing is the carrying of loads upon the back, just as the familiar thing is earning by the hands. The meaning is: they feel anguish over the good deeds they did not do, while in fact they bear the burdens of the evil deeds they did.

﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) confirming what precedes it and completing it; i.e., wretched is the thing they bear as their burden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 32:

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement.﴾ Since it was established earlier that behind the life of this world there is another life in which they will encounter the calamities they will encounter, the state of those two lives in themselves is then explained. Al-La'ib (play): an activity that occupies the soul and distracts it from what benefits it; al-Lahw (amusement): diverting it from seriousness to frivolity. The meaning is either by omitting an annexed term (idafa), i.e., "the activities of this world," or by making the life of this world itself identical with play and amusement for the sake of emphasis (mubalaghah), as in the words of al-Khansa':

"For it is nothing but advance and retreat."

That is: the activities of this world, meaning the activities connected with it insofar as they are what they are, or, insofar as it is a place for earning those activities, it is nothing but play that occupies people and distracts them with its benefit that quickly vanishes and its pleasure that swiftly perishes, away from a lofty, lasting benefit and a true, unending pleasure, which is faith and righteous deeds.

﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ which is the place of the other life.

﴿is better for those who are mindful (of God)﴾ who guard against disbelief and sins, because its benefits are pure, free of harms, and its pleasures are not marred by pains, and are everlasting.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ So that you may be mindful of the disbelief and rebellion you are upon. The fa' here is for coordination with an implied element; that is: "Will you be heedless and not reason?" or "Will you not reflect so that you reason?" It was also read as "ya'qilun" (they reason) in the third person.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 33:

﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (istie'naf) brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the grief that befalls him from what is related of the disbelievers: their persistence in denial and their exaggeration in it. It shows that he, peace and blessings be upon him, holds a station with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that what they do against him ultimately returns to Him, Exalted is He, and that He will surely take vengeance upon them with the most severe vengeance.

The word "qad" (indeed) here serves to affirm the knowledge of what has been mentioned, which conveys emphasis on the threat, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿qad ya'lamu ma antum 'alayhi﴾ ("Indeed He knows what you are upon"), and His saying: ﴿qad ya'lamu Allahu al-mu'awwiqina﴾ ("Indeed Allah knows those who hinder"), and similar verses, by taking it to the meaning of multiplication (al-takthir), in the way that "rubba" is interpreted in such a verse as:

*And if you pass by the deserted courtyard, then perhaps there has stayed in it, after the delegations, a delegation.*

This follows the custom of the Arabs when they intend extreme exaggeration in multiplication. You say to one of the commanders of the armies: "How many horsemen do you have?" and he says: "Many a horseman I have, and with him are many troops," intending by that to go to excess in multiplying his horsemen; but he wishes to show his innocence of exaggeration and to demonstrate that he is one who minimizes what he has, let alone multiplying the little. To this belongs His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿rubama yawaddu alladhina kafaru law kanu muslimin﴾ ("Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims").

This manner is adopted only when the matter is so clear that no shadow of doubt truly hovers around it, as in the noble verses mentioned, or by way of claim, as in the line of verse and His saying:

*Indeed I leave the adversary with his fingertips yellowed,*

and His saying:

*But indeed his bestowal sometimes destroys wealth.*

By the abundance of His knowledge, Exalted is He, is meant the abundance of its relation (its object). It is transitive to two objects, and what follows it stands in place of both. The subject of "inna" is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate is the sentence that explains it. The relative pronoun (al-ladhi) is the subject of "yaḥzunuka," and its returning pronoun is omitted; that is, "alladhi yaqulunahu" ("that which they say"), which is what is related of them from their saying: ﴿in hadha illa asatiru al-awwalin﴾ ("This is nothing but the fables of the ancients"), and the like. It has been read as "yuḥzinuka" (with a different vowelling), from "aḥzana," which is derived from the intransitive "ḥazina."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-innahum la yukadhdhibunaka﴾ ("Indeed they do not deny you"), it is an explanation (ta'lil) for what the preceding speech implies of the prohibition against giving weight to what they said, but not by way of being occupied with it and considering it trivial, nor by way of full attention to what is more important than it, namely magnifying their rejection of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as has been said. For this, while being entirely far from consolation, gives the impression that his grief, peace and blessings be upon him, is on account of his own person. Rather, it is by way of consolation through what it conveys of his, peace and blessings be upon him, reaching the highest degree of grandeur, elevation of rank, and nearness to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to a point beyond which there is no further limit. For He did not restrict Himself to making his denial, peace and blessings be upon him, a denial of His signs, Exalted is He, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿man yuṭi'i al-rasula fa-qad aṭa'a Allah﴾ ("Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah"); rather, He negated their denial of him, peace and blessings be upon him, and affirmed it of His signs, Exalted is He, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿inna alladhina yubayi'unaka innama yubayi'una Allah﴾ ("Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to Allah"); as an indication of the utmost nearness and the dissolution of his, peace and blessings be upon him, affairs into the affair of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Indeed, there is in it a magnification of their crimes, which points to the greatness of their punishment, as if it were said: Do not give it weight, and leave it to Allah, Exalted is He, for they, in their denial of that, do not in reality deny you.

﴿But it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of Allah﴾; that is: but rather they deny His signs, Exalted is He. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to record against them that they are firmly rooted in the wrongdoing of which this denial is one of its forms.

The turning to the Majestic Name serves to cultivate awe and to magnify what they undertook of denying His signs, Exalted is He. The use of "juḥūd" (denial) in the place of "takdhib" (denial/rejection) is to make known that the signs of Allah, Exalted is He, are so clear that everyone witnesses their truth, and that whoever rejects them does so by way of jaḥd, which is a denial while knowing the contrary, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-jahadu biha wa-istayqanat-ha anfusuhum﴾ ("And they denied them while their souls had been certain of them"). This is what is meant by the saying of one who said: it is the negation of what the heart affirms, or the affirmation of what the heart negates.

The "bi" is connected to "yajhadūna" (they deny). It is said: "jahada haqqahu wa-bi-haqqihi," when he denies it while knowing it. It has been said that it is for the verb "jaḥada" being made to include the meaning of "takdhīb" (denial). Whichever is the case, the fronting of the prepositional phrase is for restriction (al-qaṣr). It has been said that the meaning is: they do not deny you in their hearts, but they deny with their tongues, and this is supported by what is related that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq said to Abu Jahl: "O Abu al-Hakam, inform me about Muhammad: is he truthful or a liar? For there is no one here but us." He said to him: "By Allah, Muhammad is truthful, and he has never lied. But when the sons of Qusayy take the banner, the watering (al-siqaya), the custodianship of the Ka'ba (al-hijaba) and prophethood, what then will remain for the rest of Quraysh?" So this was revealed.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called the Trustworthy (al-Amin), so they knew that he does not lie in anything, but they were denying."

It has been said: "they do not deny you" because you are, in their view, the truthful one known for truthfulness, "but they deny the signs of Allah," as it is related that Abu Jahl used to say to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We do not deny you, for you are truthful among us, but we deny what you have brought us"; so this was revealed.

The truthfulness of the informant in the view of the wicked is, as it were, the agreement of his report with his belief, whereas the first is what the eloquence of the revelation requires.

It has been read as "lā yukdhibūnaka" (from ikhdhāb). It is said that both have the same meaning, like "akthara" and "kaththara," and "anzala" and "nazzala," and this is the more apparent. It has been said: the meaning of "akdhabahu" is: he found him to be a liar; and it is transmitted from al-Kisa'i that the Arabs say: "kadhdhabtu al-rajula," meaning you attributed lying to him, and "akdhabtuhu," meaning you attributed lying to what he brought, not to him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 34:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed messengers were denied before you﴾ is a consolation to him, peace and blessings be upon him, for the generality of an affliction may sometimes lessen its burden to some degree. It is also a guidance to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to follow the example of the noble messengers before him, peace be upon them, in patience over the various forms of harm they suffered from their peoples; and it is an implicit promise to him, peace and blessings be upon him, of the same victory that they were granted. The opening of the statement with an oath serves to emphasize the consolation, and the tanwin on rusul (messengers) serves to magnify and multiply them. The min (from) is either connected to kudhdhibat (were denied), or to an omitted element that falls as a qualifier of rusul; that is: "By Allah, indeed messengers of great station and great number were denied before your denial, or messengers who lived in a time before your time were denied."

﴿So they were patient over what they were denied﴾: "ma" is a verbal-masdar (ma masdariyya, a particle turning the following clause into a verbal noun).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they were harmed﴾ is conjoined to kudhdhibu (they were denied), and falls under its ruling. Thus two verbal nouns in the passive are formed from the two: that is, "so they were patient over their denial and their being harmed. So follow their example and be patient over what has befallen you from your people." By their being harmed is meant either the very denial itself, or what accompanies it of various forms of harm; it was not stated explicitly, relying on the fact that denial generally entails it. Whichever it is, there is in it an emphasis on the consolation. It is said that it is conjoined to ṣabaru (they were patient), and it is said that it is conjoined to kudhdhibat (were denied), and it is said that it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until Our help came to them﴾ is a limit to the patience, and in it is an announcement that God's help to them is a settled matter with no turning back, and that it certainly must come to them. The shift to the "we" of majesty serves to highlight the concern for the matter of help.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is none who can alter the words of Allah﴾ is a parenthetical clause confirming what precedes it concerning the coming of His help to them. By the words of Allah, may He be exalted, is meant what His saying indicates: ﴿And已 indeed Our word has preceded for Our servants the messengers, that they would surely be helped, and that Our army would surely be the victors﴾ and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾, from the earlier promises to the messengers, peace be upon them, indicating the help of the Messenger of Allah as well, not the very verses mentioned nor their like.

For the announcement that they cannot be changed only indicates the non-alteration of the promises addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in particular, not the promises made earlier to the messengers, peace be upon them. It is permissible that by His words, may He be exalted, is meant all His words, of which those noble promises are a part, and that the promises addressed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, enter it in the first place.

The shift to the exalted Name is to indicate the cause of the ruling, for divinity necessitates that no one can overpower Him in any act, and that no failure occurs from Him, may He be exalted, in any statement.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ is an oath-clause brought to establish what they were granted of victory, and to confirm what is implied in it of promise to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; or to affirm all that was mentioned of the denial of the nations and what followed from it of matters.

The prepositional phrase is in the nominative position as the subject; either in consideration of its content, that is, "some of the news of the messengers," or by estimating a modified noun, that is, "some portion of the news of the messengers," as was passed in the explanation of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among people is one who says, "We believe in Allah..."﴾, the verse.

In any case, what is meant by their news, peace be upon them, on the first reading is His help to them after hardship and adversity; and on the second reading, all that took place between them and their peoples, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken...﴾, the verse.

It is said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in jā᾽a (came), referring to what is understood from the preceding sentence; that is, "And there has certainly come to you this report, being some of the news of the messengers."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 35:**

﴿And if their turning away has been grievous to you﴾ is a resumed sentence (*kalam mustaʼnaf*, a sentence beginning a new clause and not grammatically dependent on what precedes it), brought to confirm the necessity of patience that is derived from the consolation, by showing that it is a matter from which there is no escape at all. That is: if their turning away from belief in what you have brought, the noble Qur'an, has been great upon you and hard, as is made clear by what is related of them, that they called it "the fables of the ancients," and their keeping far from it and their forbidding people from it.

It is said: al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in a gathering of Quraysh and said: "O Muhammad, bring us a sign from God as the prophets used to do, and I will believe you." God refused to bring a sign of what they proposed. So they turned away from the Messenger of God (p-129), and this was grievous to him, because he (upon him be prayers and peace) was intensely eager for the belief of his people. Thus, whenever they asked for a sign, he would wish that God the Exalted would send it down, out of hope for their belief. So it was revealed.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿their turning away﴾ is in the nominative case (*marfuʻ*) as the subject of *kabura* (was grievous). The placing of the prepositional phrase before it serves, as has been mentioned repeatedly, to give importance to what is placed first and to create anticipation for what follows. The clause is in the accusative position, as it is the predicate (*khabar*) of *kana* (was), explaining its noun (*ism*), which is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-shaʼn*). There is no need to assume *qad* (indeed).

It is also said: the subject of *kana* is "their turning away," and *kabura* is a verbal clause in the accusative position, functioning as its predicate placed before its subject, because it is a verb that bears an implicit pronoun, as is well known.

According to both analyses, the Exalted's statement ﴿So if you are able...﴾ and so on is another conditional clause whose answer is omitted, and it stands as the answer to the first condition. The meaning is: if their turning away from belief in the clear proofs you have brought, and their not counting them among the signs, has been hard upon you, and you wished to answer them in what they asked as a proposal, then, ﴿if you are able﴾.

﴿to seek a tunnel﴾: that is, a passage and an outlet.

﴿in the earth﴾ by which you may penetrate into its depths.

﴿or a ladder﴾: that is, a means of ascent.

﴿to the sky﴾ by which you may climb up into it.

﴿and bring them﴾ from both of these.

﴿a sign﴾ of what they proposed; then do so. It has been permitted that their seeking both of these may be the very bringing of the sign, so the *fa'* in *fa-ta'tiyahum* is then explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), and the tanwin on *ayah* is for magnification; that is: if you are able to seek both of them, so that you make that a sign for them, then do it.

The two adverbial phrases are related to two omitted verbs, and they are descriptive qualifiers of *nafaqan* and *sullaman*. The first serves merely for emphasis, since a tunnel exists only in the earth; or they are related to *tabtaghi* (you seek).

It has also been permitted that both are related to an omitted element that serves as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the subject of *tabtaghi*; that is: that you seek a tunnel while you are in the earth, or a ladder while you are in the sky. In this there is an indication of the extreme intensity of his eagerness (upon him be prayers and peace) for the Islam of his people, and his reaching out to the point that, if he were able to bring a sign from beneath the earth or from above the sky, he would do so, hoping for their belief, which is not hidden.

The choice of *ibtigha'* (seeking) over *ittikhadh* (taking) and similar words is to indicate that what has been mentioned, the tunnel and the ladder, is something that cannot be sought at all, so how much less can it be made.

﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾: that is, if God the Exalted had willed to gather them upon the guidance that you are upon, He would have done it, by granting them success in belief so that they would believe along with you. But He did not will it, because their choice was not turned toward the side of guidance, despite their complete capacity for it through their witnessing of the signs that call to it. It is not that God the Exalted did not grant them success in it while they were turning toward attaining it.

It is said: if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon it by bringing them a sign that compels them to it; but He did not do so, because that would have been outside of wisdom.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾ is a prohibition to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the intense eagerness he had for their Islam, and from inclining toward bringing what they proposed of signs out of hope for their belief. It is consequent upon the explanation that the Exalted's will is not connected to their guidance. The meaning is: and when you know that the Exalted did not will their guidance and their belief in either of the two ways, then do not, through intense eagerness for their Islam, or inclination toward sending down their proposals, be among the ignorant of the subtleties of His affairs, of which is what has been mentioned: that His will, the Exalted's, is not connected to their belief. As for the choice, it is because they did not turn toward it; and as for compulsion, it is because it would be outside of the legislative wisdom founded upon choice.

It is also possible that by "the ignorant" in the second interpretation is meant those who make the proposals, and that by the prohibition is meant preventing him (upon him be prayers and peace) from assisting them in their proposals. Their being mentioned under the heading of ignorance rather than disbelief or the like is to realize the ground (*manat*) of the prohibition, which is the common attribute between him (upon him be prayers and peace) and them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 36:

﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾ (p-130) This is an affirmation of what has passed, that over their hearts are coverings (akinnah) preventing understanding (fiqh), and in their ears is a deafness (waqr) barring hearing, and a confirmation that by this they are among the category of the dead, from whom faith is not conceivable at all.

And al-istijabah (response) is the answering that accompanies acceptance; that is: only those who listen to what is conveyed to them with the hearing of comprehension and reflection (tadabbur) will accept your call to faith, not the dead, of whom these are among, as in His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾.

And His exalted saying: ﴿And the dead, God will raise them﴾ is an illustration of His exclusive power to grant them success in faith, by His exclusive power to raise the dead from the graves.

It has also been said: it is an explanation of their persistence in disbelief and their not desisting from it at all, on the basis that the dead are those from the graves. And it has been said: it is a metaphorical statement for the disbelievers, based on likening their ignorance to their death; that is: and these disbelievers, God the Exalted will raise them from their graves.

﴿Then to Him they will be returned﴾ for the recompense, whereupon they will respond; but before that there is no way to it. It is also read: (yarji'un) in the active form from raja'a, ruju'an; and the well-known reading is more fitting to the requirement of the context, because it indicates that their return to Him, the Exalted, is by way of compulsion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 37:

﴿And they say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?"﴾ This is a report of another of their falsehoods, following the report of what they said concerning the Noble Qur'an and the clarification of what relates to it.

The speakers are the chiefs of Quraysh. It is said that they were al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal and his companions. Their misguidance and transgression had reached the point where they were not satisfied with the clear proofs they witnessed, which would make mountains crumble, until they dared to claim that these were not among the kinds of signs, and that the signs were rather the compelling extraordinary events they had proposed, or those that bring about punishment, as they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky...﴾ to the end of the verse.

The word tanzil (sending down) means inzal (causing to descend), as indicated by the reading with the lighter form in what follows. The reference to the title of His lordship concerning him, upon him be blessings and peace, implies a cause only by way of indirect mockery on their part.

The use of the word "sign" in His saying: ﴿Say: Indeed Allah is able to send down a sign﴾, although what is meant by it is one of the extraordinary events mentioned, not just any sign, is because the meaning would otherwise be corrupt, going along with them on their assumption. It is also permissible that what is meant is a sign that necessitates their destruction, such as the sending down of angels of punishment and the like, and that its indefiniteness is for magnification and awe. Likewise, the mention of the Great Name is to nurture awe, along with what it indicates of the cause of the awe-inspiring power. The restriction in the answer to a demonstration of His exalted ability to send it down, although it is not within the scope of denial, is to signal that His not sending it down, despite His ability to do so, is for a profound wisdom that must be known, and they are heedless of it.

This is as indicated by the resumptive statement in His saying: ﴿But most of them do not know﴾; that is, they are not people of knowledge. The object is entirely omitted, or it is "they do not know anything," with the object omitted and indicated by the context. The meaning is: He, exalted, is able to send down a sign of that kind, or any sign whatsoever, but most of them do not know, so they do not realize that the non-sending of it, despite the manifest evidence of His power over it, is because in sending it there would be a uprooting of the foundation of obligation, which is based on the principle of choice, or a total annihilation of them. So they propose it out of ignorance, and they take its non-sending as a pretext for denial.

The restriction of the lack of knowledge to most of them is because some of them are aware of the true state of affairs, and they act as they do only out of obstinacy and stubbornness. (p-131)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth...﴾ etc., is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), brought to demonstrate the perfection of His power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the breadth of His governance, so that it serves as a proof that He, exalted and mighty, is able to send down the (miraculous) sign; and that He does not send it down is only out of preservation of the wise purposes (al-hikam al-baligha).

The insertion of "min" (from/any) is to emphasise totality (al-istighraq), and "fi" (on/in) is related to an omitted element which is a description of "dabbah" (creature), conveying added generality, as if it were said: "There is not a single one of the individual creatures that settles in any region of the regions of the earth."

Likewise is the addition of the description in His saying: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾, along with what it contains of added confirmation; that is: nor any bird of the birds that flies in any direction of the directions of the air with its two wings, as is observed and customary. It was also read "wa la ta'irun" (nor a bird) in the nominative, as a coordination (ʿataf) on the place (mahall) of the preposition and its object, as if it were said: "There is no creature nor bird."

﴿Except that they are communities (umam)﴾; that is, diverse groups, and the plural is according to meaning, as if it were said: "There are no beasts nor birds except that they are communities."

﴿Like you﴾; that is, each community among them is like you in that their conditions are preserved, their affairs are regulated, their interests are observed, proceeding along the path of rectitude, and ordered within the thread of the divine decrees and the lordly arrangements.

﴿We have not neglected in the Book anything﴾. It is said: "farrata al-shay'" meaning he neglected it, i.e., lost it and left it. Saʿida ibn Huwayya said: "With him is a waterskin he does not neglect to carry", i.e., he does not leave it nor part from it. It is also said: "farrata fi al-shay'", meaning he neglected what should have been in it and overlooked it.

So His saying, ﴿in the Book﴾, i.e., in the Qur'an, according to the first reading is an adverbial phrase of incidence (zarf laghw), and His saying, ﴿anything﴾, is the object of "farrartna", and "min" is an added particle for totality; that is: We have left out in the Qur'an none of the important matters, among which is the explanation that He, exalted, takes care of the interests of all His creatures as is fitting.

According to the second reading, it is the object of the verb, and "min shay'" is in the position of a verbal noun (masdar); that is: We did not make the Book one in which anything was neglected, rather We mentioned in it everything that must be mentioned. In any case, the clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) confirming the content of what precedes it.

It has also been said: "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). The purpose of the parenthetical insertion then is to indicate that the conditions of the communities are fully recorded in the Preserved Tablet, not restricted to this general summary. It was also read "faratna" with a light vowelling (takhfif).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then to their Lord they will be gathered﴾ is an explanation of the conditions of the aforementioned communities in the Hereafter after explaining their conditions in this world. The use of their pronoun in the form of the plural of rational beings is to treat them as such, and the referring to them as "communities"; that is: to their Lord, the Owner of their affairs, they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection just as you will be, not to any other, and He will recompense them, and deal justly between one of them and another, to the extent that from His justice He takes for the hornless (sheep) from the horned. It has been said: their gathering is their death, but the context of magnifying the matter and depicting the state in its terror rejects this.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 39:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied Our signs﴾ is related to His saying, Exalted is He: "We have neglected nothing in the Book," and the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is an expression referring to those previously mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you...﴾, the verses. Its position is nominative, by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is what follows it; that is: We have set forth in the Qur'an all the important matters, and by it We have removed their pretexts and excuses.

﴿Those who denied Our signs﴾ (p-132) which are part of it.

﴿Deaf﴾ they do not hear them with the hearing of reflection and understanding; therefore they call them "the fables of the ancients," and do not count them among the signs, and they demand other than them.

﴿And dumb﴾ they are unable to speak the truth, and therefore they do not respond to your call with it.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿in darknesses﴾; that is, in the darknesses of disbelief, or the darknesses of ignorance, obstinacy and blind imitation. It is either a second predicate of the subject, on the basis that it is an expression for blindness, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿deaf, dumb, blind﴾; or it is related to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun resting in the predicate, as if it were said: "astray, existing in darknesses"; or it is an attributive (sifah) of "dumb," that is: dumb, existing in darknesses.

The purpose of this is to show the completeness of their entrenchment in ignorance and their evil state. For a deaf and mute person who is sighted may perhaps understand something through the gestures of another even if he does not understand it through speech, and likewise he may convey to another what is in his mind by gesture, even if he is cut off from speech. But if, together with that, he is blind, or is in darknesses, then the door of understanding and of making understood is completely closed to him.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whomever God wills, He leads astray﴾ is a confirmation of the truth and an affirmation of what preceded concerning their state, by showing that they are among those of sealed nature from whom faith is not at all possible. So "whomever" (man) is a subject whose predicate is what follows it, and the object of the will (maf'ul al-mashi'ah) is omitted according to the established rule of its occurring as a condition, and of its object being the content of the consequent, and of the absence of strangeness in its connection to it; that is: whoever God wills to lead astray, that is, that He create misguidance in him, He leads him astray, that is, He creates it in him. But not initially by way of compulsion, without his having any involvement at all in that; rather, when his choice is directed toward his acquisition and attainment of it.

Compare with it His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whomever He wills, He places him upon a straight path﴾. One who goes toward it does not go astray, and one whose foot is firm upon it does not slip.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 6, verse 40:**

﴿Say: Tell me﴾. This is a command to the Messenger of God ﷺ to rebuke them (*tabkit*) and to put the proof into their mouths (*yulqimahum al-hajar*) with that which leaves them no way to deny it (*nakir*, denial or rebuttal). The *kaf* in *ara'aytakum* is a particle brought in to emphasize the address and has no place in grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). Although the structure is a question about seeing, whether intellectual or visual, the intended meaning is a question about its object, that is: tell me.

﴿If the punishment of God comes upon you﴾, as it came upon the earlier nations, with the various kinds of worldly punishment.

﴿Or the Hour comes upon you﴾, from which there is no escape at all.

﴿Would you call upon other than God?﴾ This is the point of the question and the focus of the rebuke.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿if you are truthful﴾: it is connected to *ara'aytakum*, emphasizes the rebuke, and reveals their lie. The answer to the conditional is omitted, relying on what has been mentioned to indicate it. That is: if you are truthful that your idols are gods, as your well-known claim is, or if you are a truthful people, then tell me: would you call upon other than God if the punishment of God comes upon you... and so on.

For their truthfulness, in whatever sense it is taken, necessitates their reporting that they call upon other than Him, glorified is He. As for making the answer what is indicated by His words, exalted is He, "﴿Would you call upon other than God?﴾", that is, "then call upon Him", with the pronoun referring to other than God, this disturbs the eloquence (*jaza'a*) of the noble composition. How could it not, when what is required of them is only to report that they call upon other than Him, exalted is He, at the time of the coming of what is anticipated, not the act of calling upon Him itself.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 41:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon a negated clause, which is clearly indicated by the clause to which the interrogation (istikhbar) is attached, as if it were said: "You call upon none other than Him, exalted is He; rather, it is Him you call upon."

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so He removes that for which you call upon Him﴾; that is, to remove it, a conjunction upon "you call upon"; that is, He removes it immediately after your supplication.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿if He wills﴾; that is, if He wills to remove it. This is to show that the acceptance of their supplication is not constant; rather, it depends on His will, which is based on hidden wisdoms of which Allah, exalted is He, has kept the knowledge to Himself. So He may accept it, as in some of their supplications concerning the removal of worldly punishment, and He may not accept it, as in some others of them, and in everything related to the removal of the punishment of the Hereafter, of which the Hour is part.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you forget what you associate﴾; that is, you abandon completely what you associate with Allah, exalted is He, of idols; a conjunction upon "you call upon" as well. The placement of the removal between the two, despite their being joined, and the delay of the removal beyond them, is to show the full importance given to the removal and to indicate that it is consequent upon supplication specifically.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly sent﴾ is a resumed statement, brought to explain that among them are those who do not call upon Allah, Exalted is He, even at the coming of the punishment, because of their persistence in misguidance and error; they are not affected by the warnings of creation (al-zawajir al-takwiniyya) any more than they are affected by the warnings of revelation (al-zawajir al-tanziliyya).

Its opening with the oath clause is to show greater concern for its content. The object of "We sent" is omitted, because the context requires explaining the condition of those to whom the messengers were sent, not the condition of the messengers; that is: "By Allah, We have certainly sent messengers."

﴿to communities﴾ many.

﴿before you﴾; that is, existing in a time before your time.

﴿Then We seized them﴾; that is, they denied their messengers, so We seized them.

﴿with adversity﴾; that is, with hardship and poverty.

﴿and affliction﴾; that is, harm and calamities. These are both feminine forms with no masculine singular.

﴿that they might humble themselves﴾; that is, in order that they would call upon Allah, Exalted is He, to remove them through humble supplication and submission, and would repent to Him from their disbelief and their sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 43:

﴿So why, when Our might came upon them, did they not humbly supplicate?﴾ That is: they did not humbly supplicate at that time, even though what calls for it had become certain.

﴿But their hearts hardened﴾ is a *istidrak* (a corrective transition, marking a contrast with what precedes it). That is: they did not humbly submit to Him, the Exalted, with softness of heart and lowliness, even though what should have moved them to it had become certain. Instead, its opposite appeared in them, since their hearts hardened, meaning they remained as they were in hardness, or their hardness increased. This is like your saying: "He did not honour me when I came to him, but he humiliated me."

﴿And Satan made attractive to them what they used to do﴾, namely of disbelief and sins. So they did not bring to mind that what afflicted them of adversity and hardship had afflicted them only because of it.

It has also been said: the *istidrak* serves to show that they had no excuse for abandoning supplication except the hardness of their hearts and their self-admiration at their deeds, which Satan had made attractive to them.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 44:

And His saying, ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, is a conjunction (*'atf*) with an implied clause to which the noble composition leads. That is: they plunged into it, and they forgot what they had been reminded of, namely the adversities and the hardships. So when they forgot it,

﴿We opened up for them the gates of everything﴾, of the various kinds of blessings, in accordance with the method of *istidraj* (gradual lure, drawing someone on step by step toward ruin), because it is related that peace and blessings be upon him (ﷺ) said: "They were deceived concerning the people, by the Lord of the Ka'bah." It is also read as *fattahna* (ﻓَتَّحْنا) with the shadda, for intensification. In the ordering of the opening upon the forgetting mentioned, there is an indication that remembering, in some degree, is not devoid of benefit.

And *ḥattā* (حَتّى, "until") in His saying, ﴿until when they rejoiced in what they had been given﴾, is the one with which speech begins. It enters upon the conditional sentence, as in His saying, ﴿until when Our command came...﴾, and its like. And it is, nevertheless, a limit (*ghayah*) for His saying, "We opened," or for what it indicates, as if it were said: so they did what they did, until, when they became content with what was made available to them and grew insolent and exultant.

﴿We seized them suddenly﴾; that is, Our punishment descended upon them unexpectedly, so that it would be more severe in its impact upon them and more dreadful in its terror.

﴿Then, behold, they were despairing﴾, grieving with the utmost grief, hopeless, utterly dejected regarding every good. The nominal sentence indicates their remaining in that dreadful state.

﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾; that is, their last ones, such that none of them was left. *Dabara-hu dabaran wa-duburan* means he followed him, that is, *tabi'ahu*. Placing the apparent noun (*al-ism al-zahir*) in the place of the pronoun (*al-damir*) serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, since their destruction was due to their wrongdoing, which is placing disbelief in the place of gratitude and placing sins in the place of acts of obedience.

﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ for what befell them of punishment. The destruction of the disbelievers and the disobedient, insofar as it is a deliverance for the people of the earth from the ill effects of their corrupt beliefs and their wicked deeds, is a great blessing that calls for praise, especially since it exalts the word of truth which their messengers, peace be upon them, proclaimed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 46:

﴿Say: "Have you considered"﴾ is a command to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to repeat the rebuke against them and to reiterate the argument after the first argument has been completed, by showing that this is a continuous matter that has always been ongoing among the nations. This is also an interrogation about the object of the sight (ru'yah), although on the surface it appears to be an interrogation about the sight itself.

﴿If Allah were to take away your hearing and your sight﴾ by making you completely deaf and blind.

﴿and seal over your hearts﴾ by covering them with something that leaves you no intellect or understanding at all, so that you become like madmen. It is also permissible for the sealing to be an explanatory conjunction (ʿatf tafsiri) for the taking mentioned above, since hearing and sight are the two paths through which what perceptible things reach the heart. Taking them away is therefore a complete closing of its door, and this is the secret behind mentioning the taking of them before the sealing of the hearts.

As for mentioning hearing before sight, it is because it is the locus of the Qur'anic verses (mawrid al-ayat al-Qur'aniyyah), and the singular form (of "hearing") is used because its root is a verbal noun (masdar).

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Who is a god﴾, it is a subject and predicate, and "who" (man) is interrogative.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿other than Allah﴾, it is an attribute of the predicate.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿who will bring it to you﴾, i.e., "bring that," where the pronoun is used in the sense of the demonstrative noun; or "with what He took away and sealed," as another attribute of it. The clause is the object of the sight and the focus of the interrogation; i.e., tell me: if Allah deprives you of your faculties, who is a god other than Him, the Exalted, who will bring them back to you?

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Observe how We vary the signs﴾, it is an expression of wonder addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at their failure to be affected by the manifest signs they witnessed; i.e., observe how We repeat them and establish them, turning them from one style to another: at times by arranging rational premises, at times by way of encouragement and warning, and at times by alerting and reminding.

﴿Yet they turn away﴾ is a conjunction upon "We vary," included in its ruling, and it is the main point of the wonder. "Yet" (thumma) is used to express the improbability of their turning away; i.e., their aversion from those signs after they have been varied in this wonderful manner that calls for attentive acceptance of them.

﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ This is another rebuke against them, forcing them to acknowledge that the punishment is specific to them.

﴿If the punishment of God comes upon you﴾: that is, His swift punishment, specific to you, as it came upon the nations before you.

﴿Suddenly﴾: that is, unexpectedly, without any signs of its coming appearing beforehand.

Since this implies the sense of being hidden, it is contrasted with His words, ﴿or openly﴾: that is, after its signs and indications have appeared. It is said that it means at night or by day, as in His words, ﴿by night or by day﴾, because what comes at night is generally sudden, and what comes by day is generally open.

It is also recited as ﴿suddenly or openly﴾ (baghtatin aw jahratin), and both are in the position of the verbal noun (masdar): that is, the coming of suddenness, or the coming of openness. Suddenness is mentioned first because it is more terrifying and more dreadful.

His words, ﴿Will any be destroyed﴾, are the object of the interrogation, and the interrogative is for affirmation: that is, say to them, affirming to them that destruction is specific to them: Tell me, if the punishment of Him, exalted is He, comes upon you as you deserve, will anyone be destroyed by that punishment except you? That is, will anyone be destroyed who does not deserve it? The phrase was placed in its position.

﴿Except the wrongdoing people﴾: recording wrongdoing against them, and announcing that the basis of their destruction is their wrongdoing, which is their placing disbelief in the place of faith.

It is also said that the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" is the category as a whole, and they enter the ruling in the first place. Al-Zajjaj said: Will anyone be destroyed except you and those like you? This is rejected by the specification of the coming of the punishment to them.

It is also said that the interrogative carries the sense of negation, so the object of the interrogation is then omitted, as if it were said: Tell me, if the punishment of Him, exalted is He, comes upon you suddenly or openly, what will be the state? Then it was said, as an explanation of that: None will be destroyed except the wrongdoing people; that is, none will be destroyed by that punishment specific to you except you. Whoever restricts destruction to the destruction of torment and wrath, in order to achieve the restriction by excluding non-wrongdoers, on the grounds that it is not by way of torment and wrath but by way of reward and elevation of rank, has neglected what is beneficial and occupied himself with what does not concern him, and has harmed the eloquence of the noble arrangement. It is also recited as ﴿Will he be destroyed﴾ from the triliteral root.

This is a resumptive statement, brought to explain the functions of the office of messengership in general, to establish what the messengers (peace be upon them) are responsible for, and to show that what the disbelievers propose to him (peace be upon him) is not at all part of messengership. The use of the present tense (*mudari'*) indicates that this is a continuous matter, one that God's custom has followed.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except as bearers of good news and warners﴾, these are two anticipated circumstantial clauses (*hal muqaddara*) relating to "the messengers." That is: We do not send them except that their giving good news and warning is anticipated. Thus both carry the sense of a final cause (*'illah ghaa'iyyah*) with certainty; that is, so that they may give their people good news of reward for obedience, and warn them of punishment for disobedience. That is, so that they may inform them of the pleasing report and the harmful report, whether worldly or otherwise, without having any role at all in the occurrence of what is reported. On this rests the restriction (*qasr*) and the argumentative imposition (*ilzam*) that the explanation of the laws and rulings is not among the functions of messengership.

The *fa'* in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever believes and does righteous deeds﴾ is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes, and *man* is a relative pronoun.
