The *fa'* in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ is due to the resemblance of the relative construction to the conditional (*shabah al-mawsul bil-shart*). That is: there is no fear for them from the punishment with which they were warned, whether worldly or otherwise, and they will not grieve over the loss of the reward, immediate or deferred, that they were given good news of. The placing of the negation of fear before the negation of grief is in observance of the requirement of the context (*maqam*). The three pronouns referring back to *man* are plural in accordance with its meaning, just as the two preceding pronouns are singular in accordance with its wording. That is: nothing befalls them that would necessitate that (fear or grief), not that something befalls them but they do not fear or grieve.

The purpose is to state the continuity of the negation of the two (fear and grief), not to state the continuity of the two. This is what the fact that the predicate in the second clause is a present-tense verb might suggest, but it has been established in its proper place that negation, even when it enters upon the present-tense verb itself, indicates continuity and persistence according to the context. Do you not see that the nominal sentence indicates, with the aid of context, the continuity of affirmation; so when the negative particle enters upon it, it indicates the continuity of negation, not the negation of continuity? Likewise, the present-tense verb free of a negative particle indicates the continuity of affirmation; when the negative particle enters upon it, it indicates the continuity of negation, not the negation of continuity. There is no difficulty in this, for your saying *ma Zaydan darabtu* ("it is not Zayd whom I struck") indicates the restriction of the negation, not the negation of restriction, as has been explained in its proper place.

The words of His, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And those who denied﴾ is a conjunction with "those who believed" (man amana), falling under its ruling.

His, Exalted is He, words: ﴿Our signs﴾ indicate that what the Messengers, upon them be peace, utter when giving glad tidings and warning, and convey to the nations, are His signs, Exalted is He; that whoever believes in it has believed in His signs, Exalted is He, and whoever denies it has denied them. In this there is a clear encouragement to belief in it and warning against denying it. The meaning is: We send the Messengers only so that they inform their peoples on Our behalf of what will befall them from Us, of matters both pleasing and harmful, not so that they bring these about independently on their own initiative, nor on Our summons so that they propose to them whatever they propose. When the matter is thus, whoever believes in what they reported on Our behalf, as glad tidings or as warning, within Our signs, and sets right what must be set right in his deeds, or enters into righteousness, then there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.

And those who denied Our signs, which they conveyed when giving glad tidings and warning, ﴿the punishment will touch them﴾; that is, the punishment they warned of, sooner or later, or the reality of punishment and its genus, which encompasses it in an initial manner.

﴿For that they used to defiantly transgress﴾; that is, because of their persistent transgression (fisq), which is persistence in departing from belief and obedience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 50:

﴿Say, "I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah."﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) built upon the divine custom (al-sunnah al-ilahiyyah, the divine way) established concerning the sending of messengers and the sending down of scriptures. It is brought to demonstrate his (ﷺ) disavowal of what their proposals revolve around. That is: say to the disbelievers who propose to you, at one time the sending down of signs and at another other things: I do not claim that the treasuries of His (Exalted is He) capabilities have been entrusted to me, to dispose of as I wish, whether independently or by request, so that you propose to me the sending down of signs, or the sending down of punishment, or the turning of mountains into gold, or other things that are not befitting to my station. To make this a disavowal of the claim to divinity is, beyond doubt, without any basis.

And His (Exalted is He) saying: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the place (mahall) of "﴿with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾"; that is: nor do I also claim that I know the unseen of His acts (Exalted is He), so that you ask me about the time of the Hour, or the time of the descent of punishment, or the like of these two.

﴿Nor do I tell you that I am an angel﴾, so that you impose upon me extraordinary acts beyond the habits of humans, which a human cannot bear, such as ascending into the sky and the like, or so that you count my not having their attributes as a flaw in my affair, as His saying indicates: ﴿What is this messenger that eats food and walks in the markets?﴾

The meaning is: I do not claim any of these three things, so that you propose to me what is among their effects and rulings, and make my not complying with that a proof of the invalidity of what I claim of messengerhood, which has no connection whatsoever with any of what has been mentioned. Rather, it is merely an expression of receiving revelation from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and acting in accordance with its requirements, as His saying indicates: ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ — not in the sense of restricting his (ﷺ) following to what is revealed to him rather than to other things, by directing the restriction (qasr) to the object in relation to another object, as is the common usage directing the restriction to what pertains to the verb, with negation in the original and affirmation in the qualifier; but rather in the sense of restricting his (ﷺ) condition to following what is revealed to him, by directing the restriction to the act itself in relation to the acts that might be attributed to him, yet not with respect to negation and affirmation together in a specific sense, for that is certainly impossible, but rather with respect to negation regarding what it includes of the bare act, and affirmation regarding what accompanies it of the specific meaning.

For every specific verb, such as "nasara" (he helped) for example, upon examination dissolves into an absolute meaning, which is the signification of the verb's word, and into a specific meaning that it embodies; its meaning is: he performed helping. What guides you to this is the saying: "So-and-so means: he gives and withholds," i.e., he performs giving and withholding. Thus the locus of the restriction in reality is what pertains to the verb, by directing negation to the bare act and affirmation to the qualifier, as if it were said: I do nothing except following what is revealed to me, without my having any involvement whatsoever in the revelation, or in what is revealed, by way of request, or in any other respect at all.

﴿Say, "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾ This is a parable for the astray and the guided in general. The interrogation is denunciatory (inkari), and the intended meaning is the denial of the equality of one who does not know the realities mentioned and one who knows them. It contains, of indication of their complete manifestness, and of aversion from error and encouragement toward guidance, what is not hidden. And the repetition of the command is for the sake of a second rebuke and the emphasis of the obligation.

And His saying: ﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ is a reproach and rebuke falling under the command. The "fa" (then) is for conjunction upon an implied element required by the context; that is: Do you not hear this true speech, so that you do not reflect upon it? Or: Do you hear, yet do not reflect upon it? So the basis of the rebuke in the first is the absence of both matters together, and in the second the absence of reflection together with the realization of what necessitates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 51:

﴿And warn thereby those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾ after it was related to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that among the disbelievers there is a people who do not take heed from the clear display of the signs, and are not affected by witnessing the overpowering miracles. Their faculties have been utterly corrupted and they have joined the dead. He confirmed this by repeating upon them various kinds of rebuke and obligation, which silence them with a complete silencing, yet they refused except to refuse and deny. Admonition did not benefit them and warning only increased their persistence in denial. He (upon whom be blessings and peace) was commanded to direct the warning to those from whom some effect can be expected in general, namely those who consider the gathering (to be possible) in the manner that will come, whether they are firm in its principle, like the People of the Book and some of the polytheists who acknowledge resurrection but waver regarding the intercession of their forefathers, the prophets (upon them be blessings and peace), as the first group does, or regarding the intercession of the idols, as the latter group does, or who waver about both together, like some disbelievers whose condition shows that when they hear the report of resurrection they fear it may be true. As for those who deny the gathering outright, and those who affirm it but firmly hold to the intercession of their forefathers or the intercession of the idols, they are excluded from those commanded to be warned.

It has been said: they are the negligent believers in deeds. But the context and flow of the noble arrangement do not support this, and indeed there is in it what necessitates the impossibility of its correctness, as you will come to know.

The pronoun in "bihi" (thereby) refers to what is revealed, or to what it indicates of the Qur'an, and the second object of "andhir" (warn) is either the otherworldly punishment indicated by what lies in the scope of the relative clause, or the absolute punishment that the threat has been reported with. The mention of the title "Lord" (rububiyyah), which indicates absolute ownership and total disposal, serves to cultivate awe and establish fear.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿yuḥsharū﴾ (they will be gathered). The word ﴿min﴾ (besides) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from the subject of "laysa" (there is not), because it was originally an attribute of it; when it was placed before it, it took the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Except that the first circumstantial clause is to exclude the gathering that is not qualified by it from the scope of fear, and to establish that what fear is attached to is the gathering in that state, not the gathering in any form, since those who acknowledge it while firmly holding to the support of other than Him are in the same position as those who deny it regarding the absence of the fear upon which the matter of warning revolves.

As for the second circumstantial clause, it is not to exclude the protector, which was not qualified by it, from the scope of negation, because affirming His guardianship over them would corrupt the meaning, as in His saying: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides God﴾. Rather, it is to establish the basis of their fear, which is the loss of what they pinned their hope on, and that is only the guardianship of other than Him, glorified and exalted, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of God, he cannot escape in the earth, and he has no protectors besides Him﴾.

The meaning: warn with it those who fear that they will be gathered without being aided by their helpers, according to their supposition. From this it becomes clear that there is no way for the intended "those who fear" to be the negligent believers, since they have no protector other than Him, exalted is He, for them to fear the gathering without His help. What they fear is only the gathering without His help, mighty and majestic is He.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that they may fear God (la'allahum yattaqūn)﴾ is a reason for the command, meaning: warn them so that they may avoid disbelief and sins; or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the command, meaning: warn them while hoping for their piety; or from the relative pronoun, meaning: warn them, piety being hoped for from them.

And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to warn those mentioned so that they would be included among the God-fearing, he was forbidden from doing anything that would lead to driving them away.

It is narrated that some of the chiefs of the polytheists said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "If you were to drive away these slaves and the stinking ones among them," meaning the poor Muslims such as Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Salman, and their like, may God be pleased with them all, "we would sit with you and converse with you." He (ﷺ) said: "I will not drive away the believers." They said: "Then remove them from us when we come, and when we rise, seat them with you if you wish." He (ﷺ) said: "Yes," hoping for their faith.

It is also narrated that Umar, may God be pleased with him, said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: "If you did so, until we see what they become."

It was also said that Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Mut'im ibn Adi, al-Harith ibn Nawfal, Qurra ibn Ubayd, Amr ibn Nawfal, and the nobles of the Banu Abd Manaf from among the people of disbelief came to Abu Talib and said: "O Abu Talib, if your nephew Muhammad drove away our clients and allies, who are our slaves and freedmen, he would be greater in our eyes and closer to our following him." So Abu Talib came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and related to him what they had said. Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: "If you did that, until we see what they want and what they become."

Salman and Khabbab said: "This verse was revealed concerning us. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi, Uyayna ibn Hisn al-Fazari, Abbas ibn Mirdas, and their kinsmen from among those whose hearts were to be reconciled (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum) came, and they found the Prophet (ﷺ) sitting with some weak believers. When they saw them around him (ﷺ), they belittled them, so they came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and said: 'O Messenger of God, if you were to sit at the head of the gathering and remove these people from us, along with their stinking garments, then we would sit with you, converse with you, and take from you.' He (ﷺ) said: 'I will not drive away the believers.' They said: 'Then we wish that you would make for us a gathering with you by which the Arabs would recognize our merit, for the delegations of the Arabs come to you, and we are ashamed that they should see us with these slaves. So when we come to you, remove them from us, and when we have finished, sit with them if you wish.' He (ﷺ) said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Then write a document for us.' He called for the parchment and for Ali, may God be pleased with him, to write it, while we sat in a corner. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended with the verse, so he (ﷺ) cast the parchment aside and called us. We came to him and sat near him, and we used to draw so close to him that our knees would touch his knee, and when he wished to rise, he would rise and leave us. Then this was revealed: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord﴾. So he left off rising from us until we would rise from him, and he said: 'Praise be to God who has not taken me until He commanded me to keep myself patient with a people from my community, with you is my life and with you is my death.'"

The mention of the two times is meant to convey constancy. It was also said that they refer to the dawn and afternoon prayers. It has been read as (bil-ghudwa).

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿seeking His Face﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "call upon," meaning: they call upon Him, Exalted is He, sincere to Him in it. Restricting it to this serves to emphasize the causal reason for the prohibition, for sincerity is among the strongest factors calling for honor, which is contrary to driving away.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You are not accountable for their reckoning in anything﴾, is a parenthetical clause placed between the prohibition and its response, to affirm it and to repel what might be imagined as a justification for driving them away from the objections of those who criticize their religion, as was the case with the people of Noah, when they said: ﴿And we see none following you except the lowest of us, at first glance﴾. That is: you are not responsible in any way for the reckoning of their faith and their inner deeds, so that you would take it upon yourself and build upon it the rulings you see. Your duty, as is the nature of the station of prophethood, is only to consider outward deeds and to apply rulings according to what they require. As for the inner realities of affairs, their reckoning belongs to the One who knows what is in the breasts, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their reckoning is only upon my Lord﴾.

As for the mention of His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Nor are you accountable for their reckoning in anything﴾, even though the answer was complete with what preceded it, it serves to intensify the explanation of the negation of their reckoning being upon him (ﷺ), by placing it in a series with what has no doubt at all, namely the negation of his (ﷺ) reckoning being upon them, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They cannot delay an hour nor advance it﴾.

As for what has been said, that this is to treat the two sentences as one sentence serving one meaning, in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾, this is unworthy of the dignity of the revelation. The placement of "upon you" in the first sentence is for the purpose of directing the negation toward the exclusivity of their reckoning to him (ﷺ), since that is what calls him to take on their reckoning.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: you will not be held accountable for their reckoning, so that their faith would concern you and the eagerness for it would call you to drive away the believers.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so that you would drive them away﴾ is the response to the negation.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is the response to the prohibition. It has been permitted to take it as conjoined to "so that you would drive them away" in the manner of causation, but that is not the right view.

﴿Thus We tested some of them through others﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what resulted from the preceding prohibition. "Thus" (dhalika) refers to the source (masdar) of the action that follows it, which is His, exalted be He, giving precedence to the poor believers in matters of religion by granting them guidance to faith, (p-140) together with their state of utter misfortune in worldly affairs, and the sense of distance in the demonstrative, indicating the high rank of that action and the remoteness of its status in perfection.

The kaf (the "like" particle) is superfluous (muqhamah), serving to emphasize the grandeur already conveyed by the demonstrative noun. Originally its position is accusative, as an attribute (na't) of an omitted emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid). The estimated sense is: "We tested some of them through others with a testing like that testing." Then it was placed before the verb to convey restriction (qasr), which implies that the testing was not deficient only. The kaf is treated as superfluous, so the phrase becomes the emphatic verbal noun itself rather than its attribute. The meaning is: "That complete and wondrous testing is what We inflicted," that is, We tested some people through others, and no other kind of testing; in that We placed the latter (al-akhirin) ahead of the former (al-awwalin), who had precedence over them in worldly matters, with a total precedence.

The lam in His saying, ﴿so that they would say﴾, indicates consequence (lam al-'aqibah). That is, the first ones said, pointing to the latter ones, belittling them in view of the vast worldly disparity between them, and disregarding what is in truth the criterion of preference.

﴿Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?﴾ That is, by guiding them to the truth, while He has not granted them felicity with Him in preference to us, though we are the eminent ones and the leaders, and they are the slaves and the poor. Their purpose by this is to deny that any favor had occurred at all, following the line of their saying: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ It is not a belittling of those upon whom favor was bestowed while acknowledging its occurrence, by way of objecting against Him, exalted be He.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of the grateful?﴾ is a refutation of their statement and an invalidation of it, and an indication that the basis of deserving bounty is knowing the worth of the blessing and acknowledging the right of the Benefactor. The interrogative serves to affirm His complete knowledge of this; that is: Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful for His blessings, so that you find it strange that He bestowed His favor upon them?

It also contains an indication that those weak ones recognize the right of Allah's blessings in the revelation of the Qur'an and the granting of faith, and that they are thankful to Him for that, while implicitly suggesting that those who speak are far removed from all of that, which is not hidden.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 54:

﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you﴾: they are the ones who were forbidden to be driven away. They are described as believing in the signs of Allah, mighty and majestic, just as they are described as persevering in His worship with sincerity. This is an alert to their having gained both the virtue of knowledge ('ilm) and the virtue of action ('amal). The mention of this description after the first description, although it precedes it, is because the basis of the promise of mercy and forgiveness is belief in them, just as the basis of the prohibition of driving away in what came before is perseverance in worship.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Peace be upon you﴾: this is a command to give them the good news of safety from every hateful thing after warning their opponents. It has been said: it means to convey to them the peace of Him, exalted is He. It has also been said: it means that he should begin them with the greeting of peace.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy﴾: that is, He decreed it and made it obligatory upon His holy Essence, by way of bounty and benevolence, directly, without any intermediary whatsoever. This is good news for them of the vastness of His mercy, exalted is He, and of attaining their desires following the good news to them of safety from hateful things, and of His accepting their repentance.

In mentioning the title of Lordship together with the addition to their pronoun there is a manifestation of kindness toward them and an indication of the reason for the ruling.

It has been said: some people came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "We have committed great sins," and he did not respond. This is an explanation of the mercy by way of resumption (isti'naf).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in ignorance﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of the verb "did" ('amila); that is, he did it while being ignorant of the reality of the harms that follow from it. The restriction by this is to indicate that the believer does not engage in what he knows leads to harm, or that he did it while mixed with ignorance.

﴿Then he repented after it﴾: that is, after his action, or after his folly.

﴿and amended﴾: that is, what he corrupted, making amends and resolving never to return to it.

﴿then indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: that is, his affair is that He is Forgiving and Merciful, or for him there is that He is Forgiving and Merciful. It is also read ﴿fa-innahu﴾ with a kasra, on the basis that it is a resumption occurring at the beginning of the clause that is the predicate of "man" (who), taking it as a relative pronoun, or a response to it taking it as a conditional.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 55:

﴿And thus do We detail the signs﴾. What is involved in this discourse has already passed a moment ago; that is, this wondrous detailing: We detail the signs concerning the description of the people of obedience and the people of criminality, both those among them who persist (in it) and those who turn back in repentance.

﴿And that the way of the criminals may become clear﴾, with the verb in the feminine form on the basis that its subject (al-sabil, "the way") is feminine. It has also been read in the masculine, on the basis that it is masculine, for al-sabil is among the nouns that may be treated as masculine or feminine. The clause is coordinated (ʿatf, "conjunction") with a deleted causal clause (ʿillah, "reason") attached to the verb mentioned, the specific causation not being intended by it; rather, the purpose is to indicate that it has many benefits, of which what has been mentioned is one. Alternatively, it is a reason (ʿillah) for a presumed verb which is an expression for what has been mentioned, in which case it is a new independent clause; that is: and that their way may become clear, We do what We do of detailing. It has also been read with the accusative of "al-sabil" (sabila), on the basis that the verb is transitive and its ta' is for the second person address; that is: and that you, O Muhammad, may clarify the way of the criminals, so that you deal with them in what befits them.

﴿Say: "Indeed I have been forbidden﴾ He (ﷺ) was commanded to return to addressing those who persisted in polytheism, after he had been commanded to deal with everyone else among the people of warning and glad tidings in the manner befitting their condition. That is: say to them, cutting off their empty hopes of his (ﷺ) inclining towards them, and making clear that the religion they hold is pure caprice and utter misguidance: "Indeed I have been turned away and restrained by the proofs set up for me and by the signs sent down to me concerning the matter of monotheism."

﴿to worship those whom you invoke﴾; that is, from worshipping what you worship.

﴿besides God﴾, whatever they may be.

﴿Say﴾: the command is repeated despite the closeness of the context, either out of concern for the importance of the thing commanded, or to signal the difference between the two statements. The first is a report of the prohibition from His part, may He be exalted, and the second is a report of his (ﷺ) cessation, on his part, from what was mentioned of worshipping what they worship.

It was said: ﴿"I will not follow your desires"﴾ to make them appear foolish and to state explicitly that in what they are engaged in they follow vain desires, and are not upon anything that could truly be called religion at all, and as an indication of what makes the prohibition and the cessation necessary.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"Then indeed I would have gone astray"﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) emphasizing his cessation from what he was forbidden, and affirming that they are in the utmost degree of error and perdition; that is: if I were to follow your desires, then I would have gone astray.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"And I am not among the guided"﴾ is coordinated (ataf) with what precedes it, and the shift to the nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) indicates permanence and continuity; that is, the permanence and continuance of the negation, not the negation of permanence and continuance, as has been stated many times; that is: I am not, in any respect, of the guidance at the time I would be among them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 57:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed I am upon clear evidence⁠﴾ is a confirmation of the truth upon which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stands, and a statement of his following it after the refutation of the falsehood upon which the disbelievers stand, and a statement of their not following it. The bayyinah (clear proof) is the manifest argument that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and what is meant by it is the Qur'an and the revelation. It has been said that it is the rational proofs, or what encompasses them, but the context does not support this. The tanwin (nunation) is for magnification (tafkhim).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from my Lord⁠﴾ is connected to an omitted element which is an attribute of bayyinah, confirming what the tanwin conveyed of intrinsic magnificence with extrinsic magnificence. In mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) there is an honour and elevation of rank that is not hidden.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you have denied it⁠﴾ is either a resumed sentence (jumlah mustanifah) or a circumstantial clause (haliyyah) with the implied qad (قد), or without it. It is brought to express the abhorrence of its content and the improbability of its occurrence despite the existence of what requires its non-occurrence, namely the utmost clarity of the bayyinah. The pronoun in the genitive refers to the bayyinah, and the masculine form is according to the intended meaning. The meaning is: I am upon a great bayyinah from my Lord, and you have denied it and what it contains of reports, among which is the threat of the coming of punishment.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What I have is not what you seek to hasten⁠﴾ is a resumed sentence explaining their error concerning what they made the source of their denial of it, which is the non-arrival of the punishment promised in it, which they were seeking to hasten by their saying: ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?⁠﴾ — by way of mockery, or by way of challenge according to their claim. That is: what you seek to hasten of the punishment promised in the Qur'an is not in my hands, and you make its delay a pretext for denying it, as though it were in my judgment and power, until I bring it and show you its truth; or its affair is not entrusted to me.

﴿The decision belongs only to⁠﴾ — that is: there is no judgment in that, whether in hastening or delaying, or there is no judgment in all things, so that what has been mentioned enters it by primary inclusion.

﴿Allah⁠﴾ alone, without anyone else having any share in it in any way whatsoever.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He relates the truth⁠﴾ — that is, He follows it — is an explanation of His affairs, exalted is He, in the judgment of the known matter, or in all His judgments that are included under it by primary inclusion; that is: He does not judge except by what is true, so He establishes the reality of the delay.

It is read (yaqdi) [He decides], and the accusative of al-haqq (the truth) is then either as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: He decides the decision that is true; or as an object (maf'ul), meaning: He fashions the truth and arranges it, from their saying: qada al-dir'a (he made the coat of mail) when he fashioned it. The root of qada' (decision) is separation with the completion of the matter, and the root of hukm (judgment) is restraint, as if He restrains falsehood from opposing the truth, or restrains the adversary from transgressing against his companion.

﴿And He is the best of deciders⁠﴾ is a concluding parenthetical clause confirming the content of what precedes it, indicating that relating the truth here is in a specific manner, namely the separation between truth and falsehood; this is what the eloquence of the revelation requires.

It has also been said: the meaning is: I am, through my knowledge of my Lord and that there is no deity other than Him, upon a clear proof and a witness of truth, and you have denied it by associating others with Him, exalted is He.

And you know well that the course of the noble arrangement, both before and after, is upon describing them with denying the signs of Allah, exalted is He, because of the non-arrival of the punishment promised in them; so their denial of Him, glorified is He, regarding the matter of monotheism is something that has no connection to the context at all.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 58:

﴿Say: If what you are hastening for were in my power﴾; i.e., within my capacity and ability.

﴿What you are hastening for﴾, namely the punishment that the threat has announced, such that its command would be entrusted to me by Him, exalted is He.

﴿The matter would have been decided between me and you﴾; i.e., that it would descend upon you immediately after your hastening, by your saying: ﴿When is this promise?﴾ and its like.

As for the building of the verb in the passive voice, its benefits are not hidden: it signals that the agent is specifically Allah, exalted is He, it conveys the gravity of the matter, and it observes good manners. Therefore, what has been said in its interpretation, "I would have destroyed you swiftly out of anger for my Lord, and I would have quickly rid myself of you," is far from doing justice to the station of the verse.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah knows best the wrongdoers﴾, is a parenthetical clause confirming what the conditional sentence conveys: that the command of punishment is not entrusted to him, peace and blessings be upon him, which entails that the matter is not decided. It also serves as a reason for that. The meaning: (p-143) And Allah, exalted is He, knows best the state of the wrongdoers, and that they deserve to be given respite by way of gradual enticement, so that the punishment may be intensified. For this reason He did not entrust the command to me, so He did not decide the matter by hastening the punishment. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 59:

﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen (mafatih al-ghayb)﴾ is an explanation of the exclusivity of the unseen matters (al-maqdurat al-ghaybiyyah) to Him, glorified is He, in respect of knowledge, following the explanation of the exclusivity of all of them to Him, glorified is He, in respect of power.

As for al-mafatih (keys): it is either the plural of maftah, with a fatha on the mim, which means the storehouse (makhzan). In that case it is a metaphor for the place of the unseen, as though they were storehouses in which the unseen matters are stored, locked and unlocked. Or it is the plural of miftah, with a kasra on the mim, which means the key (miftah). This is supported by the reading of the one who read (mafatiyh al-ghayb), so it is a metaphor for that by which one reaches those matters, based on the first metaphor. That is: with Him, glorified is He, alone are the treasuries of His unseen things, or that by which one reaches them.

As for His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿None knows them but He﴾, it is an emphasis of the content of what precedes it, and an announcement that the intended meaning is exclusivity in respect of knowledge, not in respect of power. The meaning is: what you seek to hasten of the punishment is not within my power, so that I could compel you to hasten it, nor is it known to me, so that I could inform you of the time of its descent. Rather, it is among the things exclusive to Him, glorified is He, in power and knowledge, so He sends it down as His will requires, which is founded on wisdoms and interests.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾, it is an explanation of the relation of His knowledge, exalted is He, to the observable things, following the explanation of its relation to the unseen things, as a completion of it, and an alert that all of them are equal with respect to His all-encompassing knowledge in clarity. That is: He knows the existing things in them, detailed according to the variety of their kinds and types and the multiplicity of their individuals.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾, it is an explanation of His relation to their changing states, following the explanation of His relation to their essences. The mention specifically of the state of falling is only by way of sufficing with it over mention of all the other states, just as the mention of the state of the leaf and what is conjoined to it specifically, rather than the states of all the other kinds of existing things in them, is restricted to it, on the basis that it is a model for the states of all the rest.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor a grain﴾, it is conjoined to "leaf."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In the darknesses of the earth﴾, it is related to an elided element which is an attribute of "grain," conveying the perfection of the penetration of His knowledge, exalted is He. That is: nor a grain existing in the depths of the earth, but He knows it.

Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor anything moist or dry﴾, the two are conjoined to it and included in its ruling.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that it is in a clear Book﴾, it is a substitution for the first exception, a substitution of the whole, on the basis that the clear Book is an expression for His knowledge, or a substitution of inclusion, on the basis that it is an expression for the Preserved Tablet.

The last two were read in the nominative, conjoined to the position (mahall) of "min waraqah." It was said: their nominative is by inception (ibtida'), and the predicate is "except in a clear Book." This is the more suitable to the context, since it includes the moist and the dry in that case, including what is not of the nature of falling. The nominative reading has also been transmitted for "wa la habbatun" as well.

﴿And it is He who takes you in death by night﴾; that is, He puts you to sleep therein, using the metaphor of *tawaffi* (taking in full) for *inama* (causing to sleep), because death and sleep share the cessation of awareness and discernment. Its original meaning is the seizing of a thing in its entirety.

﴿And He knows what you have committed (*jarahtum*) by day﴾; that is, what you have earned (*kasabtum*) (p-144) therein. What is meant by night and day is the category (*jins*) realized in each of their individual instances through the *tawaffi* and the *ba'th* (raising up) that occur in them. The fulfilment of the appointed term (*ajal musamma*), which is consequent upon them, is realized through them collectively, not in only some of them.

What is meant by God's knowledge (*'ilm*) here is His knowledge prior to the committing (of the deeds), as is hinted at by the mention of it being placed before the raising up. That is: He knows what you commit by day. The use of the past tense form signifies certainty. The restriction of the *tawaffi* to night and of the committing to day, although each of them occurs in what is specified for the other, follows the customary course of things.

﴿Then He raises you up therein﴾; that is, He wakes you in the day. It is conjoined (*'atf*) to "He takes you in death." The interposition of God's words "and He knows..." etc. between them serves to explain the great benefit (*ihsan*) to them in their being raised up, by alerting to the fact that the evil deeds they earn, although they would warrant keeping them in the state of *tawaffi* — indeed their outright destruction — He bestows life upon them and grants them respite. This is indicated by the particle of delay (*thumma*), as if it were said: "It is He who takes you in death during the nights in general, then raises you up during the days in general, while knowing what you will commit therein."

﴿That an appointed term (*ajal musamma*) may be fulfilled﴾, specified for each individual, such that no one can overstep what has been appointed for him even for the blink of an eye.

﴿Then to Him is your return﴾; that is, your return through death, not to anything else at all.

﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, by requiting you for your deeds which you used to perform during those nights and days.

It has been said: the address is specific to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: you are cast down like carrion at night, earning sins by day; and He, exalted is He, is aware of your deeds, and God raises you from the graves concerning what you have consumed of your lifespans through sleep at night and the earning of sins by day, so that the term He has named and set for the resurrection of the dead and their recompense for their deeds may be fulfilled. Within this there is what is not hidden of artificiality (*takalluf*) and deficiency (*ikhlal*), since it leads to the resurrection being made dependent upon the fulfilment of the term set for it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 61:**

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾; that is: He alone disposes of their affairs, doing with them whatever He wills, bringing into existence and annihilating, giving life and causing death, punishing and rewarding, and so on.

﴿And He sends over you﴾, specifically you who are responsible (mukallafun).

﴿Guardians﴾ from among the angels, who are the noble scribes (al-kiram al-katibun). The phrase ʿalaykum (over you) is connected to yursilu (He sends), because it contains the sense of dominance (al-istila'), and its placement before the direct object is for the reason that has been mentioned repeatedly: attention to what is placed first and arousing anticipation for what comes later.

It has also been said that it is connected to a omitted verb which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of ḥafaẓatan (guardians); for if it came after, it would be a qualifier (ṣifa); that is: "being over you."

It has also been said that it is connected to ḥafaẓatan, and the object guarded (al-mahfuz) is omitted in every case; that is: He sends over you angels who guard your deeds, whatever they may be. In this there is a beautiful wisdom and a magnificent blessing, since when the responsible person knows that his deeds are guarded for him and will be displayed before the heads of witnesses, that is more restraining for him from engaging in sins and vile acts. And when a servant trusts in the gentleness of his master and relies on his pardon and concealment, he does not feel the same shame before him as he would feel before his servants who witness his circumstances.

And "ḥattā" (until) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿until when death comes to one of you﴾ is the particle with which a sentence is begun, and yet it makes what follows it in the conditional clause an endpoint for what precedes it, as if it were said: "He sends over you guardians who guard your deeds for the duration of your lives, until when the term of one of them ends, whoever he may be, and the causes and beginnings of death come to him."

﴿our messengers take him in death﴾: the others, to whom that task is entrusted, namely the Angel of Death and his assistants; and the guarding of the guardians ends there. It has been read as "tawaffahu" (in the past tense), or as a present-tense verb with one of the two tas dropped.

﴿and they﴾; that is: the messengers.

﴿do not fail﴾; that is: through negligence or delay. It has been read in the form with the lightening (mukhaffaf) from al-ifrat (excess); that is: (p-145) they do not exceed what has been prescribed for them by an increase or a decrease. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) of "our messengers." It has also been said that it is a new independent clause brought to explain their care for what they were commanded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 62:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they are returned﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "tawaffathu" (takes them in death), and the pronoun refers to the totality implied by "one of you" (aḥadakum). This is the secret of its coming by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), by way of prevalence (taghlīb): the singular is used first and the plural last, because the taking in death occurs individually while the returning occurs collectively. That is, ﴿then they are returned﴾ after resurrection (al-baʿth) by gathering (al-ḥashr).

﴿To Allah﴾; that is, to His judgment and His recompense at the station of reckoning.

﴿their true Master (mawlāhum)﴾; that is, their owner, who manages their affairs absolutely, not their helper, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that the disbelievers have no mawlā﴾.

﴿the Truth (al-ḥaqq)﴾, who does not judge except with justice. It was also read in the accusative (al-ḥaqqa) as a form of praise.

﴿Indeed, to Him belongs the judgment﴾ on that Day, in form and in meaning, belonging to no one else in any respect whatsoever.

﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾: He reckons all creatures in the swiftest and shortest time, no matter of reckoning preoccupies Him from another, nor one affair from another. And in the hadith: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, reckons all of them in the time it takes to milk a sheep."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 63:

﴿Say: "Who rescues you from the darknesses of the land and the sea?"﴾; that is: say, as a means of making them acknowledge the lowliness of their partners from the rank of divinity: "Who rescues you from their dreadful hardships, which nullify the senses and bewilder the minds?" For this reason, the darknesses, which nullify the faculty of sight, have been used metaphorically for them. It is said of a severe day: "a dark day" and "a day full of stars." Or [the darknesses are] of being swallowed up by the earth on land and of drowning at sea. It has also been read as ﴿yunjīkum﴾ (from al-injā' [the causative form]), and the meaning is one.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿tadʿūnahu﴾ (you call upon Him), it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the object of yunajjīkum, and the pronoun refers to "who"; that is: "Who rescues you from them while you are calling upon Him?" Or it is from its subject; that is: "Who rescues you from them while He is being called upon by you?"

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿taḍarruʿan wa-khufyah﴾ (in humility and in secret), it is either a circumstantial clause from the subject of tadʿūnahu, or an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar) for it; that is: you call upon Him humbly, both openly and secretly, or you call upon Him with a call of declaration and concealment. It has also been read as ﴿khifyah﴾ with a kasra on the kha'.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿la-in anjaytanā﴾ (If You rescue us), it is also a circumstantial clause from the subject, on the assumption of a verb of saying; that is: you call upon Him, saying: "If You rescue us."

﴿from this﴾ hardship and peril, which has been expressed by "darknesses."

﴿we will surely be among the thankful﴾; that is: those firmly established in gratitude, persevering in it for the sake of this blessing, or for all the blessings of which this is one. It has also been read as ﴿la-in anjānā﴾, in consideration of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿tadʿūnahu﴾.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 64:

﴿Say: "It is Allah who delivers you from them and from every distress."﴾ He (ﷺ) was commanded to state the answer himself, even though it is among their own duties to do so, to make clear that it is [already] settled in their minds, and so that the following words of the Exalted, ﴿Yet you associate partners [with Him]﴾, may be built upon it. The meaning is: Allah alone delivers you from what you call upon Him to remove of the aforementioned hardships and of other anxieties and distresses. Then, after you witness these magnificent blessings, you associate others with Him in worship. It is also read: (yunjīkum) with the lightened form (takhfīf).(p-146)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 65:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: He is the One able to send upon you a punishment﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) brought to explain that He, exalted is He, is the One able to cast them into ruin, following the explanation that He is the One who delivers them from it. In it there is an implicit threat of punishment for their associating partners (shirk), which is mentioned, in the manner of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do you then feel secure that He will not cause the earth to swallow you from the side of the land﴾ up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will not return you into it another time?﴾ ... the verse.

"Upon you" (ʿalaykum) is connected to yabʿatha (send), and its placement before its direct object is for the sake of giving it attention, hastening to explain that what is sent is something that will harm them, and to magnify the matter of what is deferred.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from above you﴾ is also connected to it, or to a deleted element that stands as a qualifier of ʿadhaban (punishment); that is: a punishment coming from the direction of above, as He did to those among the people of Lot who did so, and the companions of the Elephant, and their likes.

﴿Or from beneath your feet﴾, or from the direction of the lower part, as He did to Pharaoh and Qarun. It has been said: "from above you" means your elders and your leaders, and "from beneath your feet" means your common folk and your slaves.

The word "or" (aw) is for preventing vacancy (al-khuluww) but not for preventing combination, so there is no prohibition against what comes from both directions together, as was done to the people of Noah.

﴿Or cause you to be confused in sects (shiya'an)﴾; that is, mix you into factions, divided over various desires, each faction following a leader, so that fighting breaks out among you, and you become intermingled in the battles, like the saying of the poet of the Hamasa (al-Hamasi):

"And a host I mixed with a host, until, when they became confused, I shook my hand against them."

﴿and make some of you taste the violence of others﴾ is a conjunction with yabʿatha. It has been read with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azama), in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to magnify the matter and to intensify the warning.

The first "some" refers to the disbelievers, and the second to the believers; thus there is in it both promise and threat. From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that when he reached His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿a punishment from above you﴾", he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." And when he reached His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿or from beneath your feet﴾", he said: "I seek refuge in Your Face." And when he reached His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿or cause you to be confused in sects and make some of you taste the violence of others﴾", he said: "This is easier, or this is lighter."

And from him (ﷺ), that he said: "I asked my Lord that He not send upon my Ummah a punishment from above them or from beneath their feet, and He granted me that; and I asked Him that He not make their violence among themselves, and He refused me that."

﴿Look how We vary the signs﴾ from one state to another.

﴿That perhaps they may understand﴾: so that they may understand, and stand upon the clarity of the matter, and so return from what they are upon of obstinacy and stubbornness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 66:

﴿And your people denied it﴾; that is: the obstinate ones among them denied the promised punishment, or the glorious Qur'an which declares its coming.

﴿your people﴾; that is: the obstinate among them. The mention of them with this designation is probably to announce the utter wickedness of their state, for their denial of it, despite being from his people (ﷺ), indicates the extreme of their insolence and stubbornness. The placement of the prepositional phrase before the subject (the agent), as has been mentioned many times, serves to show concern with what is fronted and to create suspense toward what is delayed.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿while it is the truth﴾ are a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase; that is: they denied it, while it is the reality that will certainly occur, or that it is the Book that is truthful in everything it declares. It has been said: it is a resumptive (isti'nāf) clause. Whichever is the case, it indicates the magnitude of their offense and the extreme of its ugliness.

﴿Say﴾ to them, as a warning about what their affair will come to, and that you have fulfilled what is incumbent upon you of the duties of messengership.

﴿I am not a guardian over you﴾, that is, a keeper, to whom your affair has been entrusted, so that I may prevent you from denial and compel you to belief. I am only a warner, and I have discharged the obligation, since I have informed you of what you will see.

For every news there is a fixed time (mustaqarr). That is: for everything that is announced, among the reports of which your punishment is one, or for every piece of information among the reports of which is the information of its coming.

"A fixed time" means a time of settling and of actual occurrence without fail, and a time of settling by the occurrence of what it signifies.

"And you will come to know": that is, you will come to know the outcome of your news in this world, or in the Hereafter, or in both together. "Sawfa" (soon/surely) here is for emphasis, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a while﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 68:

﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk about Our verses﴾; that is, by denying them, mocking them, and disparaging them, as is the habit and custom of the Quraysh.

﴿then turn away from them﴾ by abandoning sitting with them and rising up from them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they engage in talk about something other than it﴾ is the limit of the turning away; that is: persist in turning away until they engage in talk other than Our verses. The masculine reference (in "ghayrihi," "other than it") is in view of the verses being a "speech" (hadith), for describing speech as different from them points to considering them under the title of speech. It has been said that it is in view of them being the Qur'an.

﴿And if Satan causes you to forget﴾ by occupying you so that you forget the prohibition, and you sit with them, either at the outset or continuing. It is also read "yunassiyannaka" (causing you to forget) from tanasi (the causative form).

﴿then do not sit, after the reminder﴾; that is, after you have recalled the prohibition.

﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾; that is, with them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to censure them, that by that engagement they are wrongdoers, placing denial and mockery in the place of affirmation and reverence, and firmly persisting in that.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 69:

﴿And there is not upon those who fear Allah﴾ It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that when the Muslims were forbidden to sit with them while they engaged in discourse about the verses, they said: "If we were to do so, whenever they mock the Qur'an we would not be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque and circumambulate the House." So it was revealed. That is: there is nothing upon those who fear (yattaqun) the ugly deeds and states of those who engage in such discourse.

﴿of their accountability﴾; that is: of what they are held to account for of the sins.

﴿any﴾; that is: any thing. It is in the nominative position, being the subject (mubtada'). The "ma" here is Tamimi (in which it does not operate on the predicate), or it is its noun if it is Hijazi, and "min" is extra (mazida) for totality, and "min hisabihim" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) relating to it. "Upon those who fear Allah" is in the nominative position as the predicate of the subject, or of the Hijazi "ma" according to the view of one who does not permit its operation on a preceding predicate absolutely, or in the accusative position according to the view of one who permits its operation on a preceding predicate when that predicate is an adverb (zarf) or a prepositional phrase (harf jarr).

﴿But a reminder﴾ is a corrective exception to the preceding negation; that is: rather, it is upon them to remind them and to restrain them from what they are upon of ugly deeds, by whatever admonition and reminding is possible, and to show them their disapproval and denunciation. The position of "reminder" (dhikra) is either accusative, as a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the omitted verb; that is: upon them is to remind them with a reminder, or nominative, as a subject with an omitted predicate; that is: but upon them is a reminder.

﴿that perhaps they may fear Allah﴾; that is: that they may abstain from engaging in the discourse out of shame, or out of dislike of their own offense. It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to the relative clause; that is: they remind them in hope that they will remain steadfast in their piety, or increase it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and play﴾: those who were obligated to it and commanded to establish its duties.

﴿as amusement and play﴾: in that they mocked it and ridiculed it, or they built the matter of their religion upon what a sensible person would hardly engage in seriously, and which would only issue from one if it were done in the manner of play and diversion, such as the worship of idols and the prohibition of the baḥīrah and the sā'ibah, and the like.

The meaning is: turn away from them and do not care about their deeds and their words. It has also been said that it is a threat to them, like His Exalted saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves...﴾ the verse.

﴿And the life of this world has deluded them﴾: they were content with it, to the point that they claimed there would be no life after it, ever.

﴿And admonish thereby﴾; that is, with the Qur'an, whoever is fit for admonition.

﴿Lest a soul be given over to destruction for what it has earned﴾; that is, lest it be given over to destruction, like His Exalted saying: ﴿lest you go astray...﴾ the verse; or for fear that it be given over to destruction, or out of aversion that many souls be given over to destruction, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾, and be held in pledge for its evil deeds.

The original meaning of ibsāl and basl is prevention, and from it comes asadun bāsil (a brave lion), because its prey does not escape from it, or because it is inaccessible; and bāsil (a brave man) means one who is courageous, because he refrains from his opponent. And hadha basl 'alayka means: this is forbidden and prohibited to you.

It has also been permitted that the pronoun in "bihi" (thereby) refers back to al-ibsāl (the giving over to destruction), even though it has not been previously mentioned, as in the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause is then a substitute explaining it, because of the magnification and added emphasis in mentioning it vaguely first and then explaining it second, as in the verse of poetry:

"ʿalā jūdihi la-ḍanna bi-l-māʾi Ḥātimu"

with Ḥātim in the genitive case, as a substitute for the pronoun in jūdihi. The meaning then is: and admonish concerning the pledging and confining of souls for what they have earned.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿They have, besides Allah, no protector and no intercessor﴾, it is a resumptive clause brought to inform of that. It has been said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in kasabat. It has been said that it is in the nominative position as a description of nafs, but the more apparent view is that it is a circumstantial clause from nafs, for it has the force of nafs kāfira (a disbelieving soul) or nufūs kathīra (many souls), as in His Exalted saying: ﴿a soul will know what it has presented﴾.

﴿Besides Allah﴾ is related to something omitted which is a circumstantial clause from ﴿protector﴾, as was explained in the commentary on His Exalted saying: ﴿And warn thereby...﴾ the verse. It has also been said that it is the predicate of laysa, in which case "la-hā" (for it) is then related to something omitted as an explanatory element.

﴿And if it offers every ransom﴾; that is, if that soul offers ransom, every ransom, being an emphatic infinitive.

﴿It will not be accepted from it﴾, with the verb attributed to the prepositional phrase and not to the pronoun of ransom, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿nor will ransom be accepted from it﴾; for it is the thing ransomed by which, not the infinitive as in our case.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun in terms of its being characterized by what is in its relative clause; and the distance implied in it is to indicate the remoteness of their rank in evil condition. Its position is nominative as a subject, and the predicate is His Exalted saying: ﴿Those who have been given over to destruction for what they earned﴾, and the clause is resumptive, brought after the warning about the aforementioned destruction, to explain that they are the ones afflicted with it; that is: those who have taken their religion as amusement and play, who have been deceived by the life of this world, they are the ones who have been given over to destruction for what they earned.

His Exalted saying: ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water﴾ is another resumptive clause explaining the manner of the aforementioned destruction and its outcome, built upon a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said: What will be theirs when they have been given over to destruction for what they earned? So it is said: For them is a drink of boiling water, which gurgles in their bellies and by which their intestines are cut to pieces.

﴿And a painful punishment﴾ with a fire that blazes upon their bodies.

﴿For what they used to disbelieve﴾; that is, because of their persistent disbelief in the world. It has also been permitted that "for them is a drink..." etc. is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ubsilū, and that the arrangement of the two mentioned punishments upon their disbelief, although they are also punished for all their other sins, as indicated by His Exalted saying: "for what they earned," is because it is the principal basis for the imposition of punishment and the most important in the matter of warning; or it is intended by their disbelief what is more general than it, including its consequences of sins and evil deeds.

Furthermore, it has been permitted that "those" refers to the souls indicated by nafs, its position being nominative as a subject, and the second relative pronoun is its description, or a substitute for it, and "for them is a drink..." etc. is its predicate, and the clause is brought to explain the consequence of being given over to destruction.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 71:**

﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, besides Allah, that which neither benefits us nor harms us?"﴾ It is said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) when his son 'Abd al-Rahman invited him to worship idols. The address was therefore turned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at that time, to indicate the connection and unity between them, and to exalt the rank of al-Siddiq (the Truthful) (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him). That is: "Shall we worship, going beyond the worship of Allah, Who combines all the attributes of divinity, among which is the power to benefit and to harm, that which cannot benefit us if we worship it, nor harm us if we abandon it?" The lowest degree of being worthy of worship is the power to do that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and be turned back upon our heels﴾ is conjoined to "nad'u" (shall we call upon) and falls under the same denial and negation. That is: "and be returned to polytheism." The expression of it as being "returned upon one's heels" serves to intensify its ugliness by depicting it in a form that is itself a mark of ugliness, together with the indication that polytheism is a state that has been left behind and cast behind the back. The choice of "nuradd" (we be returned) over "nartaddu" (we apostatize) directs the denial toward being turned back by another, as a clear declaration of opposition to the misguiding ones and as a cutting off of their empty hopes, and as an indication that apostasy without one who turns one back is not within the realm of possibility, so that it would need to be negated and denied.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿after Allah has guided us﴾ means: to Islam, and has rescued us from polytheism. It is connected to "nuradd" and is brought in to emphasise the rejection, not merely to establish the meaning of "being returned" and depict it. Otherwise it would have sufficed to say, "after we have been guided," as if it were said: "And shall we be returned to polytheism through the misguidance of the misguider, after Allah has guided us, the One Who has no guide other than Him?"

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿like one whom the devils have enticed﴾ is in the accusative position, being a circumstantial clause (hal) from the nominative subject of "nuradd." That is: "shall we be returned upon our heels, likened to one whom the rebellious jinn have enticed and led astray into the desert wastes and the ruinous places." Or it is an attributive adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun (masdar): "that we be returned a return like the return of one whom ... etc."

"Istihwa'" (enticement) is an verbal form (istif'al) from "hawa fi al-ard," meaning to go off into the land, as if the devils desired his descent and eagerly pursued it. It has been read as "istahwahu" with a leaning alif (imalah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the earth﴾ is either connected to "istahwat," or to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause from its object: "being in the earth."

Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bewildered﴾ is a circumstantial clause from it (the object), being a substitute for the first, or the second circumstantial clause according to those who permit that, or a circumstantial clause from "alladhi" (the one), or from the pronoun concealed in the adverbial phrase. That is: "wandering and lost from the right path, not knowing what to do."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has companions﴾ is a clause in the accusative position, being either an attributive description of "bewildered," or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun within it, or a resumed clause brought to explain his condition.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who call him to guidance﴾ is an attributive description of "companions." That is: for that one who has been enticed there is a company who guide him to the straight path. The word "guidance" is used as a verbal noun for the sake of emphasis, as if he were the very essence of guidance.

﴿"Come to us"﴾ is said with the intention of speech, and it is either a substitute for those who call him, or a circumstantial clause from their subject. That is: they say, "Come to us."

In this there is an indication (p-150) that they are rightly guided, steadfast upon the straight path, and that the one they call is not one who knows the straight path so that he might be invited to come to it; he only perceives the direction of the caller and the source of the cry alone.

﴿Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾ is that to which He guided us, which is Islam.

﴿is the guidance﴾ alone; and whatever is other than it is pure misguidance and utter error, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ and the like.

The repetition of the command is for the sake of giving attention to the matter commanded, and because what came before was a restraint from polytheism, whereas this is an exhortation to Islam, and it is a preparation for what follows, for the fact that guidance is exclusively the guidance of Allah, the Exalted, necessitates compliance with the commands that come after it.

﴿And we have been commanded﴾ is conjoined to "that the guidance of Allah is the guidance," falling under the speech.

The lam in ﴿that we may submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ is for giving the reason for the reported command, and for specifying what was meant by the three commands, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say to My servants who have believed: they should establish prayer and spend...﴾ (the verse), as if it were said: "We were commanded, and it was said to us: 'Submit,' in order that we may submit." It is also said that it has the meaning of "bi" (with), that is: "we were commanded to submit," and it is also said that it is superfluous, that is: "we were commanded that we submit," with the omission of "bi."

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And to establish the prayer and to fear Him﴾; that is, God Almighty in opposing His command, is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "that we submit" (nuslima) on the three possibilities, on the basis that the "an" (that) of the verbal noun, when it is connected to the imperative without any sense of command (tajarrud ʿan maʿnā al-amr), is like the bare connection of the verbal clause from the sense of past and future tense. So the meaning on the first (view) is: we were commanded, that is, it was said to us: "Submit, and establish the prayer, and fear God," in order that we submit, establish the prayer and fear Him, Exalted is He. And on the latter two (views): we were commanded that we submit, establish the prayer, and fear Him, Exalted is He. The mention of the attribute of His lordship over the worlds serves to give the reason for the command and to emphasize the obligation of complying with it.

Just as the Almighty's saying: ﴿And it is He to whom you will be gathered﴾ is a resumptive sentence (jumla mustanafa) that makes compliance obligatory with what was commanded of the three matters.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 73:

﴿And He it is Who created the heavens and the earth﴾. By their creation is meant also the creation of what is in them, and the absence of explicit mention of this is because it is evident that the heavens and the earth comprise all the higher and lower things.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in truth﴾ (bil-haqq), is connected to an omitted element, and it is a circumstantial phrase (hal) either from the subject of "created" (khalaqa), or from its object, or it is a qualifier of its verbal noun (masdar) that emphasizes it. That is: standing in truth, or being clothed in truth, or a creation clothed with it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the day He says: "Be," and it is, His word is the truth﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that His creation, exalted is He, of what has been mentioned of the heavens and the earth is not something that depends on matter or duration, but is completed by the mere command of bringing-into-being (al-amr al-takwini) without depending on anything else at all. And that this command, which relates to each and every individual of the created things at a specific time among the times, is true in itself, containing wisdom.

"Day" (yawm) is an adverbial complement (zarf) to the content of the clause "His word is the truth", and the conjunction (waw) is, in meaning, attached to it. Its being placed before it is for the sake of emphasis on it, since it is the locus of truthfulness. The omission of mention of what is said to it is for reliance on its being evident.

By "the word" is meant the word "Be" (kun), either literally or figuratively, as is well known. So the meaning is: His command, which relates to everything He wills to create among things, at the time of its relation to it, neither before it nor after it, among the individual times, is the truth; that is, the one attested to as true and known for it.

That said, it has been said: "His word" (qawluhu) is a subject (mubtada'), "the truth" (al-haqq) is its attribute, and "the day He says" is its predicate placed before it, as in your saying: "The fighting is on the day of Friday." Its accusative case is by the sense of "being established." The resulting meaning: His word is the truth, existing at the moment He says to a thing among things: "Be," and that thing is.

It has also been said: "Day" (yawm) is in the accusative by coordination with "the heavens," or with the pronoun in "fear Him," or by an omitted element indicated by "in truth," and "His word is the truth" is a subject and predicate, or the subject of "is" (yakun), in the sense: at the time He says to His word, the truth, "Be," and it is; that is, to His decree, the truth, "Be," and it is. The intended meaning is: at the time He brings things into being and originates them, or at the time the Resurrection occurs, so that the bringing-into-being is the gathering and revival of bodies. So reflect upon it with due reflection.

﴿And to Him belongs the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. The restriction of the exclusive dominion to Him, exalted is He, to that day, despite the general exclusivity over all times, is for the sake of the utmost clarity of that, since the figurative relationships existing in this world, which validate figurative ownership in some respect, are severed, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾; that is, He is the knower of both.

﴿And He is the Wise﴾ in everything He does.

﴿the Aware﴾ of all matters, the manifest and the hidden.

Abu al-Su'ud's Commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 6, verse 74:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ is in the accusative case as an object of an implied verb, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is conjoined to "﴿Say: Shall we call upon﴾", not to "﴿Establish﴾" as has been said, because that would corrupt the meaning. That is: "And mention to them, after you had denounced their worship of what has no power to benefit or harm, and had affirmed that guidance is the guidance of God and what follows from His affairs, the time when Abraham said, to his father Azar, rebuking him for worshipping idols" — the one whom they claim they follow in his creed — "for this is among the things that silence them and proclaim the corruption of their path."

The directing of the command of remembrance to the time, rather than to what occurred in it of events, although the events are the intended object, is because of the emphasis, repeated many times, on the importance of remembering them.

"Azar" is of the pattern of "Adam", "Aabir", "Azir", and "Falagh"; likewise "Tarah". This is reported by Muhammad ibn Ishaq, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi. He was from a village in the outskirts of Kufa. His name is not declined because of its foreign origin (ajamiyya) and its being a proper noun (alamiyya).

It is said: his name in Syriac is Tarah, and Azar is his well-known epithet. It is also said: Azar is the name of an idol, by which he was given the epithet because of his constant devotion to its worship; in that case it is an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) to "his father", or a substitute (badal) for it.

Al-Dahhak said: its meaning is "the aged, decrepit old man." Al-Zajjaj said: "the one who errs." Al-Farra' and Sulayman al-Taymi said: "the crooked one." In that case it is an attribute of him, as if it were derived from "al-azr" or "al-wizz", or it is meant as "worshipper of Azar", with the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the modified-to noun in its position.

It is also read as "Azaru" in the vocative, and this is evidence of its being a proper noun, since the vocative particle is omitted only with proper nouns.

﴿Do you take﴾ is transitive to two objects, which are ﴿idols as gods﴾; that is: "Do you make them gods for yourself?" The denunciation is directed at taking the kind (of idols) as gods without regard to plurality; the plural form is used only in consideration of what actually occurs.

It is also read as "A-azran" with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra after the interrogative hamza, a quiescent zay, and a tanween-marked fathah on the ra', and it is the name of an idol; its meaning is: "Do you worship Azar?"

Then it is said: "You take idols as gods" is for confirmation and establishment of that, and it falls under the denunciation because it serves as its explanation. It is also said: "al-azr" means strength, and the meaning is: "For the sake of strength and support, do you take idols as gods?" — a denunciation of his being strengthened by them, in the manner of God's saying: ﴿Do they seek honour with them?﴾

﴿Indeed I see you and your people﴾ who follow you in their worship,

﴿in manifest error﴾ away from the truth,

﴿manifest﴾; that is, clear that it is error with no ambiguity at all. The seeing is either cognitive, in which case the adverbial phrase is its second object, or visual, in which case it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the object. The sentence is a justification for the denunciation and rebuke.

(p-152) ﴿And thus We showed Abraham﴾. This "showing" (*ira'ah*) is derived from visual seeing (*ru'yah basariyyah*), used metaphorically for knowing and for the seeing of insight (*nazar al-basirah*). That is, "We made him know and gave him insight." The future form of the verb is used to narrate a past state, in order to bring its image vividly to mind.

"Thus" (*dhalika*) points back to the verbal noun of *nuri* ("We show"), not to another showing understood from His words "I see you" (*inni arakа*) and the sense of distance in it. This is to signal the high rank of the thing referred to, the remoteness of its station in excellence, and its complete distinction, by which it is arranged among the matters that are observed.

The *kaf* ("like") serves to emphasize the grandeur that the demonstrative noun conveys. Originally its position is in the accusative, as an attribute (*na't*) of a deleted verbal noun. The underlying sense is: "We showed Abraham a showing like that showing." It is placed before the verb to convey restriction (*qasr*). The *kaf* is regarded as superfluous (*muqhamah*) for the reason mentioned, so the thing referred to becomes the very emphasized verbal noun itself, not an attribute of it. That is: "We show him that wondrous insight."

﴿the dominion (*malakut*) of the heavens and the earth﴾. That is, His lordship (*rububiyyah*), His ownership of both, His overpowering sovereignty over them, and that they, with what is in them, are nurtured and owned by Him, exalted is He, and not another, lesser insight than this.

*Malakut* (dominion, the realm of sovereignty) is a verbal noun in the intensive pattern, like *rahabut* and *jabarut*. Its meaning is great kingship and overpowering authority. Then there is the question whether it is specific to the kingship of God, glorified is His authority, or not.
