It has been said [both ways], and the first is the more apparent, and al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) held this view.

It has also been said that *malakut* means their inner reality, their wonders and marvels. It is narrated that the heavens and the earth were uncovered for him (peace be upon him), even the Throne and the lowest of the earths. It has been said that it means their signs. It has also been said that the *malakut* of the heavens is the sun, the moon and the stars, and the *malakut* of the earth is the mountains, the trees and the seas.

These views do not require that the showing be visual, since what is meant by showing the sensible matters mentioned is not merely enabling him (peace be upon him) to see and observe them in themselves, but rather informing him (peace be upon him) of their realities and making them known to him, in terms of what they indicate about the affairs of Him, mighty and majestic.

There is no doubt that this is not something perceived by the senses, as the demonstrative noun indicates, revealing that the thing referred to is a wondrous matter. The ordinary visual seeing is far removed from that status.

It was also read as *turi* (with the letter *ta'*), with the verb attributed to *malakut*, meaning: the proofs of lordship make him (peace be upon him) see it.

The *lam* in His words, ﴿and that he might be among those who have certainty (*al-muqinin*)﴾, is connected to a deleted element placed later, and the clause confirms what precedes it. That is: "and that he might be among the company of those firmly established in certainty, who reach the degree of the eye of certainty (*ayn al-yaqin*) regarding the knowledge of God, exalted is He. We did what We did of this wondrous insight mentioned, not for any other purpose." The arrival at that remote goal is a perfection that follows from that insight, not its very essence. The restriction is not meant to show that its benefit is confined to this, since guiding creation and binding the polytheists, as will come later, are among its benefits without doubt. Rather, it shows that this is the original and principal purpose, and the rest are its consequences.

It has also been said that the clause is connected to the preceding verb, and the clause is coordinated with another deleted reason to which the speech extends: "so that he might draw evidence from them, and that he might be ..." etc. Accordingly, *malakut* of them should be understood as their wonders and their signs, because drawing inference is among the ends of showing them, not among the ends of showing the lordship itself.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 76:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When the night covered him﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the first (interpretation), which is "the Truth, the Manifest," and it is conjoined to "﴿Abraham said﴾," falling under what he was commanded to mention by the command to mention its time; and what lies between them is an interjected clause (iʿtirāḍ) confirming what preceded and what follows. For his, peace be upon him, acquaintance with His lordship (rubūbiyyah) and His dominion (mālikiyyah) over the heavens and the earth and what is in them, and with the fact that all of them are subdued under His sovereignty (malakūt), in need of Him for their existence, and with the other perfections that follow from this, and with his being among those firmly rooted in knowledge of His, exalted is He, affairs, having reached the peak of the certainty of sight (ʿayn al-yaqīn), is of the kind that requires that he, peace be upon him, judge the impossibility of the divinity of anything other than Him, glorified is He, such as idols and stars.

And upon the second (interpretation), it is an elaboration of what was mentioned concerning the showing of the sovereignty (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, and an explanation of the manner of his, peace be upon him, reasoning and his reaching the rank of firm conviction. The meaning of "covered him" (janna ʿalayhi al-layl) is: it concealed him with its darkness.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿he saw a star﴾ is the answer to "when" (lammā), for his seeing it is only realized with the removal of the light of the sun from perception, and this is explicit that it was not at the beginning of its rising, but rather its disappearance from perception was by way of being obscured by the light of the sun. The verified view is that it was close to sunset, as you will come to know. It has been said: that star was Venus (al-Zuhrah), and it has been said: it was Jupiter (al-Mushtarā).

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "This is my lord"﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) built upon a question arising from the preceding conditional clause, which is consequent upon the explanation of his, peace be upon him, being shown the sovereignty of the heavens and the earth. For that is of the sort that moves the hearer to explore what manifested from him, peace be upon him, of the effects of that showing and its rulings, as if it were said: "What did he, peace be upon him, do when he saw the star?" So it was said: he said, by way of supposition and assumption, "This is my lord," in accommodation with his father and his people, who used to worship idols and stars. For the one who argues against a view adopts it as the opinion of his opponent, then turns against it with refutation. Perhaps the adoption of this method in demonstrating the impossibility of the lordship of the stars, rather than demonstrating the impossibility of the divinity of idols, is because its falsity and impossibility are less evident than the first; for had he declared the truth from the outset, as he did regarding the worship of idols, they would have persisted in obstinacy and stubbornness and clung to their rebellion, wandering blindly.

It has also been said: he, peace be upon him, said it by way of reflection and reasoning, and that was during the time of his adolescence and the first period of his maturity. This is built upon interpreting the malakūt as the signs of the two (heavens and earth), and upon the conjunction of His saying, Exalted is He, so that it is upon the stated underlying cause, and upon taking His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿When the night covered﴾ ..." etc., as an elaboration of what was mentioned of the showing, and an explanation of the manner of reasoning.

And you are aware that all of that is of the sort that impairs the eloquence of the sublime composition and the grandeur of the station of the Friend (Khalīl), peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿When it set﴾: that is, it set (gharaba).

﴿He said, "I do not love the setting ones"﴾: that is, the lords that move from place to place, that change from state to state, that hide behind veils; for they are, beyond any doubt, far removed from deserving lordship.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 77:**

﴿When he saw the moon rising﴾; i.e., beginning to rise after the setting of the star.

﴿He said: "This is my lord."﴾ In the same manner as before.

﴿Then when it set﴾, just as the star had set.

﴿He said: "Unless my lord guides me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾ That is, to His presence, which is the Truth from which there is no deviation.

﴿I will surely be among the people who are astray﴾: for nothing of what I have seen is fitting for lordship. This is an exaggeration on his part, peace be upon him, in displaying fairness. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, was at that time in a place where, on its western side, there was a towering mountain by which the star and the moon were concealed at midday, or shortly after it, and the star was close to him, and its eastern horizon was initially unobstructed; otherwise, the rising of the moon would be after the setting of the star, and then its setting before the rising of the sun.

As indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when he saw the sun rising﴾; i.e., beginning to rise, in a manner that is hardly conceivable.

﴿He said﴾; i.e., in the same manner as before. (p-154)

﴿This is my lord﴾. The reason it is not feminine is that what is pointed to and what is ascribed lordship is the visible body as such, not as named by one of the names, let alone in respect of being named "the sun." Or the predicate is masculine to keep the Lord free from the stain of femininity.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is greater﴾ is an emphasis of what he, peace be upon him, intended of showing fairness, together with a subtle indication of the corruption of their religion from another angle, by clarifying that the greater is more deserving of lordship than the lesser.

﴿So when it set﴾: it too, just as the star and the moon set.

﴿He said﴾, addressing all of them, openly declaring the truth among them.

﴿O my people, I am innocent of what you associate﴾; i.e., of that which you associate with Him of created bodies, changing from one state to another, subjugated to their Originator; or of your associating. The ordering of this judgment and its two counterparts upon setting rather than rising and appearing is a necessity of the wise method of argumentation in this manner. For each of them, although in itself a transition incompatible with its subject deserving lordship, certainly is, yet since the first is a state necessitating the appearance of effects and judgments, suitable for the illusion of deserving in general, the first judgment was ordered upon it in the mentioned manner. And since the second is a state requiring the obliteration of effects and the nullification of judgments, which clearly contradict the said deserving, a contradiction every stubborn obstinate denier nearly acknowledges, the ordering upon it was what was ordered.

Then he (peace be upon him) disassociated himself from them, and turned toward the Originator of these created things and their Producer, saying: ﴿Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾, which are the celestial bodies that you worship, as parts of them.

﴿And the earth﴾, in which those [celestial bodies] set.

﴿Inclining (ḥanīf)﴾; i.e., turning away from all false religions and deviant creeds.

﴿And I am not of the polytheists﴾ in any of the actions or statements.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 80:

﴿And his people argued with him⦆; that is, they began to contend with him concerning the matter of tawhid (affirming the Oneness of God).

﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that comes as an answer to a question arising from the narration of their argument, as if it were said: "What did he (peace be upon him) say when they argued with him?" So it is answered: he said, rejecting what they had presumed to do against him in arguing with him, despite their falling short of that rank, the lofty nature of the claim, and the strength of his opponent.

﴿Do you argue with me concerning God﴾, with the nun of plurality assimilated into the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya), and it has been read with the deletion of the first (of the two nuns).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He has guided me﴾, it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker, emphasizing the rejection. For his being guided by God, exalted is He, and supported by Him, is among what makes it impossible for them to argue with him (peace be upon him). That is: do you dispute with me concerning His affair, exalted is He, and His oneness, while the reality is that He, exalted is He, has guided me to the truth after I had followed your way by supposition and assumption, and its falsehood became completely clear, as you have witnessed.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, it is an answer to what they frightened him with during the argument, of his being struck by harm from their idols, as when his people said to Hud (peace be upon him): ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil﴾. Perhaps they did this when he (peace be upon him) did to their idols what he did. And "mā" is a relative noun whose returning pronoun has been deleted.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that my Lord should will something﴾, it is an exceptive clause (istithna' mufragh) from the most general of times; that is: I do not fear what you associate with Him, glorified is He, from your objects of worship at any time, except at a time when my Lord, exalted is He, wills some harm to befall me from them; and that is only from Him, exalted is He, without any involvement of your gods in it at all.

Mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyya) with its attribution to his (peace be upon him) pronoun contains a display from him of submission to the judgment of Him, glorified and exalted is He, a surrender to His command, and an acknowledgment that he is under His dominion and lordship.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, it is as if it were a reason for the exception; that is: He has encompassed everything in knowledge, so it is not far that it is within His knowledge, exalted is He, that some harm should befall me from them through some cause among the causes. The explicit mention in place of the pronoun is an emphasis on the aforementioned meaning and a delight in mentioning Him, exalted is He.

﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾; that is: do you turn away from reflecting that your gods are inanimate objects, unable to do anything whatsoever of benefit or harm, so that you do not recall that they are unable to harm me? In the use of "tadhakkur" (take heed/remember) rather than "tafakkur" (reflect) and its like, there is an indication that the matter of their idols is fixed in minds and requires nothing but recollection.

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿How should I fear what you associate (with Him)?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to deny fear from him, peace be upon him, according to the presumption of the disbelievers, by way of the argumentative method (ilzami), as will come, after denying it of him on the basis of reality and the actual state of affairs. The interrogative is for denying the occurrence and negating it entirely, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists in the sight of God...﴾ and the rest of the verse. It is not for rejecting an occurrence while considering it strange despite its occurrence, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿How do you disbelieve in God...﴾ and so on. Directing the denial at the manner of fear carries an emphasis that directing it at the fear itself does not. It could be said: "Should I fear?" because every existent must have its existence in some state and some manner, certainly. So when all its states and manners are negated, its existence is negated from every aspect, by demonstrative method (burhani).

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you do not fear that you have associated with God﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "I fear", with a subject supposed, and the waw suffices for the connection without need of a pronoun returning to the one in the circumstantial state. It confirms the denial of fear and its negation from him, peace be upon him, and implies their acknowledgment of this. For since they do not fear where fear is due, it is all the more fitting and proper that he should not fear where there is safety. That is: "How should I fear what is not within the realm of fear at all, while you do not fear the danger of what is the greatest and most terrifying of dreaded things, namely your associating (partners) with God, who has nothing like unto Him in the earth or in the heaven, which is among His creatures?"

He expressed it by His words, exalted is He: ﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾; that is, by their association.

﴿upon you﴾ is in the manner of mockery (tahakkum), with the indication that religious matters rely only on the proof sent down from God, exalted is He. In making the second fear conditional upon their association there is an emphasis and a regard for good manners that is not hidden.

Furthermore, as for what has been said, that His words, exalted is He: ﴿and you do not fear...﴾ and so on, are coordinated with "I fear" and included with it in the ruling of denial and wonder, this is by no means a valid path, since it leads to corruption of the meaning with certainty. How could it not, when you know that denial in the sense of complete negation means the meaning returns to negating fear from him, peace be upon him, and negating their negation of it, and this is plainly corrupt. Taking the denial in the first instance to mean negating the occurrence, and in the second to mean considering the occurrence strange, has no justification. Moreover, His words, exalted is He: ﴿So which of the two parties has more right to safety?﴾ clearly refute it definitively. For it is a statement consequent upon denying his fear, peace be upon him, in a place of safety, while it is established that they have no fear in a place of fear, and it is driven to compel them to acknowledge his entitlement, peace be upon him, to the safety he possesses, and their non-entitlement to what they have. The comparative form was used, which implies that they too have some entitlement to it, in order to bring them down from the rank of obstinacy and injustice by driving the speech according to the paths of fairness.

By "the two parties" is meant the party secure in a place of safety and the party secure in a place of fear. The preference for the wording of the noble text over saying: "Which of us has more right to safety, I or you?" serves to reinforce compulsion toward the true answer by alerting them to the reason for the ruling, and to avoid explicitly declaring them wrong, not merely to avoid praising oneself.

﴿if you know﴾: the object is either omitted, relying on its being evident from the context; that is: "if you know who has more right to that", or intended to be general; that is: "if you know anything." Or it is left out entirely; that is: "if you are among those of knowledge." The answer to the condition is omitted; that is: "then tell me."

﴿Alladhina amanu﴾ ("Those who believe") is a resumptive clause (istinaf) from Allah, the Exalted, giving the true answer that cannot be evaded. That is, "the group who believed."

﴿Wa lam yalbisu imanahum﴾ ("and did not mix their belief") with ﴿dhalika﴾ ("that"); that is, they did not mix it.

﴿Bi-zulm﴾ ("with wrongdoing"); that is, with shirk (association of partners with Allah), as the polytheists do, claiming that they believe in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that their worship of idols is a completion of their faith and its rulings, because it is for the sake of nearness and intercession, as they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾. This is the meaning of mixing.

﴿Ulaika﴾ ("those") refers to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in terms of its being characterized by what is in its clause (silah). Pointing to it after describing it with what was mentioned indicates that they are distinguished by this from others, and are placed in the category of observed matters. The sense of distance in it serves to indicate the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in nobility. It is a second subject (mubtada' thani).

Allah's statement ﴿lahumu al-amn﴾ ("theirs is security") is a sentence consisting of a prepositional phrase (khabar muqaddam) and a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar). It functions as the predicate of ﴿ulaika﴾, and together with its predicate it is the predicate of the first subject, which is the relative pronoun. It is permissible for ﴿ulaika﴾ to be a substitute (badal) for the relative pronoun, or an explicative apposition ('atf bayan) to it, with ﴿lahumu al-amn﴾ as its predicate.

The word ﴿al-amn﴾ may be the agent (fa'il) of the prepositional phrase, since the phrase depends on the subject. It is also permissible for ﴿lahum﴾ to be a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam) and ﴿al-amn﴾ the subject (mubtada'), with the whole sentence as the predicate of the relative pronoun. It is also permissible for ﴿ulaika﴾ to be a second subject, with ﴿lahum﴾ as its predicate and ﴿al-amn﴾ as its agent, and the sentence as the predicate of the relative pronoun. That is: those characterized by what was mentioned of pure faith, free from any admixture of shirk, theirs alone is security.

﴿Wa hum muhtadun﴾ ("and they are guided"), to the truth, while those other than them are in clear error.

It is reported that when this verse was revealed, it weighed heavily on the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and they said: "Which of us has not wronged himself?" The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "It is not as you think. It is what Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with Allah; indeed, association is a great wrong﴾."

Belief in Him does not consist of affirming the existence of the Wise Creator while mixing this affirmation with associating partners with Him. Nor is it a requirement of mixing that the original remain in reality after the mixing. It has been said that the intended meaning of "wrong" is sin that makes its doer a transgressor (fasiq). The apparent meaning is the first, because it comes in the context of an answer concerning the condition of the two groups.

﴿And that﴾ refers to the argument that Abraham, peace be upon him, made, from His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿When the night covered him﴾."

It is also said that it refers to what came from His saying "﴿Do you argue with me﴾" up to His saying "﴿guided﴾." The sense of distance in the demonstrative is used to magnify the status of the one indicated and to signal his lofty rank and exalted standing in excellence (p-157). It is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence).

His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿Our argument﴾," is its *khabar* (predicate). Its attribution to the *nun al-'azamah* (the nun of majesty, the royal "We") carries an obvious magnification.

His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿We gave it to Abraham﴾," meaning: We guided him to it or taught it to him, is in the accusative position as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of "*hujjatuna*" (Our argument). The element governing it is the sense of the demonstrative, as in His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged﴾." Or it is in the nominative position as a second *khabar*, or it is itself the *khabar*, with "*hujjatuna*" being a *badal* (substitute) or *bayan* (explanatory apposition) for the *mubtada'*. "﴿Abraham﴾" is the first object of *atayna* (We gave), and the second object was placed before it because it is a pronoun.

His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿against his people﴾" is connected to "*hujjatuna*" if it is made the *khabar* of "*tilka*," or to an omitted verb if it is made a *badal*; that is, "We gave Abraham an argument against his people." It is also said that it is connected to "*ataynā*" (We gave).

"﴿We raise﴾" is with the *nun al-'azamah*. It is also read with the *ya'* (third person), by way of *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person). The same applies to the verb that follows.

"﴿degrees﴾" means: great, lofty ranks of knowledge and wisdom. It is in the accusative either as a *masdar* (verbal noun), or as a *zarf* (adverb of place or time), or by the removal of the preposition, meaning "to degrees," or as a *tamyiz* (specification), or as the object.

His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿whom We will﴾," and its postponement in the last three possibilities, is due to the concern with what is put first and to arousing eagerness for what is put later. The object of the will is omitted, meaning "whom We will," raising him as wisdom requires and as the benefit demands. The choice of the future form indicates that this is a continuous, established practice, operating among the chosen and righteous, and not restricted to Abraham, peace be upon him.

It is also read with the genitive construction to "*man*" (whom). The clause is then a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it, with no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical case analysis). It is also said that it is in the accusative as a *hal* of the subject of *ataynā*, meaning: while We are raising... etc.

"﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise﴾" in everything He does of elevation and lowering.

"﴿All-Knowing﴾" of the condition of whoever He raises, and of his readiness for it at varying levels. The sentence gives the reason for what precedes it. Placing "*Rabb*" (Lord) as a noun attached to His pronoun, peace be upon him, in place of the *nun al-'azamah*, by way of *iltifat* amid the explanation of Abraham's circumstances, shows additional kindness and care toward him, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 84:

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ is coordinated with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And that was Our argument﴾ ... and so on; for the coordination of each of the nominal and verbal clauses with the other is something about whose permissibility there is no dispute, and there is no justification for coordinating it with ﴿We gave it﴾ (ataynaha), because the latter has a place in i'rab (grammatical case), accusative or nominative, as was explained earlier. So if this were coordinated with that, it would carry the same status of being a circumstantial clause (hal) and a predicative clause (khabar), both of which require a connecting pronoun (rabit), and there is no way to that here.

﴿Each﴾ (kullan) is the object of what follows it, and placing it first is for restriction (qasr), but not restricted with respect to other than these two absolutely; rather with respect to one of them, i.e., each one of them.

﴿We guided﴾ (hadayna): not one of them to the exclusion of the other. The omission of mention of the one guided is because it is evident that it is the one to whom Abraham was given, and that the two of them are followers of him.

﴿And Noah﴾ (nuhan) is in the accusative, governed by a hidden verb that it explains.

﴿We guided before﴾ (hadayna min qabl); i.e., before Abraham, peace be upon him. He counted his guidance as a blessing upon Abraham, peace be upon him, because the nobility of the father extends to the son.

﴿And of his offspring﴾ (wa min dhurriyyatihi): the pronoun refers to Abraham, because the course of the noble composition is to explain his great affairs, from the giving of the argument, the raising of ranks, the granting of prophet-sons, and the preservation of this honour in his progeny until the Day of Resurrection, all of which is to impose the obligation upon those who belong to his religion, peace be upon him, from among the polytheists and the Jews.

It is said: it refers to Noah, because he is closer, and because Yunus (Jonah) and Lut (Lot) were not from the offspring of Abraham; so if the pronoun were for him, it would be restricted to those enumerated in this verse and the one after it. As for those mentioned in the third verse, they are coordinated upon Noah.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that all these prophets are attributed to the offspring of Abraham, even though some of them were not joined to him by birth from either mother or father; because Lut is the son of Abraham's brother, and the Arabs make the paternal uncle a father, as Allah, exalted is He, informed about the sons of Jacob that they said: ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾, although Ishmael was the uncle of Jacob.

﴿David and Solomon﴾ are in the accusative, governed by an implied verb understood from what preceded; and likewise what is coordinated upon them. To it is attached ﴿of his offspring﴾, and placing it before the explicit object is for concern for its matter, along with the length that is in the objects, which the delay of it might disturb the harmony of the noble composition; i.e., ﴿And We guided of his offspring David and Solomon﴾.

﴿And Job﴾ (Ayyub): he is the son of Amus, from the descendants of Esau (Îs) son of Isaac.

﴿And Joseph, Moses and Aaron﴾: or it is with an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause (hal) from those mentioned; i.e., ﴿and We guided them﴾ being in the state of their being ﴿of his offspring﴾.

﴿And thus﴾ (wa kadhalika) is a reference to what is understood from the noble composition of the reward of Abraham, peace be upon him; and the place of the kaf (ka) is the accusative, as it is an adjective (na't) to an omitted verbal noun (masdar).

The original estimate is: ﴿We reward the good-doers﴾ with a reward like that reward; the placing first is for restriction, and its verification has passed many times; the intended sense of "the good-doers" is the category, and by the similarity of their reward to his reward, peace be upon him, is meant absolute resemblance in repaying good with good and recompense between deeds and their returns without any diminution, not a similarity in every respect, since the reward of having numerous prophet-children is something specific to Abraham, peace be upon him.

The closer view is that the lam in "the good-doers" (al-muhsinin) is for previous mention (al-'ahd), and that refers to the verbal noun of the verb that follows it, and it is an expression for what the mentioned persons were given of the varieties of honours; and in it is the meaning of distance to signal the elevation of its rank; and the kaf is for emphasizing what the demonstrative noun conveyed of grandeur, and its place originally is the accusative as an adjective to an omitted verbal noun. The original estimate is: "And We reward the mentioned good-doers with a reward being like that reward," so it was placed before the verb to convey restriction, and the kaf was considered as an added (muqhamah) particle for the stated purpose, so the indicated thing became the very emphasized verbal noun and not an adjective to it; i.e., "And that wonderful reward, We reward the mentioned good-doers, not another reward lower than it."

The explicit mention in place of the pronoun is to praise them for good-doing, which is an expression for performing good deeds in the fitting manner, which is their descriptive goodness accompanying their essential goodness; and the Prayer and Peace upon him explained it with his saying: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." And the sentence is an interjected parenthetical remark (i'tiraq) relative to what precedes it.

**Zakariyya** is the son of Adhan, and **Yahya** is his son.

**Isa** is the son of Maryam, and in this there is evidence that *dhurriyya* (offspring) includes the children of daughters.

**Ilyas**: it has been said that he is Idris, the grandfather of Nuh, in which case the explanation applies specifically to those mentioned in the first verse. It has also been said that he is one of the descendants (asbat) of Harun, brother of Musa, peace be upon them both.

**Kull** (each one): that is, each one of those mentioned.

**Min al-salihin** (among the righteous): that is, among those who are perfect in *salah* (righteousness), which is an expression for doing what is fitting and guarding against what is not fitting. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) brought to praise them for their righteousness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 86:

﴿And Isma'il and al-Yasa'﴾ He is the son of Akhtub ibn al-'Ajuz. It is also read as (wa-al-Layasa'), and on both readings it is a non-Arabic proper name to which the definite article (al-) has been attached, and it has no derivation. It is said that he is Yusha' ibn Nun. It has also been said that it is transferred from the imperfect verb of wasi'a (to be wide/spacious), and the lam is like that in Yazid, according to the view of the one who said:

Have you seen al-Walid ibn al-Yazid, blessed, heavy-shouldered with the burdens of the caliphate?

﴿And Yunus﴾ He is the son of Matta. And Lut is the son of Haran ibn the brother of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

﴿And each﴾; that is, each one of those mentioned. ﴿We favoured﴾ with prophethood, not some of them over others.

﴿above the worlds﴾ above the worlds of their own time. The clause is a parenthetical insertion, like its sister clause.

And His saying, ﴿And of their fathers, their offspring, and their brothers﴾: it may be connected to what is connected to "from his offspring" (min dhurriyyatihi), with "min" being for the beginning of the extent (min ibtida'iyyah) and the object omitted; that is: "And We guided from among their fathers, their offspring, and their brothers many groups." Or it may be coordinated with "kullan" (each of them), with "min" being partitive (min tab'idiyyah); that is: "And We preferred some of their fathers..." etc.

﴿And We chose them﴾ is coordinated with "faddalna" (We preferred); that is, "We chose them."

﴿And We guided them to a straight path﴾ is a repetition for emphasis and a preparation for explaining that to which they were guided.

﴿That﴾ refers to what is understood from the noble composition (*al-naẓm al-karīm*) of the verbs' verbal nouns (*maṣādir al-af'āl*) mentioned. It is also said that it refers to what they adhered to. The sense of distance in ﴿that﴾ is as explained repeatedly before.

﴿The guidance of God﴾: the genitive construction is for honouring.

﴿He guides by it whomever He wills of His servants﴾: they are those who are prepared for guidance and direction. This contains an indication that He, exalted is He, bestows guidance as a favour.

﴿And if they had associated [partners]﴾: that is, these individuals mentioned.

﴿Their deeds would have been voided﴾ despite their virtue and the elevation of their ranks.

﴿What they used to do﴾ of righteous deeds that are pleasing. So how about anyone other than them? They are the ones, and their deeds are their deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 89:

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the eighteen prophets mentioned earlier, together with those joined to them in the passage, peace be upon them all. It refers to them insofar as they are characterized by the guidance mentioned and by other sublime attributes established for them. The sense of distance in it, as has been noted more than once before, signals the elevated rank of these prophets and the remoteness of their station in excellence and nobility. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the Exalted statement: ﴿whom We gave the Book﴾. That is, the genus of the Book, as realized in any single one of the heavenly scriptures. Giving it means complete understanding of what it contains of realities, and empowerment to grasp its sublime and subtle matters. This is more general than whether it came through initial revelation or through inheritance in continuity, since the ones mentioned did not each receive a specific book revealed to them individually.

﴿and the judgment﴾: that is, wisdom (al-hikmah), or the decisive settling of matters in accordance with what truth and rightness require.

﴿and prophethood﴾: that is, messengership (al-risalah).

﴿So if these disbelieve in them﴾: that is, in these three things, or in prophethood, which encompasses the rest.

﴿these﴾: that is, the disbelievers of Quraysh. For by their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and in what was revealed to him of the Qur'an, they disbelieve in what all of these confirm. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject (fa'il), as has been noted repeatedly, serves to give importance to what is fronted and to create anticipation for what is delayed.

﴿then We have entrusted with them﴾: that is, We have commanded them to observe them, and We have granted success to them in believing in them and in fulfilling their rights.

﴿a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾: that is, at no time whatsoever, but rather they are persistently upon belief in them. The affirmative nominal sentence indicates the continuity of established fact, and likewise the negative nominal sentence indicates the continuity of negation, by aid of the context, not the negation of continuity, as has been verified in its proper place.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: They are the Ansar and the people of Madinah. It was said: they are the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. It was said: every believer among the children of Adam. It was said: the Persians. For each of these groups is granted success in believing in the prophets and in the scriptures revealed to them, and in acting upon what they contain of the foundations of the sharia and its branches that remain in our sharia. By this the discharge of the obligation of the entrustment is realized, not by the abrogated (mansukhah) rulings among them, for by their abrogation (intisakh) they cease to be among its rulings. Its verification has already been discussed in the tafsir of Surah al-Ma'idah.

It was also said: they are the prophets mentioned. In that case, the entrustment means commanding what is more general than implementing their rulings, as is their condition regarding their own book, and including belief in its truth, as is their condition regarding all the other books, of which the noble Qur'an is one.

It was said: they are the angels. In that case, the entrustment is the command to bring them down, to preserve them, and to believe in their truth. Whichever of these is intended, the indefiniteness of ﴿qawman﴾ serves to magnify, and the first ﴿bi﴾ is attached to ﴿kafirin﴾, placed before it in order to preserve the rhyme of the verse endings (fawasil), while the second ﴿bi﴾ serves to emphasize the negation. As for placing the complement of ﴿wakkalna﴾ before its direct object, that is for the reason already mentioned, the giving of importance to what is fronted and the creating of anticipation for what is delayed, and also because it contains a certain length which, if fronted, might disrupt the harmony of the noble arrangement or cause a separation between the adjective and the noun it qualifies. The apodosis of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what is mentioned: that is, ﴿if these disbelieve in them﴾, then it is not to be taken into account at all. ﴿Then We have granted success in believing in them to a people of great stature who are certainly not disbelievers in them,﴾ but rather who persist in believing in them and acting upon what they contain. So in their belief there is sufficiency in place of the belief of these.

From this it becomes clear that the more correct view is that the intended ﴿people﴾ are one of the groups mentioned, since by their belief in the Qur'an and their acting upon its rulings, independence from the belief of the disbelievers in it and their acting upon its rulings is realized. As for the prophets and the angels, peace be upon them, their belief in it is not of the same kind as the belief of ordinary members of the community.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 90:

As indicated by it, ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the prophets mentioned, and the distance implied in it serves to announce the exalted rank of those prophets. It is a subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted: ﴿whom Allah has guided﴾; that is, to the truth and the straight path. The turn to the noble Name (al-ism al-jalil) serves to signal the cause of the guidance.

﴿So follow their guidance﴾; that is, single out their guidance for following, and do not follow anyone else. What is meant by their guidance is their way in faith in Allah the Exalted and His Oneness, and the fundamentals of religion, not the laws (shara'i') that are subject to abrogation (naskh), for after abrogation they no longer remain guidance.

The ha' in "iqtadih" (ihqtadih) is for pausal stopping (waqf); its proper place is to be dropped in continuous recitation (darj), but its retention in continuous recitation has also been deemed good, treating it as if it were in pause, and following the Imam. It was also recited with its vowel prolonged, considering it a pronominal suffix referring to the verbal noun (masdar).

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it﴾; that is, for the Qur'an, or for the conveying (of the message), for the flow of the speech indicates both of them, even though neither has been mentioned.

﴿A wage﴾ from you, just as those prophets before me, peace be upon them, did not ask it, and this is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow them in.

﴿It is not﴾; that is, the Qur'an is not.

﴿except a reminder to the worlds﴾; that is, an admonition and reminder to them all from Him, glory be to Him, so it is not restricted to one people to the exclusion of others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 91:

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ — this comes after the description of the magnificence of the Noble Qur'an and that it is a great blessing from Him, exalted be He, upon all nations, as His saying, exalted be He, speaks to it: ﴿And We have sent you not but as a mercy to the worlds﴾. Following this is a statement of their disdain for it and their disbelief in it, in a manner that extends to disbelief in all the divine Books.

The original meaning of qadr (measure) is testing and estimating. It is said: qadara al-shay'a yaqdaruhu bi-l-damm qadran (he measured the thing, with the dammah vowel), when he tested and estimated it in order to know its quantity. Then it came to be used for knowing a thing in its quantity, its conditions, and its attributes.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿haqqa qadrihi﴾ (with its true measure) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maf'ul mutlaq), and it was originally an adjective of the verbal noun; that is, qadrahu al-haqq (its true measure). When it was put in construct to its qualified noun, it took the case that its qualified noun would have taken. That is: they did not know God with the true knowledge regarding His kindness to His servants and His mercy toward them, and they did not observe His rights, exalted be He, in that matter; rather, they neglected them with gross neglect.

﴿When they said﴾ — denying the sending of the Messengers and the sending down of the Books, disbelieving in His magnificent blessing in both of them.

﴿God did not send down anything upon a human being﴾ — so the negation of their knowledge of His measure, glorified be He, is a metaphor (kinayah) for their belittling of His magnificent station and their ascribing to Him the opposite of His beautiful attributes, just as the negation of love in such a phrase as "Indeed God does not love the disbelievers" is a metaphor for hatred and wrath. Otherwise, the negation of knowing His measure, exalted be He, is realized even without belittling Him, indeed along with striving to attain knowledge, as in the words of one who addresses God in intimate prayer, confessing his shortcoming in knowing and worshipping Him: "Glory be to You, we have not known You with the true knowledge of You, nor worshipped You with the true worship of You." Or it may mean that they did not know Him with the true knowledge of Him in respect of His wrath upon the disbelievers and the severity of His seizing them, as the Qur'an speaks of this when they dared to utter this monstrous and abominable saying. So the negation is in its literal meaning.

The speakers were the Jews, and they said it in exaggeration of their denial that the Qur'an was sent down upon the Messenger of God ﷺ. Thus they were confronted with what they had no way at all to deny, where it is said: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book that Moses brought?﴾ That is: say to them this in the manner of rebuke and silencing.

It is narrated that Malik ibn al-Sayf, one of the rabbis and leaders of the Jews, was told by the Messenger of God ﷺ: "I adjure you by God who sent down the Torah upon Moses: do you find in it that God hates the fat rabbi? You are the fat rabbi, who has grown fat on the Malik (wealth) that the Jews feed you." The people laughed, and he became angry. Then he turned to ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, and said: "God did not send down anything upon a human being." So they took him away and put Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in his place.

It was also said: they were the polytheists, and the confrontation against them concerning the sending down of the Torah is because it was among them a well-known and widespread matter. Therefore they used to say: ﴿If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they﴾. The description of the Book as having "reached them" serves to increase the reproach and intensify the silencing.

Likewise, its restriction by His saying, exalted be He, ﴿as a light and guidance﴾ — for its being clear in itself and making other things clear is something that confirms the obligation to an extreme degree. Both words are in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of "the Book," and the governing element is "sent down," or they are a state of the pronoun in "bihi," and the governing element is "came."

The lam in His saying, exalted be He, ﴿for the people﴾ either relates to "guidance," or to an omitted word that is its adjective; that is: guidance existing for the people. The intended meaning here is not merely to oblige them to acknowledge the sending down of the Torah only, but also the sending down of the Qur'an, for acknowledging the sending down of the Torah necessarily entails acknowledging the sending down of the Qur'an with certainty, because of the evidences in it that speak to it.

He has censured them for what they did to it of distortion and alteration, where it is said: ﴿You make it into scrolls﴾ — that is, you put it into scattered pieces and separated pages, with the preposition omitted, based on treating the scrolls as an indefinite adverbial noun of place; or you make it the very scrolls in pieces. In this there is additional rebuke for their evil conduct, as though they had removed it from the category of Book and placed it in the position of blank scrolls devoid of writing. The clause is a circumstantial state, as has preceded.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿which you display﴾ is an adjective of "scrolls."

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿and you conceal much﴾ (p-162) is conjoined to it, and the returning pronoun to the relative is omitted; that is, much of it.

It was also said: it is an independent sentence with no place in the grammatical structure, and the intended meaning of "much" is the descriptions of the Prophet, upon whom be blessings and peace, and the rest of what they concealed of the rulings of the Torah. The three verbs were also read with the yā' (third person), taking the form of "they said": ﴿And they did not measure﴾.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿And you were taught what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾ — it was said: it is a circumstantial state of the subject of "you make it," with or without the particle qad, according to the difference of the two opinions.

I say: it should be taken that "what" refers to what they took from the Book of sciences and laws, so that the restriction by the circumstantial clause serves to confirm the rebuke and intensify the reproach. For what they did to the Book of separating and cutting it up, together with what was mentioned of disclosing and concealing, is a great abomination in itself, and with the consideration that it was the source of their sciences and knowledge, it is even more abominable and greater. It is not referring to what they received from the Prophet ﷺ in addition to what is in the Torah, and as clarification of what was obscure to them and to their fathers of its difficulties, as His saying, exalted be He, speaks to it: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an narrates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾, as they said; because their receiving that from the noble Qur'an is not something that restrains them from what they did with the Torah.

As for what came as an addition to what is in it, it has no connection to it, neither in negation nor affirmation. As for what came by way of clarification, the basis of what they did to it of alteration and distortion was not the obscurity and confusion of the matter that occurred in it, so that they would desist from that by its explanation and clarification; then the clause would be empty of the emphasis of rebuke at that point, and would not deserve to take the position of a circumstantial state. Rather, the proper reading then is that it is a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it regarding the coming of the Book, by way of completion, digression, and preparation, for what follows it of the coming of the Qur'an.

There is no way to take "what" as referring to what they concealed of the rulings of the Torah, as His saying, exalted be He, makes clear: ﴿There has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾. For though its manifestation would be a deterrent for them from concealment for fear of exposure, and would validate the clause's placement in the position of a circumstantial state, yet that is something the concealers know with certainty.

This is said: it was also said the address is to those of Quraysh who believed, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾.

His saying, exalted be He, ﴿Say: God﴾ is a command to the Messenger of God ﷺ to answer on their behalf, indicating that the answer is determined, such that there is no deviating from it, and as notice that they were silenced and were not able to speak at all.

﴿Then leave them in their plunging﴾ — in their falsehood in which they plunge, and there is no concern for you after the establishment of the proof and the silencing.

﴿Playing﴾ is a circumstantial state of the first pronoun; the adverbial phrase is related to the preceding or following verb, or it is related to an omitted element that is a circumstantial state of the first object, or of the subject of the second, or of the second pronoun, since it is in reality the subject; and the adverbial phrase is connected to the first.

This is a Book which We have sent down, blessed, confirming that which was before it, and that you may warn the Mother of Towns and those around it.

Translation of the passage:

"This is a Book which We have sent down" — a confirmation of the descent of the noble Qur'an after the affirmation of the descent of what the Torah gave good tidings of, and a refutation of them in their hideous statement following upon a denial.

"Blessed" — that is, abundant in benefits and copious in advantages.

"Confirming that which was before it" — from the Torah, due to its descent as described in it; or the books that came before it. For it confirms all of them in establishing monotheism and commanding it, and in negating polytheism and forbidding it, and in all the fundamental principles of the sacred laws that are not abrogated.

"And that you may warn the Mother of Towns" — a conjunction upon what is implied by "blessed": that is, for the blessings and that you may warn the people of Makkah. It is mentioned by its name, which indicates that it is the greatest of towns in status and the qibla for its people as a whole; as a notice that warning its people is a root that entails warning the people of the earth entirely. It is also read (p-163) "li-yundhira" with the ya', with the pronoun referring to the Book.

"And those around it" — from the people of settled dwellings and of tents, in the east and the west.

"And those who believe in the Hereafter" — and in what it contains of the varieties of punishment.

"Believe in it" — that is, in the Book, because they fear the consequence, and fear does not cease to move them to reflection and contemplation until they believe in it.

"And they are over their prayers ever watchful" — the singling out of their watchfulness over the prayer for mention, from among all the acts of worship that believers must perform, is to indicate its pre-eminence among all acts of obedience, and that it is the most noble of acts of worship after faith.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 6, Verse 93**

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God﴾, and claims that He has sent him as a prophet, like Musaylima the Liar (al-Kadhdhab) and al-Aswad al-'Ansi, or who invents against Him rulings concerning what is lawful and what is forbidden, like 'Amr ibn Luhayy and his followers. That is: he is more unjust than every unjust person. Although the construction (sabk al-tarkib) of the verse is in the form of negating anyone more unjust than him, and denying it, without addressing the negation or denial of an equal to him. This is because the common usage in your saying, "Who is more excellent than Zayd?" or "There is none more noble than him," means that he is more excellent than every excellent person, and more noble than every noble person. The full discussion of this has already passed.

﴿Or says, "It has been revealed to me"﴾, from Him, the Exalted.

﴿while nothing has been revealed to him﴾; that is, while the situation is that nothing at all has been revealed to him,

﴿nothing﴾ at all, like 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, who used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ). When the verse was revealed, "And We created man from an extract of clay" (﴿وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنا الإنْسانَ مِن سُلالَةٍ مِن طِينٍ﴾), and when it reached, "Then We produced him as another creation" (﴿ثُمَّ أنْشَأْناهُ خَلْقًا آخَرَ﴾), 'Abd Allah said, "So blessed is God, the best of creators" (﴿فَتَبارَكَ اللَّهُ أحْسَنُ الخالِقِينَ﴾), out of wonder at the detailed account of the creation of man. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Write it down just like that." 'Abd Allah doubted and said, "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me just as it was revealed to him, and if he is lying, then I have said just as he said."

﴿And who says, "I will reveal the like of what God has revealed"﴾, like those who said, "If we willed, we could say the like of this" (﴿لَوْ نَشاءُ لَقُلْنا مِثْلَ هَذا﴾).

﴿And if you could see when the wrongdoers﴾: the object of "see" (tara) has been omitted, because the adverbial of time (al-zarf, adverb of time) indicates it. That is: "And if you could see the wrongdoers when they are﴾

﴿in the agonies of death﴾; that is, its severities, from "ghamara" (to overwhelm) when it covers someone.

﴿with the angels extending their hands﴾ to seize their souls, like a creditor who is harsh and insistent, who extends his hand toward the one who owes him the debt, and presses him in demanding it without granting respite or leniency.

Or, "extending their hands" with punishment, saying: ﴿Bring out your souls﴾; that is: bring out your souls to Us from your bodies, and free your souls from punishment.

﴿Today﴾; that is: at the time of death, or the extended time after it, without any end.

﴿you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation﴾; that is: the punishment that includes severity and disgrace. Its being attributed to "humiliation" (al-hun, i.e., disgrace) is because of its firm establishment in it.

﴿for what you used to say about God other than the truth﴾, such as taking a son for Him, attributing a partner to Him, and claiming prophethood and revelation falsely.

﴿And you used to be arrogant toward His signs﴾, so you did not reflect upon them and did not believe in them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 94:**

﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone﴾ for the reckoning.

﴿Alone [furada]﴾ (p-164), separated from wealth and children, and from everything else that you preferred in the world; or separated from the helpers and the idols which you used to claim were your intercessors. It is the plural of fard (single), and the alif is for the feminine, like kusala (lazy). It has also been read as firadan (like rikhal), as furad (like thulath), and as fardā (like sakrā).

﴿As We created you the first time﴾ is a substitute (badal) for furada; that is, in the state in which you were born, alone. Or it is a second circumstantial clause (hal) according to those who permit multiple circumstantial clauses. Or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in furada; that is, resembling the beginning of your creation, naked, barefoot, and uncircumcised. Or it is an adjectival description of the verbal noun of ji'tumūna; that is, a coming like Our creating you the first time.

﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾, which We granted you as a favour in the world, so you were occupied with it and turned away from the Hereafter.

﴿Behind your backs﴾: you have sent forward nothing of it, and you did not carry away even a speck (naqir).

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners among you﴾; that is, partners of God Most High in lordship and in the entitlement to worship.

﴿Indeed, the connection between you has been severed﴾; that is, the severing has occurred between you, just as it is said: "The two things were joined (jumi'a bayna)"; that is, the joining was brought about between them.

It has been read as bainukum with a nominative (raf') vowel, treating the verb as ascribed to the adverbial noun (zarf), as it is said: "He was fought in front of you and behind you." Or it is because al-bayn is a noun for separation and connection; that is, your connection has been severed. It has also been read as mā baynakum.

﴿And there has gone astray from you﴾; that is, it was lost or disappeared.

﴿What you used to claim﴾ that they were your intercessors, or that there would be no resurrection and no recompense.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Splitter of the grain and the date-stone.﴾ This begins the affirmation of some of His acts, the Exalted, which indicate the perfection of His knowledge and power, and the subtlety of His craftsmanship and wisdom, following the establishment of the proofs of tawhid (the oneness of God).

Al-falq (splitting) is a cleaving with separation; that is, the Cleaver of the grain so that plants emerge, and of the date-stone so that trees emerge. It has been said that the meaning is the split that is in the grains and the date-stones; that is, their Creator in that manner, as in your saying: "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen its bottom." It has also been said that al-falq means al-khalq (creation). Al-Wahidi said: "They took fāliq in the sense of fāṭir (the Originator)."

﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾; that is, He brings forth what grows, from among animals and plants, from what does not grow, such as the sperm-drop and the seed. The clause is a resumed sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. It has been said that it is a second predicate of inna (indeed).

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and Bringer-forth of the dead﴾ such as the sperm-drop and the seed,

﴿from the living﴾ such as animals and plants, is conjoined (ʿatf) to "Splitter of the grain", not to "He brings forth" according to the first view, because bringing forth the dead from the living is not of the same kind as the splitting of the grain and the date-stone.

﴿That is Allah﴾: the Mighty in power, the Great in station, He is.

﴿Allah﴾: the One deserving worship alone.

﴿So how are you turned away?﴾ How then are you diverted from His worship to other than Him, when there is no path to it at all?

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 96:**

﴿He is the Splitter of the dawn﴾. It is another predicate (*khabar*) of *inna*, or the predicate of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, topic). *al-Isbah* (the dawn) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as the name of the morning (*al-Subh*). It is also read as *Asbah* with a fatha on the hamza, as the plural of *subh*. The meaning is: the One who splits the column of dawn (*'amud al-fajr*) from the whiteness of day and its brightening, or the One who splits the darkness of the dawn, which is the dim light that follows the morning (*al-ghabash alladhi yali al-subh*). It is also read as *fa'ilaq* (﴿Splitter﴾ in the accusative), in the sense of praise (*al-madh*).

﴿And He made the night a resting-place﴾. The tired person rests in it from the day, finding repose in it. It is from *sakana ilayhi*, meaning to be at peace with something and find comfort in it. Or the creatures rest in it, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you may rest therein﴾.

It is also read as *jā'il al-layl* (the active participle), so that *sakanan* (as a resting-place) is in the accusative by a verb implied by *jā'il*. It is said that it is governed by itself (*bi-nafsihi*), on the basis that what is meant is the continuous making that renews itself as the times renew, not the past making alone. It is also said that the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) of a verb that takes two objects governs the second object even when it has the meaning of the past, because when it is annexed to the first object, its governing of the second is fixed, since annexation is impossible after that.

﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ are conjoined to *al-layl* (the night), and on the last reading they are conjoined to its position (*mahalluhu*). It is said that they are conjoined to its position, and it is best to put them in the accusative then by a verb implied. They have also been read in the genitive and in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with the predicate omitted, meaning: *majulan* (made).

﴿As a computation﴾, i.e., in different orbits by which the times are reckoned, to which worship and transactions are tied. Or they are reckoned as a reckoning. *Husban* with a damma is the verbal noun of *hasaba*, just as *hisab* with a kasra is the verbal noun of *hasiba*.

﴿That﴾ refers to making them so, and the sense of distance in it indicates the exalted rank of what is referred to and its remoteness of station. That is: that wondrous ordaining.

﴿Is the decree of the Almighty﴾, the Victorious, the Dominant, to whom nothing among things is refractory, of which among them is ordaining them in this specific manner.

﴿The All-Knowing﴾ of all things known, among which is what is in that ordaining of benefits and interests, connected to the livelihood and the afterlife of creatures.

The Most High's words, ﴿And He it is who made the stars for you﴾, begin an account of His favour in the stars, following His account of His favour in the two luminaries (the sun and the moon). The verb *ja'ala* (to make, to bring into being) is transitive to one object, and the preposition phrase *lakum* (for you) is attached to it. The explicit object, *al-nujum* (the stars), is placed after the prepositional phrase in order to draw attention to what comes first and to create suspense about what follows. This has been noted more than once before. The meaning is: He brought them into existence and originated them for your sake.

Then His words, Most High, ﴿that you may be guided by them﴾, are a substitution (*badal*) from the prepositional phrase, with the governing verb repeated. This is a *badal al-ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), as in His words, Most High, ﴿We would surely have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾. The sense is: He made the stars for you, for your being guided. However, this does not mean that guidance is the sole purpose for which they were created. Rather, it is a method of singling out some of their benefits and purposes for mention, as the context requires.

It has also been permitted that *li-tahtadu* (that you may be guided) be a second object of *ja'ala*, with the verb meaning "to render" (*al-tasyir*). The sense would then be: He made them to be, for your guidance during your journeys, when you enter deserts or seas.

This is indicated by His words, Most High, ﴿in the darknesses of the land and the sea﴾. That is, in the darknesses of the night, on land and at sea. Their attribution to these two is by way of association, since the need for guidance by them arises only at such times. Or, it refers to confusing paths, and the darkness is used for them as a metaphor (*isti'ara*).

﴿We have detailed the signs﴾. That is, We have made clear the recited signs that remind of His favours, of which this favour is one, or the cosmic signs that indicate His affairs, set out in detail.

﴿for a people who know﴾. That is, who know the meanings of the signs mentioned and act in accordance with their requirements, or who reflect upon the cosmic signs and thereby know the reality of the matter. The detailing is specified for them, although it is general to all, because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 98:

﴿And it is He who produced you from a single soul﴾ — a reminder of another of His blessings, which indicates the greatness of His power and the subtlety of His craftsmanship and wisdom; that is: He produced you, despite your multitude, from the soul of Adam, peace be upon him.

﴿so there is a place of settlement and a place of storage﴾; that is: for you there is settling in the loins or upon the earth, and storage in the wombs or under the earth; or there is a place of settling and storage among what has been mentioned. The expression for their being in the loins or upon the earth as "settling" is because these are their natural abode, just as the expression for their being in the wombs or under the earth as "storage" is because neither of these is their natural abode. "Storage" has been interpreted as their being in the loins, but this is not clear.

It is also read: (فَمُسْتَقِرٌّ) with a kasra on the qaf; that is: "so among you there is one who settles and among you there is one who is stored," for settling is from us (p-166), unlike storage.

﴿We have detailed the signs﴾ that clarify the details of the creation of mankind from this verse and its like.

﴿for a people who understand﴾ the subtle fine points by employing discernment and scrutinizing the nuances of God's, Mighty and Majestic is He, craftsmanship in the stages of the creation of the children of Adam, which intellects are bewildered in comprehending. This is the secret in choosing "understand" (yafqahun) over "know" (ya'lamun), as occurred regarding the matter of the stars.

This is He who sends down water from the sky (﴿وَهُوَ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً﴾), a reminder of another of His blessings, indicating the perfection of His power and the vastness of His mercy. That is: He sent down from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky, a particular water, which is rain. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the direct object is for a reason already mentioned repeatedly.

﴿فَأخْرَجْنا بِهِ﴾ ("So We brought forth by it") shifts to the first-person plural, to show the great concern with the matter for which the water was sent down. That is: We brought forth, by Our might, with that water, despite its unity.

﴿نَباتَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("the growth of every thing") refers to the things whose nature is to grow, of the kinds of plants and trees and their various types, differing in quantity and quality, in properties and effects, with varying degrees of increase and decrease, as His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit﴾ (13:4).

His saying the Exalted: ﴿فَأخْرَجْنا مِنهُ خَضِرًا﴾ ("So We brought forth from it green [vegetation]") begins the detailed explanation of what was summarized in the bringing forth. It begins with the detail of the state of the plants: that is, We brought forth from the vegetation that has no stalk something tender and green. It is said: شَيْءٌ أخْضَرُ وخَضِرٌ ("a thing is akhdar and khadir"), like أعْوَرُ وعَوِرٌ ("one-eyed"). The word khadir is used most often for that whose greenness is natural, and it is what branches out from the base of the plant that emerges from the seed.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿نُخْرِجُ مِنهُ﴾ ("We bring forth from it") is an adjective of خَضِرًا ("green"), or the present-tense form is used to make the scene present to the mind because of its strangeness. That is: We bring forth from that green [vegetation].

﴿حَبًّا مُتَراكِبًا﴾ ("grain piled up") is the ear of grain containing grains layered one upon another in a specific form. It was also read: (يَخْرُجُ مِنهُ حَبٌّ مُتَراكِبٌ) ("there comes forth from it piled grain").

His saying the Exalted: ﴿وَمِنَ النَّخْلِ﴾ ("And from the date palms") begins the detailed explanation of the state of the trees, after the explanation of the state of the plants. So the phrase "مِنَ النَّخْلِ" ("from the date palms") is a fronted predicate (خَبَرٌ مُقَدَّمٌ, khabar muqaddam).

His saying the Exalted: ﴿مِن طَلْعِها﴾ ("from its spathes") is a substitute (بَدَلٌ, badal, substitution) for it, with the governing verb repeated, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for whoever hopes for Allah...﴾ (33:21), etc.

الطَّلْعُ ("al-ṭalʿ") is the thing that comes out of the date palm, as if it were two closed sandals with the fruit clustered between them.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿قِنْوانٌ﴾ ("clusters") is a subject (مُبْتَدَأٌ, mubtada', subject); that is, and from the spathes of the date palm there are clusters. It is also permissible for the predicate to be omitted, because of what is indicated by أخْرَجْنا ("We brought forth") in it; that is, and brought forth from the spathes of the date palm are clusters.

As for the one who reads (يَخْرُجُ مِنهُ حَبٌّ مُتَراكِبٌ) ("there comes forth from it piled grain"), قِنْوانٌ ("clusters") is, in his reading, coordinated (مَعْطُوفًا, ma'tuf) upon حَبٌّ ("grain"). It was also said: the meaning is: And We brought forth from the date palms palms whose spathes are clusters; or, and from the date palms is something from its spathes, clusters. قِنْوانٌ is the plural of قِنْوٌ, which is the cluster of the date palm, like صِنْوٌ and صِنْوانٌ. It was read with a ḍamma on the qāf, like ذِئْبٌ and ذُؤْبانٌ, and also with a fatḥa on it, considering it a collective noun (اسْمُ جَمْعٍ, ism jam', collective noun), because فَعْلانٌ is not one of the patterns of the plural.

﴿دانِيَةٌ﴾ ("hanging low") means easy to pick, close to the one who plucks it; for although it is small, the one sitting can reach it, and it bears fruit without needing to wait for height. Or it means: intertwined and close together. The mention of it alone is sufficient because it indicates its counterpart, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ (16:81), and to increase the blessing in it.

﴿وَجَنّاتٍ مِن أعْنابٍ﴾ ("and gardens of grapevines") is coordinated upon ﴿نَباتَ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ ("the growth of every thing"); that is, and We brought forth by it gardens consisting of grapevines. It was also read: (جَنّاتٌ) with a ḍamma ("gardens") as a beginning (مُبْتَدَأٌ) ; that is, and for you... (p-167) or there are gardens.

It has also been permitted to coordinate it upon قِنْوانٌ, as if it were said: and there are clusters, or brought forth from the date palms are clusters, and gardens of plants and grapevines. Perhaps the repetition of "gardens" here, without being content with the collective noun, is as in what precedes and what follows, because benefit from this kind is generally not attainable except when a group of its individuals is gathered together.

﴿والزَّيْتُونَ والرُّمّانَ﴾ ("and the olive and the pomegranate") are in the accusative on the basis of specification (عَلى الِاخْتِصاصِ, ikhtisas), because these two kinds are esteemed by them; or on the basis of coordination upon نَباتَ ("growth").

His saying the Exalted: ﴿مُشْتَبِهًا وغَيْرَ مُتَشابِهٍ﴾ ("resembling and not resembling") is a circumstantial state (حالٌ, ḥāl) of الزَّيْتُونِ ("the olive"), and it is sufficient for it in place of the state of what is coordinated upon it, just as the predicate of the coordinated-upon item is sufficient in place of the predicate of the coordinated item, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (9:62). Its underlying form is: the olive resembling and not resembling, and the pomegranate likewise.

It has also been permitted that it be a state of الرُّمّانِ ("the pomegranate") because of its proximity, and the omitted item would be the state of the first; the meaning: some of it resembling and some of it not resembling in form, quantity, color, taste, and other attributes that indicate the perfection of the power of its Maker and the wisdom of its Originator and Creator.

﴿انْظُرُوا إلى ثَمَرِهِ إذا أثْمَرَ﴾ ("Look at its fruit when it bears fruit"); that is: look at it with a gaze of consideration and insight: when it brings forth its fruit, how it brings it forth meager, hardly benefiting from it. It was also read: (إلى ثُمُرِهِ) ("at its fruits").

﴿وَيَنْعِهِ﴾ ("and its ripening"); that is: and [look] at the state of its ripening, how it reaches its fitting perfection, and becomes a thing combining many benefits. Originally اليَنْعُ ("yan'") is a verbal noun (مَصْدَرٌ, maṣdar) of يَنَعَتِ الثَّمَرُ ("the fruit ripened") when it became ripe. It was also said: it is the plural of يانِعٍ ("ripe"), like تاجِرٍ and تَجْرٍ. It was read with a ḍamma, and it is a dialect for it. It was also read: (يانِعِهِ) ("its ripe [fruit]").

﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكُمْ﴾ ("Indeed, in that") refers to what you were commanded to look at. The sense of distance in the demonstrative is to announce the high rank of what is pointed to and the remoteness of its station.

﴿لآياتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ ("are signs for a people who believe"); that is: indeed, there are great or numerous signs indicating the existence of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, and His oneness. For the occurrence of those diverse kinds and the varied types from one origin, and their transition from state to state in a wondrous pattern, which the minds are bewildered in understanding, can only be by the origination of a Maker who knows their details, and who prefers, from among the possible ways, what His wisdom requires over others, and whom no opposite opposing Him nor equal contending with Him can prevent from that.

Therefore it is followed by a rebuke of those who associated partners with Him, and a refutation of them, where it is said: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾; that is, they made in their belief, for God, whose state is what has been detailed within the midst of these sublime verses, partners.

﴿The jinn﴾; that is, the angels, as they worshipped them and said: "The angels are the daughters of God." They were called jinn because of their concealment (ijtinan), belittling their status in relation to the station of divinity. Or [it means] the devils, as they obeyed them as they obeyed God the Exalted; or they worshipped idols at their instigation and incitement; or they said: "God is the creator of good and of every beneficial thing, and Satan is the creator of evil and of every harmful thing," as is the view of the Dualists (al-thanawiyya).

The two objects of "made" (ja'alu) are His saying, the Exalted: ﴿partners, the jinn﴾. The second of them is placed before the first, out of extreme disapproval that God, glorified be He, should take any partner whatsoever, whatever it may be. And "for God" (lillah) is connected to "partners," and is placed before it for the aforementioned rhetorical purpose.

It is also said: they are two objects, "partners for God," and "the jinn" is an appositive (badal) to "partners," explaining it; this is stated by al-Farra' and Abu Ishaq. Or it is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, occurring as an answer to an implied question arising from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they made for God partners﴾, as if it were said: "Who did they make partners for God, the Exalted?" and it was answered: "The jinn"; that is, they made the jinn [partners]. This is supported by the reading of Abu Haywa and Yazid ibn Qutayb: (al-jinnu) in the nominative, on the assumption that they said "the jinn" in answer to one who asked: "Who are those whom they made partners for God, the Exalted?" It has also been read in the genitive, on the basis that the annexation is explanatory (lil-tabyin).

﴿And He created them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "made," with "qad" implied or not implied, according to the two opinions, emphasizing the extreme ugliness and falsehood inherent in their making that, given their knowledge of its content; that is: and indeed they knew that He, the Exalted, alone is their creator.

It is also said: the pronoun refers to the partners; that is, and the state is that God, the Exalted, created the jinn, so how can they make His creation a partner to Him, the Exalted? It was also read: (khalqahum), in conjunction with the jinn; that is, and [they made partners] what they fashion of idols; or in conjunction with "partners"; that is, and they made for Him their fabrication of falsehood, inasmuch as they attributed it to Him, the Exalted.

﴿And they forged for Him﴾; that is, they fabricated and invented for Him. It is said: "khalaqa al-ifk," "ikhtalaqahu," "kharaqahu," and "ikhtaraqahu" with the same meaning. It was also read: (kharraqu) with doubling for intensification, and it was read: (wa-harrafu lahu); that is, they falsified.

﴿Sons and daughters﴾. The Jews said: "Uzayr is the son of God," the Christians said: "The Messiah is the son of God," and a group of the Arabs said: "The angels are the daughters of God."

﴿Without knowledge﴾; that is, without knowledge of the reality of what they said, whether wrong or right, but rather hurling a saying out of blindness and ignorance, without thought or deliberation. Or [it means] without knowledge of the rank of what they said, and that it is of such heinousness and falsehood that its measure cannot be gauged. The preposition "bi" is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "kharaqu," or a qualifier of an emphatic infinitive object of it; that is: they forged while being involved in lack of knowledge, or a forging that occurs without knowledge.

﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) directed at declaring Him far exalted, Mighty and Majestic, above what they attributed to Him. "Subhanahu" is a proper noun (alam) for tasbih, which is distancing from evil in belief and in utterance; that is, the belief in His remoteness from it and the judgment of it, from "sabaha fi al-ard wa al-ma'" (to swim/glide through earth and water) when one goes far and deep in them, and from it: "faras sabuh" (a horse of wide running stride). Its accusative case is as a verbal noun (masdar), and its governing verb is hardly ever mentioned; that is, "I glorify Him" (usabbihu subhanahu); that is, I declare Him free of what does not befit Him in belief and in deed, a declaration specific to Him and worthy of His station. In it there is intensification from the aspect of derivation from "sabh," from the aspect of its transfer to the form "tafil," from the aspect of turning away from the verbal noun which denotes the genus to the noun devised specifically for Him, especially the proper noun that indicates the reality present in the mind, and from the aspect of its standing in the place of the verbal noun together with the verb.

It is also said: it is a verbal noun like "ghufran," since a verb from the triliteral root has been heard for it, as mentioned in al-Qamus.
