It is intended to mean: complete transcendence and total remoteness, so in it there is intensification in that transcendence is attributed to His holy essence; that is, He transcended by His essence in a manner fitting to Him. This is most suitable to His saying, glorified be He: ﴿and Exalted﴾, for it is necessarily conjoined to the implied verb.

And because "subhan" and "ta'ali" contain the meaning of remoteness, it is said: ﴿above what they describe﴾; that is, He is remote from what they describe Him as having, of partners or offspring.

**Badi' al-samawati wal-ard** (the Originator of the heavens and the earth): that is, their Creator and Inventor, without any pattern to imitate or any model to follow. *Badi'* is used in the sense of the one who originates, as the lexicographers have stated, like *al-sarikh* in the sense of *al-musrikh* (the one who calls for help). The verb *badaʿahu* (like *manaʿahu*) also means "he created it," as in *ibtada'ahu* (he originated it), as mentioned in al-Qamus and elsewhere. Its parallel is *al-sami'* in the sense of *al-musmi'* (the one who causes to hear) in the line of poetry:

*"Is it from Rayhana, the caller, the one who makes hear?"*

It has also been said that it is the attributive adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*) with its agent (*fa'il*) placed in the genitive case for lightness, after its being in the accusative, since it resembles the active participle, as is well known. That is: the originator of His heavens and His earth, from *bada'a*, when something is of a wondrous pattern, a remarkable form, and a delightful beauty. Or it may be taken as a noun of place (*zarf*), as in the saying "the betrayal is established," meaning that there is none like it in them. The first view is the preferred one, and the meaning is: He, exalted is He, is the originator of both regions of the world, the upper and the lower, without any material agent at all, exempt entirely from being affected. The parent is the source of the child and is affected by the transfer of his substance from himself, so how could He have a child?

It was also read as *badi'a* in the accusative, as praise, and in the genitive as a substitute (*badal*) for the noble Name, or for the pronoun in *subhanahu* (glory be to Him), according to the opinion of those who permit this. It is nominative in the well-known reading, as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as the subject (*fa'il*) of *ta'ala* (exalted is). Its being expressed in place of the pronoun serves to give the reason for the ruling, and the placing of the adverbial phrase between it and the verb is for the purpose of emphasizing its explanation.

Or it is the subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿how can He have a child?﴾. In the first two cases it is an independent sentence, brought, as the one before it was, to clarify the impossibility of what they attributed to Him, exalted is He, and to affirm His transcendence above it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He has no consort﴾ is a confirming circumstantial clause (*hal*) for the impossibility mentioned. The negation of His having a consort necessarily entails the negation of His having a child, since it is impossible for a child to exist without a mother, although it is possible for it to exist without a father. The negation of the first is beyond doubt for anyone, so from its necessity follows the negation of the second; that is: from where, or how, can He have a child, as they claimed, when, according to their own claim, He has no consort from whom the child could come?

It was also read as *lam yakun* (with the verb in the masculine), because the subject is separated from the verb, or because the subject is a pronoun referring to Him, exalted is He, and the predicate is the adverbial phrase. *Sahiba* (consort) is then the agent of the verb, raised because it depends on the subject. Or the adverbial phrase is a fronted predicate and *sahiba* is a delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of the verb *kana* (was). In this case the name may be a pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), since the clause is then suitable to explain the pronoun of the matter, but not in the first case, because it has been explained in its place that the pronoun of the matter is explained only by an explicit clause.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He created every thing﴾ is either another independent sentence brought to establish what has been mentioned of impossibility, or another circumstantial clause confirming it; that is: how can He have a child? And the case is that He created every thing that is comprised by existence and origination, from among the existents, of which is what they named a child for Him, exalted is He. So how can it be conceived that the created thing is the child of its Creator?

﴿And He is, of every thing﴾: it is proper to His nature that it be known, whatever it is, created or uncreated, as its expression by the change from the pronoun to the explicit noun indicates.

﴿Knowing﴾: intensive in knowledge, eternally and everlastingly, as the shift to the nominal sentence indicates. Nothing hidden is concealed from Him, of what has been and of what will be, of essences, attributes and states, among which are what is permissible for Him, exalted is He, and what is not permissible, among the impossibilities of which what they claimed is one instance. This sentence is a resumptive clause confirming the content of what precedes it of decisive proofs for the invalidity of their hideous doctrine, which they dared to utter without knowledge.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 102:

﴿Dhalikum﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the one described by the sublime attributes mentioned, and the notion of distance within it serves to indicate the exalted status of the one being pointed to and the remoteness of his rank in greatness. The address is to the polytheists previously mentioned, by way of iltifat (shift of address), and it is the subject (mubtada').

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is your Lord; there is no god but Him, the Creator of all things﴾ comprises four predicates in apposition (akhbar mutaradifa); that is: that One described by those great attributes is Allah, the one deserving of worship exclusively, the Owner of your affair, having no partner at all, the Creator of every thing, of what has been and of what will be. There is thus no repetition, since what is considered in the subject of the topic is only His being Creator of what has existed, as the past tense form indicates.

It is also said: the predicate is the first, and the rest are substitutes (abdal). It is said: the sublime name is a substitute for the subject, and the rest are predicates. It is said: a subject is to be supposed for each of the three predicates. It is said: the whole is treated as one single name.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him﴾ is a ruling consequent upon the content of the sentence, for whoever combines these attributes is the one deserving of worship exclusively.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾ is a conjunction with the preceding sentence (p-170); that is: He, together with the sublime attributes detailed, is the one who manages the affairs of all His creatures, of which you are part, so entrust your affairs to Him, and seek through worshipping Him the success of your worldly and otherworldly aims.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 103:

﴿No vision can grasp Him⦆ Al-basar (sight) is the faculty of seeing, and it may also be applied to the eye insofar as it is its seat. Idrak (grasping) of a thing is an expression for reaching it and encompassing it; that is, no sights reach Him or encompass Him, as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said.

ʿAtaʾ said: the sights of created beings fail to encompass Him, so there is no proof in this for those who deny the vision (of God) absolutely. It has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil, may Allah be pleased with them both: "No vision can grasp Him in this world, but He will be seen in the Hereafter."

﴿And He grasps the sights⦆; that is, His knowledge encompasses them, for nothing is hidden from Him.

﴿And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware⦆, so He grasps what sights cannot grasp. It is also possible that this is a justification for the two preceding rulings by way of al-laff (the method of wrapping, in which two matters are mentioned and each is explained by the other); that is, "No vision can grasp Him because He is the Subtle, and He grasps the sights because He is the All-Aware." Thus the meaning of "subtle" is derived from its opposite, the dense, namely that which is not perceived by the sense and does not imprint upon it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 104:

Allah's words, ﴿There have certainly come to you clear proofs (basa'ir) from your Lord﴾, form a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), uttered on the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). Basa'ir is the plural of basira, which is the light by which the soul gains insight, just as sight (basar) is a light by which the eye sees. What is meant by it is the sign (ayah) mentioned here, or all the signs that are arranged together with it in an initial arrangement.

"Min" (from) denotes the starting point of the act, used metaphorically, whether it is connected to "jaa'a" (came) or to an omitted word that serves as an attribute of basa'ir. The mention of the title Lord (rabb), together with its attachment to the pronoun of the addressees, is to show the complete kindness toward them; that is: there has come to you, from the direction of your Owner and the one who conveys to you your perfection that befits you, the revelation that speaks the truth and the right, which is like insights for the hearts; or there have come to you insights existing from your Lord.

﴿So whoever sees﴾; that is: sees the truth through those insights and believes in it.

﴿then it is for his own self﴾; that is: he sees for his own self, or his seeing is for his own self, because its benefit is specific to it.

﴿And whoever is blind﴾; that is: whoever does not see the truth after it has become clear to him through those insights, a clear manifestation, and goes astray from it. It is only expressed as blindness to disparage him and to repel others from him.

﴿then against himself﴾; that is: against himself he is blind, or his blindness is upon himself, or the burden of his blindness is upon him.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾; but I am only a warner, and Allah is the One who watches over your deeds and recompenses you for them.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 105:**

﴿And thus do We vary the signs﴾; that is: in the same wondrous manner of variation, We vary the signs that indicate the sublime meanings, which unveil the exalted realities, not with a variation inferior to it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that they may say, "You have studied"﴾ is a causal clause (ʿillah) for a verb that has been omitted, relying on the indication of the context; that is: and that they may say, "You have studied," (We do what We do of the aforementioned variation).

The lam here is of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), and the waw is parenthetical (iʿtiraḍiyyah). It has been said that it is conjunctive (ʿatifah) upon a omitted cause, and the lam is connected to "We vary"; that is: in the same manner of variation We vary the signs, so that We may establish the proof against them, and that they may say... etc.

It has also been said: the lam is the lam of command (lam al-amr), and the reading with a sukun on the lam supports it, as if it were said: "And thus We vary the signs, and let them say what they say," for there is no concern for them and no regard for their speech. This is a command whose meaning is threat, intimidation, and disregard for their words. It was rejected on the grounds that what follows it refutes it.

The meaning of "darasta" is: you read and you learned. It was also read as "darasta" (with alif), that is: you studied with the scholars. And "darasta" means: these verses became old and effaced, as they said: "the fables of the ancients." "Darusat" with a damma on the ra' is an intensive form of "darasat," that is: its effacement intensified. "Durisat" in the passive form means: it was recited, or it was effaced, or it was studied. They interpreted it as: the Jews studied with Muhammad (ﷺ), and the omission of the subject was permissible because of their being well known for study.

It has also been permitted to attribute the verb to the verses, while in reality it belongs to their people; that is: the people of the verses and their bearers studied with Muhammad (ﷺ), and they are the People of the Book. "Darasa," that is: Muhammad studied. "Darisat," that is: they are worn out; that is: ancient, or possessing study, like "a pleasing life."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that We may make it clear﴾ is conjoined to "that they may say," and the lam is in its original sense, because clarification is the ultimate aim of variation. The pronoun refers to the signs in terms of meaning, or to the Qur'an though it has not been mentioned, or to the verbal noun; that is: and that We may effect the clarification.

The lam in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for a people who know﴾ is connected to "clarification," and its specification to them is because they are the ones who benefit from it. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are His friends whom He guided to the path of right guidance. Describing them with knowledge is to announce the extent of the ignorance of the earlier ones and their complete emptiness of knowledge.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 106:

﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord.﴾ When the disbelievers' disparagement of the signs (al-tasrif al-ayat) was related, it was followed by the command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to remain steadfast in what he is upon, and not to give any weight to them or to their falsehoods. That is, persist in what you are upon of following what has been revealed to you of the laws and rulings, the foundation of which is monotheism (tawhid). And in the mention of the title of Lordship (rububiyya) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is a manifest display of kindness towards him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no god but Him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) between the two coordinated commands, emphasizing the obligation to follow the revelation, especially in the matter of monotheism. It has also been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "your Lord," meaning: singular in divinity.

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾: do not concern yourself with them and their false sayings, of which is what has been related about them just now. And whoever holds that this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf) understands turning away as encompassing refraining from them (al-kaff 'anhum).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 107:

﴿And had God willed﴾; that is, that they not associate partners (with Him), in accordance with the established rule regarding the omission of the object of the verb of willing (mashi'ah) when it occurs as a conditional, and the object being what is implied by the consequent (jaza').

﴿they would not have associated﴾. This is evidence that He, exalted is He, does not will the faith of the disbeliever. However, this is not in the sense that He, exalted is He, prevents him from it while he is directed towards it; rather, it means that He, exalted is He, does not will it from him, because his partial choice (ikhtiyar juz'i) is not turned towards faith, and he persists in disbelief. The clause is a parenthetical (i'tiraD) that emphasizes the turning away (i'raD).

Likewise is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And We have not appointed you a guardian over them﴾; that is, a watcher, a overseer from Our side, who keeps watch over their deeds.

Likewise is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Nor are you a trustee over them﴾ on their behalf, who manages their affairs and arranges their interests. And "over them" (alayhim) in both places is connected to what follows it, placed before it for emphasis on it, or for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (fawasil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 108:

﴿And do not revile those who call upon other than Allah﴾; that is: do not insult them with regard to their worship of their deities, such as by saying: "Perish you and what you worship," for example.

﴿lest they revile Allah in enmity﴾ transgressing from truth into falsehood, by saying to you the same as what you say to them.

﴿without knowledge﴾; that is: in ignorance of Allah, the Exalted, and of what is due to be mentioned about Him. It is also read as ('udwan) [عُدُوًّا], from: ʿadā yaʿdū, ʿudūwan, ʿidāʾan, and ʿudwānan.

It is related that they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when there was revealed His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship other than Allah are fuel for Hell﴾: "You will surely cease reviling our gods, or we will surely revile your God." It was also said: the Muslims used to revile them, so they were forbidden from that, lest their reviling lead to their reviling of Him, glorified and exalted be He. In this is the principle that when obedience leads to a greater disobedience, it becomes obligatory to abandon it, for that which leads to evil is itself evil.

﴿Thus﴾; that is: like that strong adornment.

﴿We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ of good and evil, by bringing about that which empowers them to them and drives them toward it, through success or abandonment. It is also permissible that by "every community" is meant the communities of disbelievers, since the discussion concerns them; and by "their deeds" is meant their evil and corruption, and the thing likened is the adornment of reviling Allah, the Exalted, for them.

﴿Then to their Lord﴾, the Master of their affair, ﴿is their return﴾; that is: their return by resurrection after death, ﴿and He will inform them﴾ without delay

﴿of what they used to do﴾ in the world, persistently, of the evil deeds made attractive to them. This is a threat of recompense and punishment, like a man's saying to one who threatens him: "I will inform you of what you did." In this there is a secret subtlety founded on a noble wisdom: that everything that appears in this creation, whether substances or accidents, appears in a borrowed form different from its true form by which it appears in the Hereafter. Sins are deadly poisons that have emerged in the world in a certain form, which the souls of the sinners find pleasing, as this noble verse expresses.

Likewise acts of obedience: although they are the most beautiful of beauties, they have appeared to them in a hateful form. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and Hellfire is surrounded by desires." Thus the deeds of the disbelievers have appeared to them in this creation in an adorned form that the deviant find pleasing and the tyrants love, but they will manifest in the Hereafter in their true, repugnant and terrifying form. At that point they will know what their deeds really are. So the manifestation of these deeds in their true forms is expressed by informing them of them, because each of the two is a means of knowing their reality as it is. So let it be pondered.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they swore by God﴾. It is narrated that the Quraysh proposed some signs, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If I do some of what you say, will you believe me?" They said: "Yes," and they swore that if he did it, they would all believe. The Muslims then asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to send it down, hoping for their faith, and he (ﷺ) intended to supplicate; so it was revealed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with their most emphatic oaths﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); that is, they swore by Him, may He be exalted, exerting themselves in their oaths.

﴿If a sign comes to them﴾ from among what they proposed, or from the kind of signs, and this is most fitting to their state of obstinacy and stubbornness, and the extent of their affair in insolence and corruption, since they did not regard the dazzling miracles they witnessed as being of the kind of signs.

﴿they will surely believe in it﴾. The aim of their request was nothing but to dictate to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in seeking a miracle, and to disregard the clear proofs they had witnessed from him, which deserve that the earth be cut through by them and the mountains be set in motion.

﴿Say: Signs are only with God﴾; that is, all of them, so what they proposed enters into it by primary inclusion.

﴿with God﴾; that is, their affair is in His judgment and decree specifically, He disposes of them according to His will, which is based on profound wisdoms; no one's power or will has any connection to them or to any of their affairs, neither independently nor jointly in any manner, so that I could undertake to bring them down by request. This, as you see, is a closing of the door of proposing in the most eloquent and finest manner, (p-173) by explaining the exalted status of signs, the difficulty of attaining them, and their loftiness above being subject to request and proposal.

As for what has been said: that the meaning is: signs are with God, the Exalted, not with me, so how can I respond to you with them or bring them to you, since He is the One able to do so, not I, so that I could bring them to you; this has no fitting relation to the context. How could it, since their proposal is not for their coming apart from God's power and will, so that they would be answered with this?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come, they will not believe?﴾ is a resumed statement, not included under the command, delivered from Him, may He be exalted, to explain the wisdom motivating what the preceding answer implied of the non-coming of the signs. It was addressed to the Muslims, either specifically by way of shifting address (talwīn), since they were eager for their descent hoping for their Islam, or together with him (ﷺ) by way of generalization, in light of what is narrated from him (ﷺ) of intending to supplicate; and it has been made clear therein that their oaths are sinful, and that their faith is among what does not fall under existence, even if they were answered in what they asked.

The "mā" is interrogative of denial, but not on the basis that the denial's reference is the occurrence of what is implied; rather it is the very act of implying together with the realization of what is implied in itself. That is: what thing makes you know that the sign they propose, when it comes, they will not believe, but will remain upon their disbelief and obstinacy? That is, you do not know that, so that you would wish for its coming in hope of their faith. This is, as it were, an expression of excuse on the part of the Muslims in their wishing for the descent of the signs.

It has been said: "lā" is extra (ṣilah), so the denial is directed at both the implication and the implied together: what thing makes you know their faith upon the coming of the signs, so that you wish for their coming in hope of their faith? This would be a correction of the opinion of the Muslims.

It has been said: "anna" means "la'alla" (perhaps). It is said: "Enter the market, perhaps (annaka) you will buy meat," and "ʿannaka," "ʿallaka," and "la'allaka" are all with the same meaning. This is supported by the reading: (la'allahā idhā jā'at lā yu'minūn), with the statement being complete before it, and the second object of "yush'iruka" being omitted, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will make you know that he may purify himself?﴾

The clause is a resumption to give the reason for the denial and its confirmation; that is: what thing makes you know their state and what will be when the signs come: perhaps when they come they will not believe in them? Why then do you wish for their coming? For his wishing is only fitting when their faith in them is certain to exist upon their coming, not when its non-existence is hoped for.

It is also read: (innahā) with a kasra, on the basis that it is a resumption as previously, with added confirmation of their non-faith. It is also read: (lā tu'minūn) with the second person, so the address in "wa-mā yush'irukum" is to the polytheists. It is also read: (wa-mā yush'iruhum annahā idhā jā'athum lā yu'minūn), so the reference of the denial is the polytheists' undertaking of the aforementioned oath, together with their ignorance of the state of their hearts upon the coming of the signs, and of its being then as it is now.

﴿وَنُقَلِّبُ أفْئِدَتَهم وأبْصارَهُمْ﴾ ["and We turn their hearts and their sights"] is in conjunction (ʿaṭf) with "﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾" ["they will not believe"]. It falls under the ruling of "﴿ما يُشْعِرُكم﴾" ["what will make you aware"] and is restricted by the same restriction that applies to it. That is: "And what will make you aware that We turn their hearts away from grasping the truth, so that they do not understand it, and their sights away from witnessing it, so that they do not see it? But not while they are directed toward it and prepared to accept it. Rather, it is because of their complete aversion from it and their total turning away." This is why its mention is delayed beyond the mention of their not believing, to indicate that they are original in disbelief, and to preclude the assumption that their not believing arises from God's turning their perceptive faculties by way of compulsion.

﴿كَما لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا بِهِ﴾ ["as they did not believe in it"]: that is, in what came of the signs.

﴿أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾ ["the first time"]: that is, at the time the preceding signs came. The kāf (ك) is in the accusative position, as it is an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar) in the accusative, governed by "﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾". The mā (ما) is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah). That is: "they will not believe, but will disbelieve, with a disbelief like their disbelief the first time." The placement of the turning of hearts and sights between them is because it is among the completions of their not believing.

﴿وَنَذَرُهُمْ﴾ ["and We leave them"] is in conjunction with "﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾", falls under the ruling of the rhetorical interrogative (al-istifhām al-inkārī), and is restricted by what restricts it. It clarifies what is meant by the turning of hearts (p-174) and sights, and indicates its reality: it is not in its outward sense, namely that God, glorified is He, turns their perceptive faculties away from the truth while they are directed toward it and prepared for it, by way of compulsion. Rather, it means that He leaves them to themselves after it has been known that their preparedness is corrupt, their aversion from the truth is extreme, and the gentle guidance (luṭf) has no effect on them at all. He seals their hearts in accordance with what their preparedness requires, as we have indicated.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فِي طُغْيانِهِمْ﴾ ["in their transgression"], is connected to "﴿نَذَرُهم﴾".

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ ["wandering blindly"], is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in the accusative position in "﴿نَذَرُهم﴾". That is: "We leave them in their transgression, bewildered, not guiding them with the guidance given to the believers." Or it is a second object (mafʿūl thānin) of "﴿نَذَرُهم﴾", meaning: "We make them heedless."

It is read as "﴿يُقَلِّبُ﴾ and ﴿يَذَرُ﴾" with the yā' (ي), attributing both verbs to the pronoun of the Divine Name (ḍamīr al-jalālah). It is also read as "﴿تُقَلَّبُ﴾" with the tā' (ت) and in the passive form, attributing it to "﴿أفْئِدَتَهم﴾" ["their hearts"].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 111:

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels﴾ — an explicit statement of what was implied by His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: "And what will make you know that when they come they will not believe?" — part of the wisdom that calls for not granting what they demanded of the signs, following the clarification that they are, in His judgment and decree, which is founded upon the far-reaching wisdoms, such that no one has any role in their matter in any way; and it is a demonstration of the falsity of their profane oaths in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. That is to say: even if We had not confined ourselves to granting what they demanded here of a single sign from the signs, but rather had sent down to them the angels, as they asked Him by saying: ﴿Why has not the angel been sent down to us?﴾ and their saying: ﴿Why do you not bring the angels to us?﴾.

﴿And the dead had spoken to them﴾ and bore witness to the truth of faith after We had revived them, as they demanded by their saying: "Bring us our fathers."

﴿And We gathered﴾; that is, We assembled.

﴿Against them everything, in groups﴾ — with two dammas; it is also read with the ba' sukun. That is, guarantors of the correctness of the matter and the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), taking it as the plural of qabil meaning "guarantor," like raghif and rughuf, and qadib and qudub. This is the more fitting with His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Or you bring Allah and the angels as a guarantee﴾; that is, even if We had not confined ourselves to what they demanded, but added to that by bringing before them every thing from which a guarantee and testimony to what has been mentioned could come about, not individually, but together, or in groups, taking it as the plural of qabil. This is more suited to the generality of "everything" and its inclusion of the kinds and categories; that is, We gathered every thing kind by kind, category by category, and group by group. Its being in the accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal), and its collective form is in view of the collective whole that necessarily belongs to each individual whole. Or it is "before them" and "face to face," taking it as a verbal noun like qibalan, and it has been read thus as well.

Its accusative in both cases is as a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state. It has been transmitted from al-Mubarrad and a group of the people of language that the latter means "direction," as in your saying: "I have a right with (qibal) so-and-so," and that its accusative is as an adverb of place.

﴿They would not have believed﴾; that is, it would not have been right or proper for them to have faith, because of their persistence in disobedience and their extremity in rebellion and insolence. As for the prior decree against them with unbelief, it is among the rulings that follow from that, as His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying indicates: ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾ is an exception of the emptied type from the most general of states, and the turning to the Glorious Name is for the cultivation of awe and the introduction of dread; that is, they would not have believed, after the gathering of what has been mentioned of the matters that necessitate faith, in any state of the states that call to it, completing its mentioned requirements, except in the state of His, Exalted is He, willing their faith; or it is from the most general of causes; that is, they would not have believed for any cause of the counted causes and others, except by His, Exalted is He, willing it for them. In any case, the meaning of the exception is not to show that their faith is at risk of occurring, on the basis that His will, exalted is He, is also such, but rather to show the impossibility of its occurring on the basis of the impossibility of their occurrence, as if it were said: they would not have believed except that Allah wills, and far-fetched is that, and their state is their state, by the evidence of what preceded from His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts...﴾ the verse.

How could it be otherwise, when His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾ is a resumption from the content of the conditional clause after the mention of the exception, not before it. And there is no doubt that what they are ignorant of, whether the intended ones are the Muslims, which is the apparent meaning, or the swearers, is not that their non-faith is without the will of Allah, Exalted is He, as is the necessary implication of carrying the noble wording upon the first meaning, for it is not something the former believe, nor something the latter claim. Rather, it is only their non-faith due to the absence of His will for their faith, and its reference is to their ignorance of the absence of His will for it. So the meaning is: their state is as explained, but most of the Muslims are ignorant that they would not have faith when the signs come, because of their ignorance of the absence of His, Exalted is He, will for their faith; so they wish for its coming, hoping for what will not be.

Thus the sentence confirms the content of His, Exalted is He, saying: "﴿And what will make you know﴾ ... " etc., according to the well-known reading; or: "But most of the polytheists are ignorant that they will not have faith when the signs come, because of their ignorance of the absence of His, Exalted is He, will for their faith at that time, so they swear by Allah with their most emphatic oaths that such a thing will not come to be."

Thus the sentence, according to the previous reading, is an initiating explanation of the source of the error of the swearers and the basis of their oath, and a confirmation of it according to the reading "لا تُؤْمِنُونَ" with the second-person ta', and likewise according to the reading "ما يُشْعِرُهم أنَّها إذا جاءَتْهم لا يُؤْمِنُونَ".

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 6, verse 112:**

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾ is an independent statement, brought in to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for the enmity of the Quraysh toward him, peace be upon him, and for the baseless words and deeds they built upon it. It shows that this is not peculiar to you: it is a trial that every prophet before you (peace be upon them all) also faced.

The kaf (ك) in ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ is in the accusative case, as a *naʿt* (qualifying adjective) of an omitted *maṣdar* (verbal noun) to which *dhālika* points. That verbal noun is governed by its omitted verb and serves to emphasise what follows. *Dhālika* refers to what is understood from what precedes it; the meaning is: We have appointed for every prophet an enemy.

The fronting of the phrase before the verb (*al-taqdīm ʿalā al-fiʿl*) gives restriction, which conveys emphasis. The meaning is: like that appointing which We made in your case, when We appointed for you enemies who oppose you, harm you, and do not believe; who seek to bring about your ruin and plot to nullify your affair; We appointed for every prophet before you enemies who did to them what your enemies did to you, not an appointing less than that. This indicates that the enmity of the disbelievers toward the prophets (peace be upon them) is by the creation of Allah, the Exalted, as a test.

﴿Shayāṭīn al-ins wal-jinn﴾ means: the rebellious ones of both groups. The genitive construction here is in the sense of *min al-bayāniyya* (the "min" of explanation): the devils who are humans and jinn.

It is also said that this is an annexation of a qualifier to the qualified, and that the original is "the humans and the jinn are devils." It is also said that the annexation has the sense of *lām* (belonging): the devils belonging to mankind and those belonging to the jinn. In that case it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾ (an enemy).

The verb *jaʿala* (to appoint) is transitive to one object or to two. Its first object is the one that comes first, and the second object has been placed before it to hasten the explanation of the enmity. The *lām* in ﴿likull﴾ is, on both readings, connected with *jaʿalnā*, or with an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿They inspire one another with decorated speech﴾, this is a new statement (*kalām mustaʾnaf*) brought to explain the modes of their enmity and to clarify the aspect of resemblance between the compared and that to which it is compared. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from "the devils," or a qualifier of ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾. The pronoun is plural in accordance with the meaning, since ﴿ʿaduwwan﴾ denotes enemies, as in the verse of the poet:

*When I do not benefit my friend with my affection, my enmity toward them does not harm them with my hatred.*

*Al-waḥy* (inspiration) here denotes indicating and rapid speech. That is: the devils of the jinn whisper to the devils of mankind, or some of each group to others.

﴿Zukhruf al-qawl﴾ means: its outward appearance is embellished and its inward reality is false, from *zukhruf* (ornamentation), since they adorned it.

﴿Ghurūran﴾ is an object of purpose (*mafʿūl lahu*) for *yūḥī*: that is, in order to deceive them. Or it is a *maṣdar* in the position of a circumstantial clause: that is, deceiving. Or it is a *maṣdar* emphasising an omitted verb that is itself a circumstantial clause from the subject of *yūḥī*: that is, they deceive with deception.

﴿And had your Lord willed﴾ returns to explaining the affairs that took place between him (ﷺ) and his people, which are understood from the narration of what occurred between the prophets (peace be upon them) and their nations, as the shift of address (*iltifāt*) indicates. The mention of the attribute of lordship together with its attachment to his pronoun (ﷺ) expresses the completeness of gentleness in consolation. That is: and had your Lord willed the non-existence of the matters mentioned, not their faith. It has been said that the established rule is that the object of the will is omitted only when the will occurs as a condition.

The object of the will is the content of the apodosis, which is the Exalted's words ﴿they did not do it﴾: that is, they did not do what has been mentioned of enmity toward you and the inspiring of some of them to others of embellished false speech, concerned with your affair in particular, not with what includes it and the affairs of the prophets (peace be upon them) as well, as has been said.

For the Exalted's words ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾ are clear that the intended people are the disbelievers contemporary with him (peace be upon him). That is: if what they did of the matters of enmity toward you, of all kinds of corruption, is by His will, the Exalted, then leave them and their fabrication, or what they fabricate of kinds of schemes. For them there are severe punishments in that, and for you there are praiseworthy outcomes, because the will of the Exalted is founded on perfectly sound wisdoms.

"And so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it"; that is, toward the ornamented speech. On the first interpretation, this is another reason for the inspiring, conjoined to "delusion," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. It is not put in the subjunctive (manṣūb) because its condition is absent: the delusion is the act of the one who inspires, while the inclining of hearts is the act of the one to whom it is inspired. That is, some of them inspire into others ornamented speech in order to delude them with it and so that they incline toward it.

"The hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter": the mention is specifically of their not believing in the Hereafter, rather than of the other matters that must be believed in and which they also disbelieve in. This is to indicate what is the basis of the inclining of their hearts toward what is cast to them. The pleasures of the Hereafter are surrounded in this world by hardships, and its pains are adorned with desires. Those who do not believe in it, nor in the conditions of what is in it, do not realize that behind those hardships there are pleasures, and beneath those desires there are pains. They look only at what appears to them in this world at first glance, so they are compelled to love the desires, among which are ornamented sayings and embellished falsehoods.

As for those who believe in the Hereafter, since they stand upon the reality of the matter and look to the outcomes of affairs, it is not conceivable that they would incline toward those embellishments, because of their knowledge of their falsehood and the wretchedness of their end.

On the last two interpretations, it is a reason for a deleted verb indicated by the context; that is, "and because of that We made what We made." The Mu'tazilah took the lam to be the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), or the lam of oath, or the lam of command, and its weakness is most evident.

"And that they may be pleased with it": for themselves, after their hearts have inclined to it.

"And that they may commit": that is, they may acquire by the requirement of their being pleased with it.

"That which they are committing": of the vices for which it is not fitting to mention them.

(p-177) ﴿Shall I seek a judge other than God?﴾ This is a resumed statement, addressed as if a speech had been intended. The hamza is for denial, and the fa' links it to an implied element that the sentence requires. The meaning is: Say to them, "Shall I incline toward the ornate deceptions of the devils, and seek a judge other than God who will decide between us and separate the one who is right from the one who is wrong?"

It is said that the polytheists of Quraysh said to the Messenger of God ﷺ, "Appoint between us and you a judge from among the rabbis of the Jews or the bishops of the Christians, so that he may inform us about you from what is in their Book concerning your affair." So this was revealed.

The attribution of the denied seeking to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and not to the polytheists, is as in His saying, ﴿Is it other than the religion of God that they seek?﴾ Although it is they who are seeking, this is to show complete fairness, or to take into account their statement, "Appoint between us and you a judge."

"Ghayra" (other than) is either the object of "abtaghi" (I seek), with "hakaman" (a judge) as its circumstantial qualifier (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject or object), or the reverse. Whichever it is, placing it before the verb that is actually the element joined by the fa' is to signal that the focus of the denial is the seeking of someone other than Him, as a judge, and not seeking in general.

It is said that "hakaman" is a specifier (tamyiz, a noun clarifying an ambiguity) for the vagueness in "ghayra," as in their saying, "We have other than them as camels." They said: "al-hakam" (the judge) is more emphatic than "al-hakim" (the ruler) and points more strongly to firmness, because it is used only of one who is just, and of one from whom judgement has repeatedly issued, unlike "al-hakim."

His saying, ﴿And He it is who has sent down to you the Book﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) that emphasises the denial of seeking someone other than Him as a judge. The attribution of the sending down specifically to them, although the situation calls for showing that His relation to the parties in dispute is equal, is for the purpose of inclining them toward what was sent down, and drawing them down to accept His judgement, by implying the strength of His relation to them. That is: Shall I seek other than Him as a judge, when He is the one who has sent down to you the Book, and you are an unlettered people who do not know what you do or what you leave undone? [He sent down] the Qur'an, which speaks the truth and the right, and which deserves to be the one to which the name "Book" is exclusively applied.

﴿Fully detailed﴾: that is, with truth and falsehood, the lawful and the unlawful, and the other rulings made clear in it, to such an extent that no confusion or ambiguity remains in matters of religion. So what need is there, after this, for a judge? As you see, this is plainly evidence that the noble Qur'an is sufficient in the matter of religion, and needs nothing else, through its own explanation and detailing. As for whether its inimitability (i'jaz) has a role in this, as has been said, that is not so.

His saying, ﴿Those whom We have given the Book know that it is sent down from your Lord in truth﴾, is a resumed statement, not included within the implied speech, and it is brought from Him, glorified is He, to establish the truthfulness of the Book on which the matter of arbitration has been hung, and to confirm that it has been sent down from His presence, mighty and majestic is He, by explaining that those whom they trusted and with whose arbitration they were content, as was reported just above from the scholars of the Jews and the Christians, know that it is true and that it was sent down from Him, exalted is He.

In referring to the Torah and the Gospel by the name "Book" there is an allusion to the kinship between them and the Qur'an, which requires that they share in truthfulness and in being sent down from Him, exalted is He, together with the brevity this entails. The mention of the two groups under the heading of having been given the Book is to indicate that they knew it from their own Book, since they found it as it had been described in it, and they witnessed it agreeing with it in the fundamentals and in what does not differ among the secondary matters, and reporting matters for which there is no way of knowing except through revelation.

By the relative pronoun is meant either the scholars of both groups, which is the apparent meaning, and then "giving" (itha') is making understand in actuality; or it means all of them, and they are included in it as a first inclusion, in which case it is more general than what was mentioned and includes making understand in potential. There is no doubt that all of them are able to do this.

It is said that what is meant is the believers among the People of the Book. It is also read as "munzal" (sent down), from the causative form "inzal." The mention of the title of Lordship together with its attribution to his pronoun ﷺ is to honour him, peace and blessings be upon him. The "bi" in His saying ﴿in truth﴾ is connected to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial qualifier of the hidden pronoun in "munazzal"; that is: connected with the truth.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾: that is, concerning their knowing this, because of what you do not observe from them in the way of the marks of knowledge and the judgements of certainty. So the fa' is for ordering the prohibition upon the report of the People of the Book's knowledge of the matter of the Qur'an; or concerning its being sent down from your Lord in truth, in which case it is of the kind of stirring up and inflaming, as in His saying, ﴿and do not be among the polytheists.﴾

It is said that the address is in reality to the community, although it has the form of being addressed to him ﷺ. It is also said that the address is to everyone, in the sense that the proofs have mutually reinforced and supported one another, so it is not fitting for anyone to doubt it. On these views the fa' is for ordering the prohibition upon the very fact of their knowledge of the state of the Qur'an.

The commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 115:

﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾. This begins an explanation of the perfection of the aforementioned Book in itself, following the explanation of its perfection in terms of its attribution to Him, the Exalted, by being sent down from Him with truth. The verification of this is by the knowledge of the People of the Book concerning it. It was expressed as "word" (kalimah) because it is the foundation of the attribute of truthfulness and justice, and through it the effects of judgment become manifest. It has also been read as: ﴿the words of your Lord﴾ (kalimat).

﴿In truth and justice﴾: these are two verbal nouns (masdar) put in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (hal). It has also been said that they are in the accusative as specification (tamyiz), and it has been said that they are in the accusative as cause ('illah).

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿None can change His words﴾, it is either a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining its superiority over other things, following the explanation of its superiority in itself, or it is another circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "has been fulfilled", on the basis that the noun in apparent form (al-zahir) suffices in place of the connecting pronoun (damir rabit). The meaning: it has reached the utmost limit in truthfulness in reports and promises, and in justice in decisions and rulings. No one can substitute any part of that with something more truthful and more just, nor with something of its like. So how can one conceive of seeking a judge other than Him, the Exalted?

﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ of everything that hearing relates to.

﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of everything that can be known, so that within this are included the statements of those who go to judgment and their conditions, the apparent and the hidden, by primary inclusion.

Furthermore, it has been said: the meaning is that no one is able to distort it as was done to the Torah, so this is a guarantee from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of its preservation, like His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardian﴾; or (the meaning is) that there is no prophet or book after it to abrogate it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 116:

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾ When the exclusivity of Him, the Exalted, in judgment (al-hakamiyya) was established, owing to His independence in what necessitates it, namely the sending down of the complete Book that distinguishes between truth and falsehood, the perfect truthfulness of His speech, the complete justice of His rulings, the impossibility of anyone altering any part of them, and His, the Exalted's, sole comprehensive encompassing of all that is heard and known, the discussion was followed by an explanation that the disbelievers are characterized by the opposites of those perfections, namely the opposite qualities of misguidance and leading others astray, the following of corrupt conjectures that arise from ignorance, and lying against Allah, glorified and exalted be He. This shows the complete contrast between their condition and what they aspire to, and warns against leaning towards them and acting upon their opinions.

By "those on earth" is meant mankind, and by "most of them" is meant the disbelievers. It has also been said: the people of Makkah, and "the earth" refers to their land; i.e., if you obey them by making them judges.

﴿they will lead you astray from the way of Allah﴾ from the path that leads to Him, or from the law that He has prescribed for His servants.

﴿They follow only conjecture﴾ and this is their conjecture that their fathers were upon the truth, so they follow in their footsteps, or their ignorance and their false opinions. This is so because the meaning of "conjecture" here is what stands opposite to knowledge.

The sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the conditional form, as if it were said: how do they go astray? So it is answered: they follow in matters of their religion only conjecture, ﴿and conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾, so they go astray in manifest error. And there is no doubt that the misguided person who sets himself up to guide others only guides them to the path of his own self, so they are both misguided and misguiding.

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿and they are only guessing﴾ is coordinated (atf) with what precedes it and falls under its ruling; i.e., they lie against Allah, glorified be He, in what they attribute to Him, the Exalted, such as taking a son for Him, and making the worship of idols a means of drawing near to Him, the Exalted, and making lawful the carrion, and forbidding the baheera and their like. Or they assume that they possess something, and how could they have it, when beyond it is the bounds of the Pleiades (al-'Ayyuq), and its reality is what is said on the basis of conjecture and guesswork.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 117:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ This is a confirmation of the content of the conditional clause and what follows it, and an emphasis on what it conveys of warning; that is: He is most knowing of the two groups, so beware lest you be among the first.

"Man" (مَن) is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a qualifying noun (mawsufah) in the accusative position, not governed by "a'lam" itself, for the comparative (af'al al-tafdil, the elative form) does not govern an explicit noun in such constructions; rather it is governed by a verb implied by it. Or it is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) in the nominative position as a subject of inception (mubtada'), with the predicate being "yadillu" (strays), and the clause is one in which the implied verb is suspended (mu'allaq 'anha al-fi'l al-muqaddar), meaning its action is blocked from governing the interrogative.

It was also read as "yudillu" (with a dammah on the yaʼ), with "man" as the subject of "yudillu," its object omitted, and its position in the accusative by virtue of the implied verb mentioned; that is: He is most knowing, He knows who misleads people, so this constitutes an emphasis on the warning against obeying the disbelievers.

As for the view that the subject is God Most High and "man" is in the accusative governed by what was mentioned (that is: He knows whom He misleads), or in the genitive by the annexation of "a'lam" to it (that is: He is the most knowing of misleaders), from the words of God Most High: ﴿whomever God misleads﴾, or from your saying: "I found him astray" (adlaltuhu, meaning: when you find him to be astray), then this is not supported by the preceding context (al-siyaq) nor the surrounding context (al-sibaq). The superlative here refers to the abundance of knowledge, its comprehensiveness regarding all the aspects to which knowledge can attach and which it necessarily entails, and its being essential to Him rather than derived from another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 118:

﴿So eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned﴾ is a command that follows from the prohibition of following those who lead astray, among whose misguidance is making lawful what is forbidden and making forbidden what is lawful. This is because they used to say to the Muslims: "You worship Allah, so what Allah has killed is more worthy that you eat it than what you have killed yourselves." So the Muslims were told: eat of that over which the name of Allah alone, exalted is He, has been mentioned at its slaughter, not that over which the name of another has been mentioned alone, or together with His name, or that which died a natural death.

﴿If you are believers in His signs﴾ — among which are the verses that come in this matter.

﴿believers﴾ — for belief in them necessitates permitting what Allah has made lawful and avoiding what He has forbidden. The response to the condition is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 119:

﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not eat of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned?﴾ This is a rebuke against there being any reason that would move them to abstain from eating what has had the name of Allah Most High mentioned over it, [such as] the baheera, the sawaiba, and the like.

His Most High saying: ﴿And He has already detailed for you...﴾ etc., is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) emphasizing the rebuke, as in His Most High saying: ﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we do not fight in the way of Allah, when we have been driven out of our homes and our children?﴾ That is: what cause do you have for not eating of that over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, or what purpose compels you to refrain from eating it and prevents you from it?

The situation is that He has already detailed for you ﴿what He has forbidden to you﴾ by His saying: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden...﴾ etc. So everything other than that remains permitted. [This detailing is] not by His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion...﴾ etc., because that [verse] is Medinan. As for the delay in recitation, it does not necessitate a delay in revelation. The two verbs are read in the passive voice, and the first is also read in the active voice, with the second in the passive.

﴿Except what you are compelled to﴾ of what has been forbidden, for it too is then permitted.

﴿And indeed many﴾; that is, of the (p-180) disbelievers,

﴿will surely mislead﴾ people by making the permitted forbidden and the forbidden permitted, like 'Amr ibn Luhayy and his like. It is also read: (yadilluna) "they go astray."

[They] go astray by their deviant desires and their false appetites.

﴿without knowledge﴾, that is, not drawn from the noble Shari'a and not grounded in revelation.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the limits of truth into falsehood, and of the lawful into the unlawful.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 120:

﴿And leave the outward and the inward of sin﴾; i.e., what is openly committed of sins and what is kept secret, or what is done by the limbs and what is done by the heart. It has also been said: fornication in the shops and taking secret lovers (akhdan).

﴿Indeed, those who earn sin﴾; i.e., they acquire it from the outward and the inward.

﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to commit﴾ whatever it may be. So it is necessary to avoid both of them, and the clause is a causal justification (ta'lil) for the command.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 121:**

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned﴾. This is apparent in the prohibition of what is left without the invocation of God's name (*tasmiyah*), whether deliberately or through forgetfulness. Dawud went this way, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal is reported to have held the same. Malik and al-Shafi'i held the opposite, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The slaughtered animal (*dhabihah*) of a Muslim is lawful even if the name of God has not been mentioned over it." Abu Hanifa distinguished between deliberate and forgetful omission, and interpreted the verse as referring to carrion (*maytah*), or to that over which the name of other than God has been invoked, on the basis of His words: ﴿And indeed it is a transgression (*fisq*)﴾. For *fisq* is that which has been dedicated to other than God. The pronoun refers to *ma* (that which). It is also possible that it refers to the act of eating, which is implied by ﴿do not eat﴾, and the clause is then a new, independent sentence. It has also been said that the clause is in the circumstantial accusative (*hal*).

﴿And indeed the devils inspire their allies﴾. By "the devils" is meant Iblis and his armies, so their inspiring is their whispering to the polytheists.

It has been said that they are the rebellious ones among the Magians (*majus*), and their inspiring to their allies is what they conveyed to the Quraysh in writing: that Muhammad and his companions claim they follow the command of God, yet they claim that what they kill themselves is lawful and what God kills is unlawful.

﴿to dispute with you﴾; that is, with satanic whisperings, or with the falsehoods transmitted from the Magians. This supports the interpretation of the verse as referring to carrion.

﴿And if you obey them﴾ in making lawful what is unlawful and assist them in their falsehoods.

﴿indeed you are polytheists﴾, since whoever abandons the obedience of God for the obedience of another and follows him in his religion has associated that other with Him, Exalted is He; indeed he has preferred that other over Him, glorified be He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 122:

﴿Is he who was dead⦆ and it is read: (mayyitan) according to the original form.

﴿Then We gave him life﴾ is a parable brought forth to warn the Muslims away from obeying the polytheists, following on from the warning against it by indicating that they (the Muslims) are illumined by the lights of Divine Revelation, while the polytheists are floundering in the darknesses of disbelief and transgression. How, then, could it be conceived that they would obey them?

The hamzah (interrogative particle) is for rebuke and negation, and the waw is for conjoining the nominal clause to a similar one that the context implies; that is: "Are you then like them? And is he who was dead, then We gave him life, and what follows from it of the faculties of perception and motion?"

﴿And We made for him﴾ in addition to that, from outside, ﴿a light﴾, a great one.

﴿by which he walks﴾; that is, by means of it. The clause is a resumptive (istiʾnaf) construction built on a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said: "What does he do with that light?" So it was said: "by which he walks."

﴿among the people﴾; that is, among them, safe from their harm, or it is an attribute of his (the light).

﴿like one whose likeness﴾; that is, whose attribute is wondrous, and it is the subject (mubtada').

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in darknesses﴾ is its predicate, on the basis that (p-181) the intended meaning of the two is the wording and not the meaning, as in your saying: "Zayd, his attribute is dark-complexioned." This clause is a relative clause (silah) for "man" (in the phrase "man"), and it is in the genitive after the kaf (prefix), and it together with its genitive is the predicate of the first "man."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿not coming out of them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in the adverbial phrase. It was said: from the relative pronoun; that is, "not coming out of them in any state."

This, as you see, is a parable intended to describe the one who remains in error, to the extent that he never departs from it at all, just as the first is a parable intended to describe the one whom God Almighty created upon the fitrah of Islam and guided by clear signs to the path of truth, which he follows as he wills. However, this does not mean that each of these meanings is indicated by the words appropriate to it in the two parables through a comparison with what corresponds to it from their meanings; rather, the words of the parable remain in their original meanings. Instead, from the multiple matters considered in each side of the two parables a distinct configuration is abstracted, and from the multiple matters mentioned in each side of the two parables a distinct configuration is abstracted; thus the first two are likened to these two and take their place, and what indicates the latter two is used for the former two by a kind of figurative extension.

It has already been indicated, in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts...﴾ and the rest of the verse, that the parabolic image is a category in its own right, with no way to making it a metaphor in the strict sense, and that the parabolic metaphor (al-istiʿarah al-tamthiliyyah) is among the expressions of the later scholars. Indeed, this may proceed according to the pattern of metaphor, by not mentioning the comparandum, as in these two parables and their like; and it may proceed according to the pattern of simile, as in the poet's saying:

"And people are but like the abodes and their inhabitants, in which, on the day they dwelt there and then departed, they were desolate."

﴿Thus﴾; that is, like that eloquent adornment.

﴿was made fair-seeming﴾; that is, from God Almighty's side by way of creation, at the suggestion of the devils, or from the side of the devils by way of embellishment and enticement.

﴿for the disbelievers﴾, who follow the satanic whisperings, who take up the embellishments that they inspire in them.

﴿what they were doing﴾; that is, what they persisted in doing of the various kinds of disbelief and sins, of which is what is related of them of ugly deeds, for had these not been made fair-seeming to them they would not have persisted in them, nor would they have disputed the truth through them.

It was said: the verse was revealed concerning Hamzah, may God be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. It was also said: concerning Umar or Ammar, may God be pleased with both of them, and Abu Jahl.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 123:

﴿And thus﴾. It has been said: its meaning is: just as We placed in Makkah the greatest of its criminals, that they might plot therein.

﴿We placed in every town﴾, among the rest of the towns,

﴿the greatest of its criminals, that they might plot therein﴾. The two objects of "placed" (*ja'alna*) are "the greatest of its criminals," with the second object placed first, and the adverbial phrase "therein" is *laghw* (a dependent phrase that does not complete the sense on its own). Or the two are the adverbial phrase and "the greatest" (*akabir*), with "its criminals" (*mujrimiha*) being an apposition (*badal*) or a genitive complement (*mudaf ilayhi*). When the elative form (*af'al al-tafdil*, the comparative/superlative pattern) is followed by a genitive complement, it may be used in the singular or agree in number. For this reason it has been read as: *akbara mujrimiha* (the singular form "greatest").

It has also been said that "the greatest of its criminals" is the first object, and the second is "that they might plot therein." It is not hidden that whatever meaning is intended from these meanings must be well established and known among people, familiar among them, so that the demonstrative may be turned away from the context of the noble composition, directed toward that meaning, and made a measure for its counterparts by being brought out in the manner of a comparative verbal noun.

It is clear that the matter is not so, and there is no way to direct it toward what is understood from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus the deeds they used to do were made attractive to the disbelievers﴾, even if the intended people are the greatest of Makkah. For the meaning then, after "the one and the other," becomes: just as We made the deeds of the people of Makkah attractive to them, We placed in every town the greatest of its criminals... and so on.

So the closer view is that "thus" refers to the known disbelievers, by virtue of their being characterized by their attributes. The singular form is by interpreting it as "the group" or "the one mentioned." The place of the *kaf* (thus) is in the accusative, as the second object of "We placed," and it was placed before it (the verb) to convey restriction (*takhsis*), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus you were before...﴾, the verse.

The first is ﴿the greatest of its criminals﴾, and the adverbial phrase is *laghw*. That is: and like those disbelievers who are the chieftains of Makkah and its criminals, We placed in every town its greatest criminals. That is: We made them characterized by the attributes of those mentioned, their deeds made attractive to them, persisting in falsehood, disputing the truth with it, ﴿that they might plot therein﴾; that is, that they might carry out plotting therein. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they do not plot except against themselves﴾ is a parenthetical statement (*i'tiraद*) by way of promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and threat to the disbelievers; that is: the harm of their plotting does not fall except upon themselves.

﴿And they are not aware﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "they plot," with the consideration that the exception (*istithna'*) comes after the negation. That is: they only plot against themselves, while they are in a state in which they are not aware of this at all; rather, they assume that they are plotting against others.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 124:

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when a sign comes to them﴾ is a return to explaining the condition of the criminals of Makkah, after it had been made clear, by way of consolation, that the condition of others as well is likewise, and that the outcome of the plotting of all of them is what has been mentioned, for the great [plot] that was related proceeded only from them and not from the rest of the criminals. That is: when a sign comes to them through the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿They say: We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Until it is revealed to us and Jibril (peace be upon him) comes to us and informs us that Muhammad is truthful, just as they said: Or you bring Allah and the angels as a surety (qabil)." And it is related from al-Hasan al-Basri the like of this.

This, as you see, is explicit that what was made dependent upon being given what the messengers (peace and blessings be upon them) were given is their belief in the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and in what was sent down to him, a true belief, as is what is understood from it when stated without qualification; except that it requires that what was given to the messengers of Allah be taken to mean revelation in general, and speaking with Jibril (peace be upon him) in some manner.

And that the word "risalah" (message) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah knows best where He places His message﴾ be turned away from its apparent meaning and be taken to mean the message of Jibril (peace be upon him) in the manner mentioned, and that its "placing" be understood as delivering it to the one to whom it is sent, not placing it in its proper place, which is the Messenger, so that it may be a response to their demand and a rejection of it: that the meaning of the demand is: "We will not believe that that sign has descended from Allah the Exalted to the Messenger until it comes to us in person, visibly, just as the Messenger comes and informs us of that."

And the meaning of the rejection: Allah knows best who is fit for sending Jibril (peace be upon him) to him for some matter; as a notice that they are far from deserving that honour. And in this there is a great deal of contrivance, which is not hidden.

And Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl when he said: "We have competed with the Banu 'Abd Manaf in nobility, until when we have become like two racehorses, they say: 'From us is a prophet to whom revelation is sent.' By Allah, we will never accept him or follow him, until revelation comes to us just as it comes to him."

And al-Dahhak said: Each one of the people asked to be singled out for messengerhood and revelation, as Allah the Exalted informs of them in His saying: ﴿Rather, each one of them wants to be given scrolls spread out﴾. And it is not hidden that each of these two statements, although it is suitable to the aforementioned rejection, nevertheless requires that by the belief made dependent upon being given what the messengers were given is meant merely their affirmation of his message (peace and blessings be upon him) in general, without including all people; and that the word "until" (hatta) in the words of the accursed one: "until revelation comes to us just as it comes to him..." be a limit to non-acceptance and not to non-following, for it is established under both suppositions: the giving of revelation and its absence.

So the meaning: "We will not believe in his message at all until we ourselves are given, of revelation and prophethood, the like of what the messengers of Allah were given," or "a giving like the giving to the messengers of Allah."

As for what has been said: that al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "If prophethood were true, I would be more deserving of it than you, since I am older than you in age and greater than you in wealth and children"; so it was revealed. Then it has no connection to their rejected statement, except that by the belief made dependent upon what has been mentioned is meant merely belief that the revealed sign is a true revelation, not belief that it was sent down to him (peace and blessings be upon him); so the meaning would be: "When a sign sent down to the Messenger comes to them, they say: We will not believe that it has descended from Allah until its descent is to us and not to him, for we are the ones deserving it rather than him." For the summary of the meaning of his saying: "If prophethood were true..." is: "If what you claim of prophethood were true, I would be the prophet, not you; and since the matter is not so, it is not true." And it has no making belief in the truth of prophethood dependent upon himself being a prophet.

And "﴿mithla ma ute﴾" (like what was given) is in the accusative as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah); that is: "until we are given it a giving like the giving to the messengers of Allah." The attribution of the giving to them is because they deny his receiving it (peace and blessings be upon him). "Hayth" (where) is in the accusative as an object by extension, not by the verb "a'lamu" itself, since, as you know, it does not operate on the apparent, but by a verb that it indicates; that is: "He knows the place in which He places it."

And the meaning: that the station of messengership is not something attained by abundance of wealth and children, nor by the support of means and numbers; rather it is attained by inner virtues which Allah the Exalted singles out for whom He wills of His sincere servants. And it has been read: (risalatihi) in the singular.

﴿Those who committed crime will suffer﴾: another resumption, condemning them for what they will meet of various kinds of evil, after condemning their deprivation of what they had hoped for. The particle "sa" is for emphasis, and placing the relative pronoun in the place of the pronoun indicates that the afflicting of what afflicts them is because of their criminality, which entails all evils and vices; that is: there will befall them certainly, in place of what they wished for, and upon which they set their empty desires, from the glory of prophethood and the nobility of messengership.

﴿Humiliation﴾: that is, abasement and lowliness after their pride.

﴿with Allah﴾: that is, on the Day of Resurrection; and it has been said: from Allah.

﴿and severe punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, or in this world.

﴿because of what they used to plot﴾: that is, because of their constant plotting, or in return for it. And since this was among the greatest sources of their criminality, its causation was explicitly stated.

﴿Whoever Allah wills to guide﴾: that is, He makes him know the path of truth and grants him success in faith.

﴿He opens his breast to Islam﴾, so that it expands and becomes open. This is a kinaya (metonymy, an indirect expression) for making the self receptive to the truth, prepared for it to settle within it, and purified of whatever prevents it or contradicts it. The Prophet (ﷺ) alluded to this when he was asked about it, and he said: "It is a light that Allah casts into the heart of the believer, and so it expands and opens." They said: "Is there a sign by which one can recognise it?" He said: "Yes: turning in repentance towards the abode of eternity, turning away from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it comes."

﴿And whoever He wills to lead astray﴾: that is, He creates misguidance in him by directing his choice towards it.

﴿He makes his breast tight, constricted﴾, such that it recoils from accepting the truth, so that faith hardly enters it. It is also read as ﴿ضَيْقًا﴾ (ḍayqan) with the letter ya' unstressed, and ﴿حَرِجًا﴾ (ḥarijan) with a kasra on the letter ra'; that is, extremely constricted. The first (ḍayq) is a verbal noun described with it for emphasis.

﴿As if he were climbing﴾: the ﴿ما﴾ (mā) here is a particle called muhayyi'a (a preparatory particle), which prepares ﴿كأنَّ﴾ (ka'anna) to enter upon verbal sentences.

﴿up into the sky﴾: this is a simile for the extremity of his breast's constriction, likened to one who attempts what he can hardly do, since climbing into the sky is an image for what lies outside the scope of capability. It also contains an indication that faith is barred to him just as ascending is barred to him.

It is also said that the meaning is: "as if he were ascending to the sky", recoiling from the truth and fleeing far from it. The original form of ﴿يَصَّعَّدُ﴾ (yaṣṣa'ʿadu) is ﴿يَتَصَعَّدُ﴾ (yatasa'ʿadu), and it has been read in that form. It is also read as ﴿يَصّاعَدُ﴾ (yaṣṣā'adu), whose original form is ﴿يَتَصاعَدُ﴾ (yatasā'adu).

﴿Thus﴾: that is, in the same manner as that placing, which is making the breast constricted, in the manner mentioned. (p-184)

﴿Allah places the rijs﴾: that is, the punishment, or abandonment. Mujahid said: "Rijs is that in which there is no good." Al-Zajjaj said: "Rijs is the curse in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter."

﴿upon those who do not believe﴾: that is, upon them. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-ladhīna) in the position of the pronoun is to indicate that His placing (the rijs) is caused by what is contained in the relative clause, namely their complete recoil from faith and their persistence in disbelief.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 126.

﴿And this﴾; i.e., the clarification brought by the Qur'an, or Islam, or what preceded of divine guidance (tawfiq) and abandonment (khidhlan).

﴿is the path of your Lord﴾; i.e., His way which He approves, or His custom and manner which His wisdom has required. And in mentioning the title of Lordship (rububiyyah) there is an indication that the straightening of that path is for nurture (tarbiyah) and the bestowing of perfection.

﴿straight﴾, without crookedness, or just and consistent. It is a confirmatory circumstantial state (hal mu'akkidah), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is the truth, confirming﴾, and the element governing it is the meaning of the demonstrative (al-isharah).

﴿We have detailed the verses﴾; we have made them clear in detail.

﴿for a people who remember﴾; who recall what is within their contents, so they know that everything that occurs of events, whether good or evil, occurs only by the decree (qada') and creation of God, exalted is He, and that He, exalted is He, is knowing of the states of the servants, wise and just in what He does to them. The specifying of the people mentioned by the mention is because they are the ones who benefit from the detailing of the verses.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 127:

﴿For them is the Abode of Peace﴾; i.e., for those who remember, the Abode of Safety from every hardship, which is Paradise.
