﴿فَتَفَرَّقَ بِكُمْ﴾ (so that it scatters you): with one of the two taa' omitted, and the ba' is for transitivity; that is: "so that it scatters you" according to their scattering, as the "Ayadi Saba'" (scattered tribes of Saba'). Thus, as you see, it is more eloquent than "tufarriqakum," just as it has been said that "dhahaba bihi" is more eloquent than "adhhabahu," because of what it indicates of continuance.

﴿عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ﴾ (from His way): that is, the way of Allah in which there is no crookedness or hardship, which is the religion of Islam, some of whose rulings have been mentioned. It was also said: it is following revelation and adhering to proof. In this there is an indication that his (ﷺ) path is the very way of Allah the Exalted.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾ (That): a reference to what has passed of following His way and abandoning the following of all other ways.

﴿وَصّاكم بِهِ لَعَلَّكم تَتَّقُونَ﴾ (He has commanded you with it, that you may be righteous): following the ways of disbelief and misguidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 154:

﴿ثُمَّ آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ﴾ [*Then We gave Moses the Book*] is a statement set down from the side of Allah, the Exalted, to confirm the charge (*wasiyya*) and to establish it, and to prepare for what follows concerning the sending down of the Glorious Qur'an. This is indicated by the change of style through *iltifat* (the shift of grammatical person) to the first person plural of speech. It is conjoined (*ma'tuf*) to an implied clause that the context requires and the arrangement calls for, as if it were said after His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿ذَلِكم وصّاكم بِهِ﴾" [*That is what He has enjoined upon you*], by way of *isti'naf* (resumption of a new sentence), confirming it and establishing its content: "We did that, then We gave ... etc." In the same way, His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿وَنَطْبَعُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾" [*and We set a seal upon their hearts*] is conjoined to what the meaning of "﴿أوَلَمْ يَهْدِ ...﴾" [*Did it not guide them...*] implies, as if it were said: "They are heedless of guidance, and We set a seal ... etc."

As for its being conjoined to "﴿ذَلِكم وصّاكم بِهِ﴾" and being placed with it in the same string of speech, as the majority agreed, this is among things that do not befit the eloquence (*jaza'a*) of the noble arrangement. So reflect on this.

"Thumma" (*then*) here indicates delay in the reporting (*li-al-tarakhi fi al-ikhbar*), as in your saying: "It reached me what you did today, then what you did yesterday is more astonishing." Or it indicates difference in rank (*li-al-tafawut fi al-rutba*), as if it were said: "That is what He enjoined upon you, anciently and recently; then greater than that is that We gave Moses the Torah, for giving it, comprising the mentioned charge and other things, is greater than merely enjoining it."

﴿تَمامًا﴾ [*completion*] is for the honour and the blessing; that is, a completing of both of them. It is a *masdar* (verbal noun) of *atamma* with the augmenting letters removed.

﴿عَلى الَّذِي أحْسَنَ﴾ [*upon the one who did good*]; that is, upon the one who performed it well, whoever he may be. This is supported by the reading "عَلى الَّذِينَ أحْسَنُوا" [*upon those who did good*], and *tamaman* [completion] is upon the good-doers. Or it means upon the one who conveyed it well, namely Moses, peace be upon him. Or *tamaman* is upon what Moses, peace be upon him, performed well; that is, perfected it of knowledge and laws; that is, an increase upon his knowledge, in the manner of completion.

It is also read in the nominative (*raf'*), on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject; that is, "upon that which is the best religion and most pleasing," or "We gave Moses the Book complete (*tamaman*); that is, perfect and complete, upon the best state in which books can be."

﴿وَتَفْصِيلا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [*and a detailing of all things*], and a detailed exposition of everything that is needed in the religion. It is conjoined to *tamaman*. The accusative of both is either as a causative (*al-'illiyya*), or as a verbal noun (*al-masdariyya*), as indicated, or as a circumstantial (*al-haliyya*). Likewise His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿وَهُدًى ورَحْمَةً﴾" [*and a guidance and a mercy*].

The pronoun in "﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ﴾" [*so that they*] refers to the Children of Israel, implied by the mention of Moses and the giving of the Book.

The *ba'* (*with*) in His saying, Exalted is He, "﴿بِلِقاءِ رَبِّهِمْ﴾" [*in the meeting with their Lord*] is connected to His saying, "﴿يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾" [*they may believe*]. It has been placed before it in order to preserve the rhyme (*fawasil*). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "That they may believe in the Resurrection and affirm the reward and the punishment."

This and (demonstrative: the One whose commands and prohibitions have been recited to you), i.e., the Qur'an.

Book: of great standing, whose worth cannot be measured.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have sent it down; blessed⦆ — i.e., abundant in benefits, both religious and worldly, are two attributes of "Book." The mention of the attribute of sending down before the attribute of blessedness, though it is not explicit, is because the discourse is with those who deny it. Or they are two other predicates of the demonstrative: "We have sent it down, comprising the various kinds of religious and worldly benefits, a portion of which has been detailed to you."

The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So follow it⦆ indicates the consequence of what follows from what precedes. The great standing of the Book in itself, and its being sent down from His presence, the Mighty and Majestic, entailing religious and worldly benefits, make following it obligatory in the highest degree.

﴿And fear God⦆ (i.e., by opposing it), ﴿that you may receive mercy⦆ through following it and acting upon its ruling.

**(Lest you say)** is a reason (*ʿillah*) for "We sent it down," where "it" refers to what was indicated by what was mentioned, not to the Book itself. Otherwise there would be a separation between the governing element (*al-ʿamil*) and the governed element (*al-maʿmul*) by a foreign element that is blessed, whether as an attribute or as a predicate. The meaning is: We sent it down in this way, out of aversion to your saying on the Day of Resurrection: "Had You not sent it down..."

**(Only the Book was sent down)** that speaks of those general rulings common to all nations.

**(upon two groups)** existing.

**(before us)** These are the Jews and the Christians. The sending down is specified to their two scriptures because, at that time, these were the best known among the heavenly books for containing rulings, especially the rulings mentioned.

**(And indeed we were)** The "in" here is the lightened form of *inna*, and the *lam* distinguishes it from the negating *in*. The pronoun of the matter is omitted. Their purpose in this is to repel what might be raised against them: that its being sent down upon the two does not preclude the generality of its rulings, so why did you not act upon its general rulings? That is, and indeed we were.

**(heedless of their study)** We did not know what was in their Book, since it was not in our language so that we could receive from it those general rulings and preserve them, even though it had not been revealed to us. By this it becomes clear that their excuse is this, even though they were not commanded with what is in the two books, because those books contain the mentioned rulings that encompass all nations. Likewise, cutting off that excuse is by the sending down of the Qur'an, because it also contains them, not merely the other laws and rulings.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 157:**

﴿Or [lest] you say﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*, coordination) to "lest you say," and both of them have been read with the *yāʾ* (third person, "they say"), by way of *iltifāt* (shift from address to third-person reference) from the address in "follow it and fear [God]."

﴿Had the Book been sent down to us﴾ as it was sent down to them.

﴿we would have been better guided than them﴾ to the truth, which is the ultimate goal, or to what lies within its folds of the great rulings and laws and their subtleties, owing to the keenness of our minds and the acuteness of our understanding. For this reason we have acquired from the various branches of knowledge, such as stories and reports, sermons and poetry, and the like, a sound portion, even though we are unlettered.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Now there has come to you﴾ is connected to an omitted element indicated by the eloquent *fa'* (*al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa*). It is either the cause of that omitted element, meaning: do not offer this as an excuse, for there has come to you ... etc.; or it is a condition for it, meaning: if you are truthful in what you used to claim for yourselves, namely that you would be better guided than the two groups had the Book been sent down to you, then what you supposed has come about, and it has come to you.

﴿a clear proof﴾: and what a proof! That is, a conclusive argument whose true nature cannot be fathomed.

And His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to "has come to you," or to an omitted element that is an attribute of "a proof," meaning: a proof issuing from Him, exalted is He. In either case it indicates its relative excellence, just as its glorifying nunation (*tanwīn al-tafkhīm*) indicates its intrinsic excellence.

Mentioning the attribute of lordship together with the attachment to their pronoun adds further emphasis to the obligation of following.

﴿and guidance and mercy﴾ are conjoined to "a proof," and their nunation is likewise glorifying. The Qur'an is expressed as "a proof" to signal their complete capacity to study it; then as "guidance and mercy" to alert that it includes what the Torah included of guidance and mercy for people, indeed it is the very essence of guidance and mercy.

﴿Who then is more unjust﴾: the *fa'* connects what follows to what precedes, for the coming of the Qur'an, which contains guidance and mercy, necessitates the utmost injustice of whoever denies it. That is: since the matter is so, who then is more unjust?

﴿than one who denies the signs of God﴾: the relative pronoun has been placed in the position of their pronoun by way of *iltifāt*, to specify their being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause, to indicate the cause of the judgment, and to remove them from the rank of direct address. The phrase "the signs of God" is used for what came to them, to magnify the matter and to alert that denying any single sign of God is sufficient for the utmost injustice; so what then is your opinion about denying the Qur'an, which comprises all of them?

The meaning is: a denial that anyone could be more unjust than one who does that, or equal to him. Although the structure of the expression does not explicitly address the denial or negation of equality, when one says "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "No one is more excellent than him," what is meant, necessarily by the prevailing custom and the consistent usage, is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. This has been mentioned many times.

﴿and turns away from them﴾ (p-203): that is, he diverts people away from them, thereby combining misguidance with leading others astray.

﴿We will recompense those who turn away﴾ people

﴿from Our signs﴾: a threat against them by stating the recompense for their leading others astray, such that the recompense for their own misguidance is also understood from it. Placing the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun serves to establish the ground of the recompense.

﴿with a terrible punishment﴾: that is, a punishment that is evil and severe in its harm.

﴿for what they used to do of turning away﴾: that is, because of what they were continually and habitually doing of diverting and turning away. This is an explicit statement of what was indicated by attaching the judgment to the relative pronoun, namely that what is in the sphere of the relative clause is the cause of it.

﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ ("Are they waiting?") is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) introduced to show that faith cannot come from them even on the arrival of the signs mentioned, and that they will not refrain from persisting in obstinacy and from demanding signs that contradict the wisdom of the law, namely the compelling signs. It also shows that faith at the time of their coming is of no benefit at all. This is an emphasis on conveying the message, warning, and removing excuses. The meaning is: "What are they waiting for?"

﴿إلا أنْ تَأْتِيَهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ أوْ يَأْتِيَ رَبُّكَ﴾ ("Unless the angels come to them, or your Lord comes") corresponds to what they proposed when they said: ﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us, or do we see our Lord?﴾ and when they said: ﴿Or you bring God and the angels as a guarantee﴾, and when they said: ﴿Why was an angel not sent down to him?﴾ and similar statements. Or it means: unless the angels of punishment come to them, or the command of your Lord comes with punishment. The waiting is understood figuratively, as will be explained. It is also read as ( يَأْتِيَهم ) with a ya', because the feminine gender of "angels" is not real (non-literal).

﴿أوْ يَأْتِيَ بَعْضُ آياتِ رَبِّكَ﴾ ("or some of the signs of your Lord come"): that is, other than what was mentioned, as they proposed when they said: ﴿Or cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claim﴾, and similar great signs upon which they made their faith conditional. The expression "some" is used for dread and magnification. Likewise, the attribution of the signs in both places to the name of the Lord, which indicates total ownership of that, and its attribution to his pronoun ﷺ is for honour.

It has been said: the meaning of "the angels" is the angels of death, and the coming of Him, glorified and exalted, is the coming of all His signs, meaning the signs of the Resurrection and total destruction, by the indication of what follows: the coming of some of His signs, exalted be He. The meaning of this is the portents of the Hour, which are: the smoke, the beast of the earth, a sinking in the east, a sinking in the west, a sinking in the Arabian Peninsula, the Dajjal, the rising of the sun from its west, Gog and Magog, the descent of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and a fire that comes out of Aden, as the famous noble hadith states.

Since the coming of these matters is not something they are waiting for, like the coming of the signs they proposed, making their faith conditional on their coming is, apparently, waiting on their part for it. Thus the waiting is understood as a figure of speech, based on likening their state of persisting in disbelief and continuing in stubbornness until those tremendous matters come upon them, at which point faith is absolutely necessary upon witnessing them, to the state of those who await them.

You know that the noble composition, with its preceding context which indicates their persistence in denying God's signs and not regarding them, and its following context which declares that faith is of no benefit when what they await comes, requires that this be understood as tremendous matters specific to them, either as an expression of what they proposed, or as punishments consequent upon their crimes, such as the coming of the angels of punishment and the coming of His command with punishment. This is the most appropriate reading for His saying, exalted be He, what follows: ﴿Say: Wait, we too are waiting﴾.

As for understanding it as the coming of the angels of death, and the coming of all the signs of the Resurrection, and the appearance of the portents of the Hour, together with the fact that their coming encompasses every righteous and wicked person and its danger includes every believer and disbeliever, this is not supported by the context, since some portents of the Hour are not such that the door of faith and obedience is closed by them.

Yes, it is permissible to understand some of the signs in His saying, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come﴾ as including what they proposed and other great calamities that nullify choice, on which the sphere of obligation revolves. For this is like the major premise in the first figure of syllogism (al-shakl al-awwal), so the approximation is completed when they occur, by the inclusion of what they await in that as a primary inclusion.

﴿يَوْمَ﴾ ("the day") is in the accusative, governed by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿does not benefit﴾, because the negation of the operation of "mā" after "lā" when it occurs as the answer to an oath is impossible here. It is also read as ( يَوْمُ ) in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate being the clause, and the returning pronoun omitted, meaning: "it does not benefit in it."

﴿نَفْسًا﴾ ("a soul") refers to any soul among souls.

﴿إيمانُها﴾ ("its faith") at that time, because the matter is uncovered and the affair is witnessed directly. The basis of accepting faith is that it be in the unseen, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So their faith did not benefit them when they saw Our might﴾. It is also read as ( لا تَنْفَعُ ) with a feminine ta', because faith is attributed to the feminine through the association of the attributed-to noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) with the feminine gender.

His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Who had not believed before﴾, that is, before the coming of some of the signs, is an attribute of "nafsan," separated from it by the agent (al-fa'il) because the agent includes a pronoun referring to the described noun. There is no defect in this, because it is not foreign to it, since both share the same governing element.

﴿أوْ كَسَبَتْ في إيمانِها خَيْرًا﴾ ("or had not earned good through its faith") is conjoined to ( آمَنَتْ ) ("had believed") by introducing an alternative (tardid) to the negation, which indicates that one of the two negations suffices for the absence of benefit. The meaning is: faith does not benefit at that time a soul that did not previously put forward its faith, or that put it forward but did not earn good through it. It necessarily follows that benefit is conditioned on both matters being realized together, namely prior faith and the good earned through it. The meaning is that what is beneficial is the realization of both.

Later faith is vain and the obtaining of what is already obtained, not that it is the beneficial thing, and the realization of both being a condition for its benefit, as when the one put forward is not the same as the one postponed in essence. For your saying: "Fasting and charity do not benefit one who did not believe before them" means that they benefit him when they occur after faith. The Mu'tazila have used this to argue that faith without deeds is not valid. This is not conclusive, because it is valid to understand it as negating the alternation, which necessarily implies its generality. Its explicit meaning indicates that benefit is conditioned on the absence of both matters together, and its implicit meaning indicates that benefit is conditioned on the realization of one of them, by way of prohibiting a void, not by way of real exclusivity. So the meaning is: faith does not benefit at that time a soul from which neither of the two matters previously proceeded. As for bare faith, or good earned through it, benefit is realized by whichever of them exists, as the noble texts of the verses and hadiths state.

As for what has been said, that the absence of prior faith necessarily entails the absence of earning good through it, so mentioning it would be repetition without benefit, and that what necessitates eternal abiding in the Fire is the first absence without the second having any role in that at all, so mentioning it while explaining what necessitates eternal abiding would be idle speech, this is based on the assumption that the purpose of describing the soul with the two stated absences is merely to explain that they necessitate eternal abiding in it, and that the newly arising faith does not save it from it. That is not so. Otherwise it would suffice to say: "faith that arises newly does not benefit a soul." Rather, the principal purpose of describing it with those two absences, in the course of explaining the non-benefit of newly arising faith, is to establish that the cause of benefit is one of the two qualities, namely prior faith and good earned through it, with the method and encouragement to acquire them included within the warning against abandoning them.

There is no way to argue: just as the absence of the first is independently sufficient for necessitating eternal abiding in the Fire, so mentioning the absence of the second is idle, and likewise its existence is independently sufficient for deliverance from it, so mentioning the second is idle, because this is an analogy with a difference. How could it not be, since eternal abiding is a matter in which multiple causes cannot be conceived? As for deliverance from it along with entrance into Paradise, it has degrees, some of which follow from faith itself, and some from its branches (furu') which vary in quantity and quality.

It was not limited to explaining what necessitates the basic benefit, which is prior faith, although it is the opposite of what does not necessitate it at all, namely newly arising faith. Rather, what necessitates the additional benefit was joined to it as well, as guidance toward seeking the highest, and an alert that the lesser suffices, and as despairing the disbelievers of what they have set their vain hopes on, namely the deeds of righteousness they performed in disbelief, such as maintaining family ties, freeing slaves, releasing captives, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, and other matters of nobility, by showing that all of that is pure vanity, because it is built on no foundation. This is as His saying, exalted be He, indicates: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like ashes which the wind blows violently﴾, and similar noble texts.

And that newly arising faith, just as it does not benefit them alone, does not benefit them when joined with their prior and subsequent deeds. You may say: the purpose of describing the soul with the two absences mentioned is an allusion to the state of the disbelievers in their rebellion and their negligence regarding each of the two obligatory matters, even if the obligation of one of them is conditioned on the other, as in His saying, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿So he neither affirmed nor prayed﴾, recording their complete transgression and announcing the multiplication of their punishment, because it is established that the disbelievers are addressed with the branches of the laws regarding accountability, as His saying, exalted be He, indicates: ﴿Woe to the polytheists who do not give zakat﴾.

Having understood this, you will realize that the noble verse is more deserving of being an argument against the Mu'tazila than an argument for them.

This is what has been said. It has also been said that it is an instance of the implicit reference (al-laff al-taqdiri, "the estimated wrapping"), meaning: "It does not benefit a soul its faith, nor its earning in faith, [if] it had not believed before, or had not earned in it." But this is not clear.

The basis of the estimated implicit reference is that what is estimated must be among the completing elements of the speech and the requirements of the context, and its mention has been omitted relying on the indication of the spoken words and their implication of it, as was explained in the interpretation of His saying, mighty and majestic be He: ﴿And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant, He will gather them to Himself all together﴾. For the mention of the gathering of the believers has been omitted in the detailed statement, trusting in the reports of the detail about it, namely His saying, exalted be He: ﴿As for those who believed...﴾ and the rest of the verse.

There is no doubt that what is estimated here is not something requiring His saying: "or earned good through its faith," nor is it one of the requirements of the context, because it is not something they were promised and made conditional on the coming of the mentioned signs, like faith, so that it would be refuted for them by showing that it does not benefit at that time. Moreover, that indicates that after the calamities that befell them, they would have remained in safety for a period in which earning and acting would be possible for them. This contains a failure to observe the context of magnifying the severity of the matter and making the situation grave, which is evident.

Other answers have been given to the argument, but their final outcome is only to remove this noble verse from the rank of opposing decisive texts, which are strong in indicating what has been mentioned: that bare faith without deeds is sufficient for deliverance from eternal punishment, even after a long time of trouble and difficulty, because it is established that the speculative (zanni) is far from opposing the decisive (qat'i).

﴿قُلِ﴾ ("Say") to them, after the explanation of the reality of the situation, in the form of a threat.

﴿انْتَظِرُوا﴾ ("Wait") for what you are waiting for of the coming of one of the three matters, so that you may see what it is that you are waiting for.

﴿إنّا مُنْتَظِرُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, we too are waiting") for that, in order that we may witness what evil end will befall you. In this is confirmation that what they await is the coming of the angels of punishment, or the coming of His command with punishment, as has been indicated, and an implicit promise to the Messenger of God ﷺ and the believers that they will witness what punishment will overtake the disbelievers. Perhaps this is what they witnessed on the day of Badr. And God, glorified be He, knows best.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 159:

﴿Indeed, those who divided their religion﴾ is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining the condition of the People of the Book after the explanation of the condition of the polytheists; that is, they scattered it and split it into parts, so that each group clung to one part of it.

It is also read as (فارقوا) "faraqu", meaning: they separated themselves from it, for abandoning part of it, even if one takes up another part of it, is abandonment of the whole and a departure from it.

﴿And they became sects (shiya')﴾; that is, factions, each faction following a leader of its own. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Jews split into seventy-one sects, all of them in the Hellfire except one; the Christians split into seventy-two sects, all of them in the Hellfire except one; and my community will split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Hellfire except one."

The exception of one sect from the sects of each of the two groups of the People of the Book applies only in view of the past era before abrogation. As for after it, all of them are in the Hellfire, even though the causes of their entry differ.

So the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿You have nothing to do with them in anything﴾ is: you are not concerned with investigating their division, or with confronting and taking to account those among them who are your contemporaries through debate and censure. It has been said: it means you are not concerned with fighting them, beyond conveying the message and manifesting the symbols of the true religion to which you were commanded to call, and so this would be abrogated by the verse of the sword.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Their affair is only with Allah﴾ is a justification for the aforementioned negation; that is, He alone takes charge of their affairs, first and last, and manages them as He wills, according to what wisdom requires. He takes them to account in this world whenever He wills, and commands their fighting when He wishes.

It has been said: "those who divided" refers to the people of innovations and deviant desires from this community. This is rejected, since he (ﷺ) is commanded to take them to account, and the explanation that the meaning of ﴿You have nothing to do with them in anything﴾ would then be: you are free of them and of their way, and they are free of you, is incompatible with the justification mentioned.

﴿Then He will inform them﴾; that is, on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿of what they used to do﴾. He expressed their being made to know by "informing," because of the connection between the two as two causes of knowledge; as an alert that they were ignorant of the state of what they committed, heedless of its evil outcome. That is, He will make it manifest to them before all witnesses and let them know what shameful thing they used to continually do in the world, and will then assign to it the recompense that befits it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 160:

And His saying, ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the measures of the recompense of those who act, and it was introduced with the explanation of the recompense of the good-doers, which is indicated by mention of their opposites.

ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He means: whoever among the believers does a good deed, ten good deeds are written for him; that is, whoever comes on the Day of Resurrection with good deeds from among the believers, since there is no good deed without faith, then for him are ten good deeds like it, as a bounty from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It has been read ʿashrun (ten) with tanwin, and amthaluha (its likes) in the nominative as an adjective. This is the least of the multiplications promised, and the promise has come of seventy, of seven hundred, and of without reckoning. Therefore it has been said: the purpose of mentioning ten is to indicate abundance, not to restrict the number to that specific figure.

﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed﴾; that is, with evil deeds, whoever he is among the doers.

﴿He will not be recompensed except with its like﴾, by the rule of the promise, one for one.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ by a reduction of reward or an increase of punishment.

﴿Say: Indeed my Lord has guided me﴾ The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to explain to them the true religion that he is upon, the religion they claim to follow while they have completely abandoned it. The opening of the sentence with the particle of emphasis (harf al-tahqiq) shows the full importance given to its content. The mention of the title "Lord" (al-Rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) is for the greater honouring of him. That is: say to those who divide their religion: "My Lord has guided me by revelation, and by the signs of creation He has set up in the horizons and within the selves."

﴿to a straight path﴾ leading to the truth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a religion﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿to a path﴾, since its position is in the accusative, as in His saying: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾. Or it is an object of a suppressed verb indicated by what has been mentioned.

﴿upright﴾ (qiyaman) is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis. The analogical form would be qiwaman, like ʿiwadan, but it was altered (i'lal) to match the alteration of its verb, as in al-qiyam. It was also read as qayyiman, which is fa'il-form from qama, like sayyid from sada. In terms of its morphological pattern (al-zinah) it is more emphatic than "straight" (al-mustaqim), although in terms of its form (al-sighah) the latter is more emphatic.

﴿the creed of Abraham﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf al-bayan) to "religion".

﴿a man of pure faith (hanifan)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from Abraham; that is, turning away from the false religions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) confirming his purity (ﷺ) from what those who divide his religion hold, in belief and practice. That is: he was not of them in any matter of their religion, in its fundamentals or its branches. He stated this in refutation of those who claim to follow his creed (peace be upon him), from among the people of Makkah, the Jews, and the polytheists, by their saying "Uzayr is the son of God," and the Christian polytheists by their saying "The Messiah is the son of God."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 162:

﴿Say: Indeed, my prayer and my sacrifice﴾. The command is repeated because what is commanded here pertains to the subsidiary branches of the sacred laws (furu' al-shara'i'), whereas what preceded it pertains to their foundations (usul); that is, "my worship, all of it." It has also been said: "and my sacrifice" (dhabhi) is meant, being joined with the prayer, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾. And it has been said: "my prayer and my pilgrimage" (hajji).

﴿And my life and my death﴾; that is, what I am upon during my life, and what I will be upon at my death of faith and obedience; or the acts of obedience during life and the good deeds attributed to death, such as bequest (wasiyyah) and disposition of affairs (tadbir). It has been read as "mahyaya" (with the yaʾ pronounced with sukun), treating the connected reading as if it were a pause (wuquf).

﴿For Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 163:

﴿Has no partner﴾: sincerely devoted to Him, without my associating anything else with Him in it.

﴿And of that﴾: a reference to sincerity (ikhlas), and the sense of distance in it (the use of "that" for something near) signals the loftiness of its rank and the great distance of its standing in excellence; i.e., of that sincerity.

﴿I have been commanded﴾: not commanded with anything other than it.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am the first of the Muslims﴾ explains his (peace be upon him) hastening to comply with what he was commanded, and that what he was commanded is not among his peculiar features (peace be upon him); rather, all are commanded with it, and whoever among them has submitted follows his example (peace be upon him).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 164:

﴿Say: Shall I seek a lord other than Allah, while He is the Lord of all things?﴾ That is, shall I seek another lord and associate him with Him in worship?

﴿And He is the Lord of all things﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah ḥāliyyah) serving to reinforce the denunciation. That is: while the state of affairs is that everything other than Him is a creature (marbūb) belonging to Him just as I am, how could it be conceived that it would be a partner to Me in being worshipped?

﴿And no soul earns [sin] except against itself﴾. The polytheists used to say to the Muslims: ﴿Follow our way, and let us bear your sins﴾. This may mean either: let the sins that you have committed be recorded against us and not against you; or it may mean: let us bear on the Day of Resurrection the sins that have been recorded against you. The verse is therefore a refutation of the first meaning: that is, no wrongdoing of any soul among souls is borne except by that soul itself, and it is impossible that its commission should proceed from one person while its burden settles upon another person, so that what you have mentioned could come about.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ is a refutation of the second meaning. That is: on that Day no soul carrying its own load shall carry the load of another soul, so that your statement could be valid.

﴿Then to your Lord is your return﴾ is a shift in address (talwīn lil-khiṭāb) and a turning of it toward all of them, to reinforce the promise and intensify the warning. That is: to the Owner of your affairs and to your return on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then He will inform you﴾ on that Day

﴿of that over which you used to differ﴾, through the clarification of right guidance from error, and the distinguishing of truth from falsehood.(p-208)

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 6, verse 165:**

﴿It is He who made you successors (khala'if) on the earth﴾, in that you succeeded the earlier nations, or some of you succeed others, or He made you vicegerents (khulafa') of God, Exalted is He, on His earth, to dispose of its affairs, with the address being general.

﴿And raised some of you﴾ in nobility and wealth.

﴿above others in degrees﴾, many and varying.

﴿That He may try you in what He has given you﴾ of wealth and standing; that is, that He may deal with you as one who tests you, to see what you do of thanks and its opposite.

﴿Indeed your Lord﴾: the address is directed solely to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the name of the Lord being attached to his pronoun (ﷺ), to show extra kindness towards him (ﷺ).

﴿is swift in punishment﴾; that is, His punishment comes swiftly upon those who do not observe the rights of what God, Exalted is He, has given them and do not give thanks for it, since everything that is to come is near; or He is swift in completing (it) when He wills, because He is exalted above using causes and instruments.

﴿And indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward those who observe them as they should. In making the predicate of this sentence one of the essential attributes, expressed in the intensive form and emphasized with the lam, while making the predicate of the first sentence an attribute applied to other than its subject, there is an indication that God, Exalted is He, is Forgiving and Merciful by essence, intensely so in both, and that He is the doer of punishment only incidentally, and is lenient in it, as is not hidden. And God knows best.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "The surah of al-An'am was sent down to me all at once, escorted by seventy thousand angels who have a loud sound of glorifying (tasbih) and praising (tahmid). Whoever recites al-An'am, those seventy thousand angels will send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him, for the number of every verse of the surah of al-An'am, for a day and a night." And God, Exalted is He, knows best.
